clippings.quote: We usually discover this after we’ve committed. Rather than back out, we push on. In Africa, while shooting a sequence for Dead Reckoning Part Two, he came up with an idea that I told him could not be done, simply because no camera rig existed that could capture it. By that afternoon, our team had built it.
clippings.title: Meet Christopher McQuarrie, wingman to Tom Cruise’s death-defying maverick
clippings.context: Same Q&A, asked whether Cruise ever had an idea too complex to do; the film was then titled Dead Reckoning Part Two.

clippings.speaker: Christopher McQuarrie
clippings.quote: At the start of this movie, I said to Tom, 'What do you want to do?' … He said, 'I want to drive a motorcycle off of a cliff. What do you want to do?' And I said, 'I want to wreck a train.'
clippings.film: Mission: Impossible – Dead Reckoning Part One
clippings.title: ‘M:I 7’ Director Was Determined to ‘Wreck’ a 70-Ton Train Like Buster Keaton
clippings.context: IndieWire quoting McQuarrie's Entertainment Weekly interview about how he and Cruise picked their dream stunts.

clippings.speaker: Tom Cruise
clippings.quote: That's McQ [Christopher McQuarrie]. McQ designed that whole thing and we had to build the train for that. … But, as a kid, I played with trains. McQ played with trains. We always wanted to throw a train off a cliff or blow it up.
clippings.film: Mission: Impossible – Dead Reckoning Part One
clippings.title: Tom Cruise Dreamed of Throwing a Train Off a Cliff as a Kid, So He Did in ‘Mission: Impossible 7’
clippings.context: Q&A with Ben Felderstein, answering the first question about the film's train sequence.

clippings.speaker: Tom Cruise
clippings.quote: You see what's right in front of him. McQ has a tremendous ability to be able to do that. And he has a tremendous ability to be able to write for actors.
clippings.film: Mission: Impossible – Dead Reckoning Part One
clippings.title: Tom Cruise Dreamed of Throwing a Train Off a Cliff as a Kid, So He Did in ‘Mission: Impossible 7’
clippings.context: Same Q&A, on how the franchise avoids feeling repetitive by building each film around what the actors do well.

clippings.speaker: Tom Cruise
clippings.quote: You look at McQ [Christopher McQuarrie], McQ has such an understanding and appreciation of rhythm as an editor. He just has a brilliance with rhythm [when] he and I edit the film, it has to have a natural rhythm and you feel it. And then the icing is the score.
clippings.title: “I never made a movie to just go make a movie, it was always an exploration of filmmaking”: our world exclusive interview with Tom Cruise
clippings.context: Interview with Isabel Stevens for the BFI Fellowship, on why he dislikes editing to music.

clippings.speaker: Spike Lee
clippings.quote: Very much so. I think it's evident by the work we've done. And we have acquired sort of like a shorthand. You know, we do most of our discussion, rehearsals, but we're on the set, we know what we have to do. So there's not a lot of need for a whole lot of talking.
clippings.title: A Conversation with Spike Lee
clippings.context: Lee talked with Scott Simon on NPR about Inside Man, his fourth film with Washington.

clippings.speaker: Spike Lee
clippings.quote: Same way a coach, you're not gonna let everybody take the last shot when the game is on the line. In a movie, you put the ball in Denzel's hands.
clippings.title: A Conversation with Spike Lee
clippings.context: Lee talked with Scott Simon on NPR about Inside Man, his fourth film with Washington.

clippings.speaker: Spike Lee
clippings.quote: I've become a better director working with Mr. Denzel Washington. … It's not about just what's on the script. It has to be deeper than that.
clippings.title: Spike Lee and Denzel Washington on a Reunion Making “Highest 2 Lowest”
clippings.context: Joint interview of Lee and Washington by David Remnick before Highest 2 Lowest opened; the page notes the transcript was produced on a rush deadline.

clippings.speaker: Denzel Washington
clippings.quote: When I started acting, there were two or three actors that I followed. De Niro, Hoffman, Pacino, the filmmakers that made those films never called me. I was never asked to be in any of their films. When Spike called me, we developed a relationship, and we made our own films.
clippings.title: Spike Lee and Denzel Washington on a Reunion Making “Highest 2 Lowest”
clippings.context: Washington on why he and Lee built a partnership beginning with Mo' Better Blues (1990), in the same joint interview.

clippings.speaker: Denzel Washington
clippings.quote: Which is why I call Spike, Trust. I trust Spike completely. … I completely, 1000% trust Spike and I do my part and he does the rest.
clippings.title: Spike Lee and Denzel Washington on a Reunion Making “Highest 2 Lowest”
clippings.context: Washington on the shorthand built over five films, in the same joint interview.

clippings.speaker: Denzel Washington
clippings.quote: In this case, the script came to me first. I hoped that Spike would be interested in, so I called him up, he said, ‘Send it to me.’ He read it, he said, ‘Let's make it,’ and here we are.
clippings.title: Spike Lee and Denzel Washington on a Reunion Making “Highest 2 Lowest”
clippings.context: Washington on how Highest 2 Lowest came together, in the same joint interview.

clippings.speaker: Samuel L. Jackson
clippings.quote: But Quentin would say, no, take your time. And I'd do it again. I'd count to, like, five, and he'd say, no, no, no. … Which consequently led me to that almost, you know, 20-second pause in that film that he left in it. … But Quentin trusts audiences like I do.
clippings.title: Celebrating movie icons: Samuel Jackson
clippings.context: Terry Gross interview recorded in 2000, rebroadcast 2024-09-02; Jackson recalls shooting the Jackie Brown van scene.

clippings.speaker: Samuel L. Jackson
clippings.quote: He knows the movies that we like. I tend to go on location with about 30 Hong Kong films — I have a lot of Asian crime films in my trailer just to pass the time. Every time he’d pass my trailer he’d ask, ‘what are you watching now?’ and we’ll talk about it. We had long conversations about those movies. We tend to watch the same kind of bullshit. Entertainment.
clippings.title: Samuel L. Jackson Lets Loose On ‘Django’, Tarantino, Slavery, Oscars And Golden Globes – Interview
clippings.context: Deadline interview during the Django Unchained release, on shared taste in genre movies.

clippings.speaker: Samuel L. Jackson
clippings.quote: We are the constant — we’re the base flavor for that bouillabaisse he makes, we’re the tomato consommé or whatever.
clippings.title: ‘Hateful Eight’ Star Samuel L. Jackson Says He’s the Base in Quentin Tarantino’s Bouillabaisse
clippings.context: Q&A on what it takes to be the right actor for Tarantino films, around The Hateful Eight release.

clippings.speaker: Quentin Tarantino
clippings.quote: I love him because nobody says my dialogue quite the way Sam Jackson does. It's not poetry but it's poetic. It's not song, but it's musical and he sings it. It's not stand-up comedy but it has a comedic rhythm…
clippings.title: Pieces of eight
clippings.context: Tarantino chatting with the writer after The Hateful Eight press conference.

clippings.speaker: Quentin Tarantino
clippings.quote: Not only has it become easy to write for him, it’s become hard not to write for him.
clippings.title: Quentin Tarantino Defends Violence in ‘Hateful Eight,’ No Cell Phone Policy; Reveals Why Samuel L. Jackson Is His Muse
clippings.context: Variety 'Contenders Conversations' interview on The Hateful Eight; caption quotes Tarantino on Jackson.

clippings.speaker: Quentin Tarantino
clippings.quote: I remember after I gave Sam Jackson the first draft of the script, I go to him, I go, ‘What's your favourite part of it?’ He goes, ‘I like when I start figuring shit out, and I turn into Hercule Négrô.’
clippings.title: Interview: THE HATEFUL EIGHT Los Angeles And New York Press Conferences
clippings.context: Tarantino at Hateful Eight press events (Dec 2015), as transcribed by ScreenAnarchy.

clippings.speaker: Martin Scorsese
clippings.quote: He has range. He keeps growing. He also has a lot of courage. I know he'll go to places that other people might pull back from… I've been working with him over the years he's been growing as a person. He's maturing from a young kid to a young man. As he changes in life, he's changing on film.
clippings.title: Martin Scorsese Details Working With Leonardo DiCaprio and How He's Matured as an Actor (Exclusive)
clippings.context: Scorsese to ET at the New York premiere of Killers of the Flower Moon.

clippings.speaker: Martin Scorsese
clippings.quote: And then finally Leo said, ‘If I play Ernest, we could turn it upside down and go in from the ground level.’ And I said, ‘Absolutely.’ So DiCaprio was the first driver of that change. Absolutely.
clippings.title: Martin Scorsese, the Interview: On Reframing 'Killers,' Subverting DiCaprio's Star Power — and 'The Wager'
clippings.context: Scorsese recounts how DiCaprio's decision to play Ernest Burkhart rather than the FBI agent reshaped the script.

clippings.speaker: Martin Scorsese
clippings.quote: We have this ability to collaborate together, and it's based on trust and love. We go to places sometimes that at times feel almost impossible.
clippings.title: Why Leonardo DiCaprio and Martin Scorsese 'Debate for Months' Before Every Movie
clippings.context: Scorsese on stage with DiCaprio at TIME's 'A Year in TIME' event, as they prepare their seventh film together.

clippings.speaker: Leonardo DiCaprio
clippings.quote: I know the trust level has built over the years. (Scorsese) has taught me not only about being a better actor, but the history of cinema and the importance of cinema as an art form.
clippings.title: SBIFF: Double Dose – Martin Scorsese and Leonardo DiCaprio share the stage at SBIFF
clippings.context: DiCaprio, in a Variety interview earlier that week (during The Wolf of Wall Street press run), quoted in Ted Mills's SBIFF report.

clippings.speaker: Leonardo DiCaprio
clippings.quote: Well, in a lot of ways these two men that we're speaking to have been like cinematic father figures to me… He told Marty about me, and I've gotten to do six films with him now. And here we are 30 years later.
clippings.title: Leonardo DiCaprio Views Martin Scorsese and Robert De Niro as Special 'Father Figures'
clippings.context: DiCaprio at a Nov. 15, 2023 press conference, speaking of Scorsese and Robert De Niro together ('these two men'; 'Marty' is Scorsese).

clippings.speaker: Leonardo DiCaprio
clippings.quote: Marty's very obsessive as a filmmaker, he thinks about every single detail. Over the years, I've learned the times when there's a malleability and ways to pivot in the storyline, but I've also learned the times where you have a specific shot list.
clippings.title: Why Leonardo DiCaprio and Martin Scorsese 'Debate for Months' Before Every Movie
clippings.context: DiCaprio in conversation with Scorsese at TIME's 'A Year in TIME' event.

clippings.speaker: Song Kang-ho
clippings.quote: When we first started together, it was over 20 years ago. I was a novice actor in his second film. Back then, we were both new to the craft as a director and actor. After twenty years, it's much more than that. We're now friends.
clippings.title: Interview: Song Kang Ho and Park So Dam On 'Parasite' and Becoming A Family
clippings.context: Song on how his relationship with Bong has changed since Memories of Murder, during Parasite press (translated).

clippings.speaker: Song Kang-ho
clippings.quote: I met the two men who would later become master filmmakers. They were like college students with crop hair. We had a cup of tea and parted without saying a word about movies. Later, they told me that they had wanted to see me to cast me in a film.
clippings.title: [Interview] Song Kang-ho, "The Title Is 'Parasite,' But the Film Is about Symbiosis"
clippings.context: Song recalls his first meeting with Bong (then an assistant director on Motel Cactus), in a Seoul interview before Parasite's release (translated).

clippings.speaker: Song Kang-ho
clippings.quote: What I really like about him is his realism; his worldview on the society and the people that we live with. I feel like his views have become more relentless, persistent, and meticulous over the years, and I think Parasite is really the concentrated result of all those years of effort.
clippings.title: PARASITE Interview: Acting Legend Song Kang-ho on his "Relentless" Relationship with Bong Joon-ho
clippings.context: Song answers what is special about their collaboration from Memories of Murder through Parasite (translated).

clippings.speaker: Bong Joon Ho
clippings.quote: I don't think of it as me directing actors. I'm just entering Song's world, the vast universe that he occupies. He has a unique rhythm and tempo. Working with Song is something I feel confident in.
clippings.title: Clutch For A Villain: An Interview With Bong Joon-Ho And Song Kang-Ho
clippings.context: Bong on directing Song, in a joint interview at the Locarno Film Festival (translated).

clippings.speaker: Bong Joon Ho
clippings.quote: he acts with insight with every small detail and nuance, and never goes against the big context that surrounds the film. When he plays a scene, I think the audience is more convinced that something like that could happen.
clippings.title: "All Characters in 'Parasite' Are in the Gray Zone." Bong Joon-ho on the War of the Classes in His New Masterpiece
clippings.context: Bong, asked why he keeps returning to Song, in a New York interview (translated).

clippings.speaker: Bong Joon Ho
clippings.quote: For my second movie, 'Memories of Murder,' I thought, I'd really love to work with Song Kang-ho, but my debut had been a disaster. I thought I was about to get chased out of the industry, and he was a star. But he remembered that meeting fondly.
clippings.publication: Bong Joon Ho: Dissident Cinema (Karen Han, Abrams)
clippings.title: How Bong Joon Ho Discovered Song Kang-ho for 'Memories of Murder' — and Made Them a Dream Team
clippings.context: Book excerpt quoting Bong ('Bong has said') on why he wanted Song for his second film; the original interview is not identified.

clippings.speaker: Pedro Almodóvar
clippings.quote: Penélope has done ballet when she was younger and that gave her a very gracious and light way of walking. I wanted her to have more weight, so you could feel the sense of gravity attaching her to the Earth.
clippings.title: Women are more interesting: Talking with Pedro Almodóvar and Penélope Cruz
clippings.context: Almodóvar explains how he reshaped Cruz's physicality for Volver; interview at the film's 2006 release (translation not stated).

clippings.speaker: Penélope Cruz
clippings.quote: I was so happy that he called me again and gave me the most challenging, difficult, complex character of my career up to now. When I read it, it was more than what I dreamt about. He was actually my biggest motivation to becoming an actress.
clippings.title: Interview with Penelope Cruz
clippings.context: Q&A at a Tribeca Cinema Series advance screening; she speaks of Volver as the new film (Tribeca's page is dated Nov 2007, the screening was presumably 2006).

clippings.speaker: Penélope Cruz
clippings.quote: I have fear, always on the set. Insecurity to the point where the first week I always think I could be fired. I think that’s a fear most actors have. But Pedro can intimidate me more than anybody. Because I care so much about him and I don’t want to disappoint him.
clippings.title: Penelope Cruz talks Broken Embraces - RT Interview
clippings.context: Interview at Cannes 2009 for their fourth film together (page later updated in 2015).

clippings.speaker: Pedro Almodóvar
clippings.quote: With Penélope, before we begin shooting, she needs to really rehearse a lot so she really feels that she’s able to enter into that role. That’s not the case with Antonio Banderas, it’s very much about directing him in the moment.
clippings.title: Pedro Almodóvar discusses drugs, Penélope Cruz and not understanding camp
clippings.context: Asked about his long working relationship with Cruz while promoting Pain and Glory in London (translation not stated).

clippings.speaker: Pedro Almodóvar
clippings.quote: The nature of muses is not only to inspire you, but also to give you confidence in yourself
clippings.title: Penélope Cruz Takes on Her Dream Role for Pedro Almodóvar
clippings.context: Almodóvar to the writer by phone from Madrid, for W's Directors Issue photo story starring Cruz (translation not stated).

clippings.speaker: Pedro Almodóvar
clippings.quote: She needs to feel what she’s doing. But because she’s so emotional, every time she read the script she would be overcome and would start crying. At first, I let her cry all she wanted, but then I dedicated myself to draining her of her tears, until the very end.
clippings.title: Pedro Almodovar and Penelope Cruz on Pain, Friendship and Sexy Mothers
clippings.context: On directing Cruz through the long rehearsal period for Parallel Mothers (translation not stated).

clippings.speaker: Penélope Cruz
clippings.quote: I love him and I trust him 100% of the time, and at the same time I’m scared. Not scared of him. I’m scared of… I don’t want to disappoint him. And I know he’s going to be honest and he’s going to be tough. And that is a great fear to have on the set. I’d much rather have that than have somebody that always tells you everything is right, because we know it’s not.
clippings.title: 'Parallel Mothers' star Penelope Cruz on her intense working relationship with Pedro Almodovar
clippings.context: Cruz on how their friendship and working relationship differ on set, awards-season interview for Parallel Mothers.

clippings.speaker: Penélope Cruz
clippings.quote: He literally had to pick me up from the floor, because I could not come out of the fiction. It took me a while and he got worried. He said, ‘No, but why it has to be this way? I want you to do the same thing, but not suffer.’
clippings.title: 'Parallel Mothers' star Penelope Cruz on her intense working relationship with Pedro Almodovar
clippings.context: Cruz recalls a Parallel Mothers shoot day when she could not shake a devastating scene.

clippings.speaker: Christopher Miller
clippings.quote: The reason this collaboration is successful is because each of us respects and values the other person and what he brings. And we’re each like a life preserver rather than a weight. The second it feels like a nuisance, it’s doomed.
clippings.title: Dynamic Duo
clippings.context: Answering how their collaboration has evolved, in a joint Q&A with fellow Dartmouth alumnus Jake Tapper (interview held May 20, 2019).

clippings.speaker: Phil Lord
clippings.quote: Our first 10 years we would have our frustrations, but the work was always better when it was the two of us. It’s just more fun to do it with your buddy, and it’s more interesting to be challenged.
clippings.title: Dynamic Duo
clippings.context: Same joint Q&A, on how the partnership has changed over time.

clippings.speaker: Christopher Miller
clippings.quote: We’re like brothers, where we fight and love each other and respect each other. We’ve had such a long history together. We’ve known each other for 20 years.
clippings.title: '22 Jump Street' Directors Phil Lord and Chris Miller Discuss How Friendship Turned Into Comedy Gold
clippings.context: Joint interview ahead of 22 Jump Street's release, on the trouble of two directors sharing one film.

clippings.speaker: Phil Lord
clippings.quote: It takes just as long to do another take [as] it does to argue about whether you should do another take. Just do one. And I trust this guy if he has something that he wants to do, we should just do it.
clippings.title: '22 Jump Street' Directors Phil Lord and Chris Miller Discuss How Friendship Turned Into Comedy Gold
clippings.context: Same joint interview, on settling disagreements on set.

clippings.speaker: Christopher Miller
clippings.quote: During college, we were friends, we would help each other on each other's films, but Phil's films were his and my films were mine, and we'd never been in an equal partnership where neither one was the boss. It was a lot to figure out how to be in a partnership, which was really challenging. It's like a marriage, and luckily we stuck with it, because we weren't very good at it at the beginning.
clippings.title: Phil Lord and Chris Miller Prove the Power of Partnership With Variety's Creative Impact in Animation Award
clippings.context: Variety profile on the pair receiving its Creative Impact in Animation Award, recalling their first year as Disney-era partners.

clippings.speaker: Phil Lord
clippings.quote: One of the things that's neat about being partners for so long is the partnership grows to accommodate a lot of different facets of each of us… You have to allow for each partner to grow and develop and do their thing. It's been really lovely to be able to support Chris, and we were on the set together the whole time…
clippings.title: Chris Miller And Phil Lord On The Afterparty And The More Ambitious Spider-Verse Sequels - Exclusive Interview
clippings.context: Exclusive interview on Miller creating and directing The Afterparty while Lord supported him.

clippings.speaker: Ben Affleck
clippings.quote: That’s why we stayed friends: because we lie for each other in crucial moments. It gets you through a development meeting, I can tell you that.
clippings.title: New Again: Ben Affleck
clippings.context: Joint interview with Ingrid Sischy as Good Will Hunting was about to open; the page is Interview's 2014 online republication of the December 1997 piece.

clippings.speaker: Ben Affleck
clippings.quote: Matt and I had identical interests, so whether we ended up successful or making hot dogs at Dodgers games, we knew we’d end up doing the same sort of thing. The remaining friends part was pretty consistent. We saw each other all the time, we talked on the phone all the time.
clippings.title: New Again: Ben Affleck
clippings.context: Answering whether he and Damon were sure they'd stay friends after high school and end up writing together.

clippings.speaker: Ben Affleck
clippings.quote: It was a very gracious and kind gesture that’s characteristic of how Matt’s treated me, and this friendship, his whole life … It’s a testament to why we are still friends.
clippings.title: A duo once more, Ben Affleck, Matt Damon come up for 'Air'
clippings.context: On Damon's support when Affleck directed him for the first time, in an AP profile by Jake Coyle.

clippings.speaker: Matt Damon
clippings.quote: Ben’s too modest to tell you this, but he’s the most well-read person I know. He’s certainly a lot smarter than I am.
clippings.title: New Again: Ben Affleck
clippings.context: Teasing Affleck, who had just joked about dropping out of college, in the same joint interview.

clippings.speaker: Matt Damon
clippings.quote: Once we started, we really got into a groove. While I was away, I’d write and fax the stuff to Ben, and Ben would fax stuff to me, and we’d write on and edit each other’s faxes.
clippings.title: New Again: Ben Affleck
clippings.context: Describing how they co-wrote the Good Will Hunting screenplay when apart.

clippings.speaker: Matt Damon
clippings.quote: After my dad passed in 2017 — and Ben was very, very close with him — it changed something in us, I think … You start to see the end game and you start to feel like, ‘I want to make every second count. I don’t want to fritter away time anymore.’
clippings.title: Matt Damon Says His Friendship with Ben Affleck 'Changed' After His Dad Died
clippings.context: TODAY quotes Damon from the July 21, 2023 episode of 'Who's Talking to Chris Wallace?', on why he and Affleck began working together more often.

clippings.speaker: Guillermo del Toro
clippings.quote: A good Bunraku artist moves the creature or character, but an excellent Bunraku artist fuses with the puppet, and that's what Doug does. … there's the rarest of the rare, which is a guy who can actually act and be an actor under make-up, and that's Doug Jones. He can do it.
clippings.title: Guillermo del Toro on The Shape of Water and Beautiful Monsters
clippings.context: Asked what makes Jones such a great monster actor, during an awards-season directors' panel.

clippings.speaker: Guillermo del Toro
clippings.quote: He came in and Doug was eating a bagel and sipping coffee from a foam cup, and Richard came to me and said, ‘What the fuck is this?! There's a guy in a fish suit! What are we doing here?!’ … And then, I said, ‘Action!,’ and Doug instantly started acted. He became a creature that had never seen a bathtub and never said tiles.
clippings.title: Guillermo del Toro on The Shape of Water and Beautiful Monsters
clippings.context: Del Toro's anecdote about Richard Jenkins's first day shooting opposite Jones in the bathtub scene.

clippings.speaker: Guillermo del Toro
clippings.quote: It needed a human inside because of the nuance of the characters looking at one another. It needed a lot of things that only Doug can deliver.
clippings.title: On The Set Of 'The Shape Of Water' - Guillermo Del Toro Interview
clippings.context: On-set piece; del Toro explains why the Amphibian Man had to be a performer in a suit rather than a puppet.

clippings.speaker: Guillermo del Toro
clippings.quote: And Doug Jones is Doug Jones. Only he could have played this river god.
clippings.title: Shape of Water Is Guillermo del Toro's Passion Project
clippings.context: Press interview in which del Toro runs through what each lead actor brought to the film.

clippings.speaker: Doug Jones
clippings.quote: He's never let me play a human, and that's fine. He doesn't think of me as a human and I'm going to take that as a compliment because he loves his monsters so much. He has said, ‘I will always have a monster on my call sheet.’ … I've been 12 different characters for him now.
clippings.title: Meet Doug Jones, Guillermo del Toro's go-to monster man and star of 'The Shape of Water'
clippings.context: KPCC radio interview on The Frame about Jones's two decades playing del Toro's creatures.

clippings.speaker: Doug Jones
clippings.quote: I'll get a call usually late in the game. He's told me before when he's got something in development, ‘I've got something for you, but I'm not going to tell you about it because if we don't get to do the movie I don't want you to kill yourself.’
clippings.title: Meet Doug Jones, Guillermo del Toro's go-to monster man and star of 'The Shape of Water'
clippings.context: Jones on how del Toro brings him onto projects.

clippings.speaker: Doug Jones
clippings.quote: And only Guillermo del Toro could fashion a movie together where the monster and a human form a romantic bond that the audience is actually rooting for. … I'm just so proud of Guillermo for having the vision and pushing forward with it
clippings.title: Interview [Part 2]: Doug Jones on Playing Saru in STAR TREK: DISCOVERY and Working with Guillermo del Toro on THE SHAPE OF WATER
clippings.context: Jones in a press interview ahead of The Shape of Water's release, which he calls his sixth film with del Toro.

clippings.speaker: Simon Pegg
clippings.quote: We still use a flip chart to lay out all our ideas. We start on a large canvas and then refine and refine until we have the screenplay we want to shoot. We never stop writing, all through the shoot and even through the edit. … I love writing with Edgar, I think we bring out the best in each other.
clippings.title: Simon Pegg Talks THE WORLD'S END, the Film's Soundtrack, Writing with Edgar Wright, and More
clippings.context: Pegg describing how he and Wright co-wrote The World's End, ahead of its release.

clippings.speaker: Simon Pegg
clippings.quote: I try and stay present, so that I'm there for Edgar if he needs me and Edgar won't lock the film until we are both happy.
clippings.title: Simon Pegg Talks THE WORLD'S END, the Film's Soundtrack, Writing with Edgar Wright, and More
clippings.context: Pegg on his role in the edit, which Wright and editor Paul Machliss lead.

clippings.speaker: Simon Pegg
clippings.quote: Well, this one was me and Edgar (Wright). We write in a collaborative way with a brainstorming session, and then brought Nick into the process for his input on the rest of the script. … Edgar has an idea of how the scenes are cut, so there is no need for extra nonsense, money wasted.
clippings.title: Interview: The World's End with Edgar Wright, Simon Pegg & Nick Frost
clippings.context: Pegg, interviewed with Nick Frost on the Australian press tour, on their writing process; the Q&A format does not label speakers, but he refers to writing with Edgar himself.

clippings.speaker: Edgar Wright
clippings.quote: No, I don't think we have really done anything separately on all three films. The only fancy thing that we do now is to plug the laptop into the TV; prior to that, it was like battleships with two laptops opposite each other and one person is typing and the other person is pacing.
clippings.title: Edgar Wright Exclusive Interview
clippings.context: Wright answering whether he and Pegg ever write separately, for the home-video release of The World's End.

clippings.speaker: Edgar Wright
clippings.quote: The characters are an amalgamation of friends that both Simon and I had; there weren't any specific people. … I would say that there are parts of me and Simon in all of the main characters.
clippings.title: Edgar Wright Exclusive Interview
clippings.context: Wright on how the World's End gang was drawn from his and Pegg's own lives.

clippings.speaker: Edgar Wright
clippings.quote: Simon has less body fat after appearing on screen with Tom Cruise (Mission Impossible 3 & 4) inspired him to get ridiculously gym fit, Simon is suddenly ripped. His hair is longer too, he wanted to wear a wig but I insisted he had to dye it.
clippings.title: Interview: The World's End with Edgar Wright, Simon Pegg & Nick Frost
clippings.context: Wright, asked how Pegg and Frost had changed over years of working together, on Pegg's look for Gary King.

clippings.speaker: David Cronenberg
clippings.quote: And that’s often how Howard Shore and I work, because so much movie music is hammering you over the head with what’s obviously there in the scene, you know? … And Howard and I never have done that in all the films we’ve done together, which is many. We’ve always felt that the music should be another level, an added level to the film, that brings in an element that actually wasn’t there, and wouldn’t be there without the music.
clippings.title: David Cronenberg on the Hollywood horror of Maps To The Stars
clippings.context: Interview with Calum Marsh, on why the Maps to the Stars score plays against the scenes.

clippings.speaker: David Cronenberg
clippings.quote: When I was talking to Howard Shore about the music, one of the things we wanted the music to do was to suggest the other part of him — the non-controlled part, the part that was in total agony, and despair, and melancholy over his wife’s death.
clippings.title: Interview: Director David Cronenberg on Melancholy and ‘The Shrouds’
clippings.context: Release interview for The Shrouds, on what the score says about Vincent Cassel's grieving widower.

clippings.speaker: David Cronenberg
clippings.quote: It's very difficult to talk about music, so it's a kind of a telepathy. … I think we've done 17 films together, and we both come from Toronto.
clippings.title: Grave New World: A Conversation with David Cronenberg on The Shrouds
clippings.context: Interview with Mark Asch, answering when Shore joins the process on his films.

clippings.speaker: Howard Shore
clippings.quote: Yeah, and it’s interesting, because the relationship is still exactly the same. He still seems older and brighter somehow, and whatever he’s doing is always way ahead. He’ll say something and years later I’ll think, ‘Oh, David said this would happen, and he was right.’
clippings.title: Howard Shore
clippings.context: Interview with Cory Reynolds; Shore had met Cronenberg as a boy in their Toronto neighbourhood and looked up to him.

clippings.speaker: Howard Shore
clippings.quote: That’s why Cronenberg was so perfect to start with — he’d never worked with a composer, and I’d never worked with a director. We had no preconceptions. There was no studio. There was nobody telling us what we could or couldn’t do. It was completely experimental.
clippings.title: Howard Shore
clippings.context: Same interview, on how their collaboration began with the low-budget early films.

clippings.speaker: Howard Shore
clippings.quote: In Dead Ringers I think he changed four bars of the entire score. In Videodrome he did not change a note. It was funny because I recorded that score without him being present at most of the sessions. I gave it to him and he put it in the movie, and I knew he felt that it was strange -- even for him. Another director would have asked me to think about changing it, but not David.
clippings.title: Howard Shore: Composing with a very wide palette
clippings.context: Edited transcript of a 1998 conference talk, published in Cinesonic (AFTRS, 1999) and reposted by its editor Philip Brophy.

clippings.speaker: Howard Shore
clippings.quote: With Cronenberg I'm more working as a fellow artist. He's made his experiences, he made a lot of films and I've done a lot of films with him so there's really a great trust there.
clippings.title: Locarno 2016 Interview: Howard Shore Talks His Career and Lifelong Collaborations
clippings.context: Interview at the Locarno Film Festival, comparing Cronenberg with Scorsese and Peter Jackson.

clippings.speaker: Howard Shore
clippings.quote: I’d only done one film before that, but he took me on, and we started a collaboration. Now we’ve done 16 films since that period and we kind-of grew up together, making different films, and trying different ways of using music in film, which has made the collaboration so interesting.
clippings.title: Composer Howard Shore on his Crimes of the Future score, and a lifetime working with David Cronenberg
clippings.context: Interview around Crimes of the Future, recalling how he approached Cronenberg to score The Brood.

clippings.speaker: Joel Coen
clippings.quote: It's fantastic, there's nothing like it, when people ask if I have directing advice I tell them, 'find a partner,' … It's an enormous advantage in every way. You have someone you can turn to when things go pear-shaped and, in crass terms, you can gang up on people. I missed him a lot.
clippings.title: Joel Coen wouldn't have made 'Macbeth' with his brother Ethan. Here's why
clippings.context: Kenneth Turan interviews Joel about directing his first film without Ethan.

clippings.speaker: Joel Coen
clippings.quote: I knew I'd be directing the next one by myself … If I was working with Ethan I wouldn't have done 'Macbeth,' it would not be interesting to him.
clippings.title: Joel Coen wouldn't have made 'Macbeth' with his brother Ethan. Here's why
clippings.context: Joel on what changed after Ethan told him, at the end of The Ballad of Buster Scruggs, that he wanted to do other things for a while.

clippings.speaker: Joel Coen
clippings.quote: But it's also the case that frequently Ethan will just sit down and or I'll sit down at the computer and just type up dialogue in a scene. You know? And then the other person will look at it and maybe adjust it or change it or something like that. But it's all in the context of this ongoing conversation.
clippings.title: The Coen Bros. On Writing, 'Lebowski' And Literally Herding Cats
clippings.context: Joint Fresh Air interview with Terry Gross; the transcript labels both as COEN, but the speaker refers to Ethan in the third person, so it is Joel.

clippings.speaker: Ethan Coen
clippings.quote: I think it's just wrong to separate out and try to analyse out who adds what to which, you know what I mean? Because it's all either between Joel and myself or Trish and myself. [It's not] that when I write scripts with Joel, I'm the funny one. And he's the serious one. That's just wrong. I mean, the fun and the comedies that we've done together is a product of both of us talking, not of one of us trying to jolly the other one.
clippings.title: Ethan Coen on streaming, Drive-Away Dolls and his split with Joel
clippings.context: Asked to compare writing with his brother to writing with his wife, Tricia Cooke.

clippings.speaker: Ethan Coen
clippings.quote: The last couple [movies] I'd done before were just really difficult, in terms of production. They were difficult movies to make … Not that it wasn't fun, it was still intermittently fun, but Joel felt the same way – 'Those last two. Man, they were hard.' I'd not decided anything definitively, but took some time off.
clippings.title: How 'Drive-Away Dolls' Artistically Reinvigorated Ethan Coen
clippings.context: Ethan on why he stepped back after Hail, Caesar! and The Ballad of Buster Scruggs.

clippings.speaker: Ethan Coen
clippings.quote: We actually wrote another alternate ending, which I thought my brother was going to talk about. Instead of having Tommy Lee Jones telling the story, we had Cormac McCarthy, the author of the novel, leaning on the fence, telling the story directly to the camera.
clippings.title: INTERVIEW – Joel and Ethan Coen: "We let our films live their own lives"
clippings.context: Joint interview while the brothers were jury presidents at Cannes; Ethan picks up after Joel describes one alternate ending.

clippings.speaker: J.J. Abrams
clippings.quote: I made him promise, when we were first doing the ‘Alias’ pilot, that he would do everything that I ever did, and so he said he would. And so, though I didn't get it in writing, I plan to.
clippings.title: 'Lost,' 'Alias' Composer Michael Giacchino
clippings.context: Abrams in an NPR radio profile of Giacchino, then scoring both Alias and Lost.

clippings.speaker: Michael Giacchino
clippings.quote: I had never worked on a television series before, but the thing that I remember is that J.J. and I just got along instantly. You know, he loved everything that I loved as far as music goes and what that meant to movies and, in particular, what live music meant to movies and television.
clippings.title: 'Lost,' 'Alias' Composer Michael Giacchino
clippings.context: Giacchino recalling how Abrams hired him, a video game composer, for Alias.

clippings.speaker: J.J. Abrams
clippings.quote: He understands character and structure. So while it's wonderful to work with him as a composer, I give him the scripts in advance and get his comments and notes and show him cuts and scenes and rough cuts of the whole piece, just to get his reaction.
clippings.title: Michael Giacchino: Driven by stories
clippings.context: Abrams in a Variety profile of Giacchino on how early he brings the composer into a project.

clippings.speaker: J.J. Abrams
clippings.quote: Michael's music was the kind of music that I would find myself listening to in headphones when I was writing. And it just felt like clearly whoever was writing this music was as obsessed with the scores that I was familiar with growing up.
clippings.title: Michael Giacchino On Coming Home To Write Music For 'Jurassic World'
clippings.context: Abrams recalling discovering Giacchino through his Medal of Honor video game scores.

clippings.speaker: Michael Giacchino
clippings.quote: I was involved in Lost thanks to J. J. Abrams: I already worked with him for Alias . Besides our professional relationship, I have a special friendship with J. J., I really owe him a lot.
clippings.title: An interview with Michael Giacchino
clippings.context: Interview by Marco Bellano; Giacchino on how he came to score Lost (may be translated/edited from an Italian-conducted interview).

clippings.speaker: Michael Giacchino
clippings.quote: Well the great thing about working with J.J. is that he has a very good sense of getting a point across without hammering it over your head. … He has this really good sense of keeping things simple and I love that in his work, and it helps me as well, because I can be simple too.
clippings.title: A Conversation with Super 8 Composer Michael Giacchino
clippings.context: Giacchino discussing the home-movie scene in Super 8 and Abrams's restraint.

clippings.speaker: Michael Giacchino
clippings.quote: We both grew up making 8MM movies, Super 8, 16MM movies and as we got older we had a similar path just making films so there's this love of getting together with your friends and making something that we both shared. One of the reasons we get along very well is because we had that shared experiences growing up.
clippings.title: Exclusive: Interview…Film Composer Michael Giacchino
clippings.context: Giacchino, ahead of a Dallas Symphony concert, on meeting Abrams and scoring Super 8.

clippings.speaker: Jordan Peele
clippings.quote: Michael's a man of immense empathy — very soft-spoken, a very sweet person, very loving. … I think that the best horror is created by those who are in touch with their empathetic side. And that's him.
clippings.title: Michael Abels, Composer Of Jordan Peele's 'Us', Balances Terror With Empathy
clippings.context: Peele explaining to NPR's Tim Greiving why Abels makes a great horror composer, around the release of Us.

clippings.speaker: Jordan Peele
clippings.quote: I knew he was capable of creating a chimera effect of music genre … to take what, to me, sounded like jazz and western score and sweeping Chinese epic — and combine it into this new flavor. That's what I wanted to do with 'Get Out' and 'Us.' I wanted a new flavor of film. I wanted a new flavor of thriller.
clippings.title: For Jordan Peele, the 'Nope' score provides the 'spectacle and the spectrum'
clippings.context: Peele recalling what he heard in Abels' concert piece Urban Legends on YouTube before hiring him for Get Out.

clippings.speaker: Jordan Peele
clippings.quote: the piece of the puzzle that I think really surprised me … was how much the warmth, and the sibling love story and the heart of the film needed to translate through his music. That was a very new thing for me.
clippings.title: For Jordan Peele, the 'Nope' score provides the 'spectacle and the spectrum'
clippings.context: Peele on what Abels' score for Nope added beyond horror: the Haywood siblings' bond.

clippings.speaker: Michael Abels
clippings.quote: It's in no way music for a horror or suspense film. … But it really spoke to Jordan, so that made me feel confident that I could really stretch myself creatively and find an open ear in him.
clippings.title: How The 'Us' Composer Used Silence, Children's Voices And Gibberish To Terrify You
clippings.context: Abels, speaking with KPCC's The Frame, on Peele discovering him through his YouTube concert piece Urban Legends.

clippings.speaker: Michael Abels
clippings.quote: From my very first conversation with Jordan before Get Out, he said, ‘I want silence to be part of the score.’ That has become a touchstone for me, not just with Jordan.
clippings.title: "Nope" Composer Michael Abels on Scoring Jordan Peele's Sci-Fi Epic
clippings.context: Abels, in a Motion Picture Association interview about Nope, on Peele's earliest instruction to him.

clippings.speaker: Michael Abels
clippings.quote: Jordan is someone who's not afraid to look outside his immediate network for people who he thinks he can see a possibility in. … And I count myself among those.
clippings.title: How composer went from posting music to YouTube to working with Hollywood director Jordan Peele
clippings.context: Abels in an interview with TODAY's Craig Melvin about going from schoolteacher to Peele's composer.

clippings.speaker: Michael Abels
clippings.quote: So, when I'm coming up with rhythms, I always want them to be ones that make people want to dance a little, and sometimes [Jordan will] say, 'That's not scary enough.' And I have to go back and I'll make it less dancey and more scary.
clippings.title: How Composer Michael Abels Created a Soundtrack of Horror for 'Nope' (Exclusive)
clippings.context: Abels, in an Academy conversation with Nope star Brandon Perea, on his back-and-forth with Peele over rhythms.

clippings.speaker: Federico Fellini
clippings.quote: Nino is an angelic friend made of music, always with an angel of music by his side, with its huge wings about him.
clippings.title: A portrait of composer Nino Rota
clippings.context: Fellini's tribute quoted by Jon Burlingame in a CSO profile of Rota; original source and date not given.

clippings.speaker: Federico Fellini
clippings.quote: stress vanished and everything became a party. The film entered a light, serene, fantastical phase, an atmosphere from which it gained a kind of new life.
clippings.title: A portrait of composer Nino Rota
clippings.context: Fellini on what happened when Rota arrived near the end of each project, quoted in a CSO profile; original source not given.

clippings.speaker: Federico Fellini
clippings.quote: You felt his creativity so near at hand that it gave you a feeling of inebriation, the sensation that it was you producing the music. It entered so completely into the characters, the atmosphere, the colours of my films as to permeate them with his music.
clippings.title: Nino Rota
clippings.context: Fellini's verdict on Rota's contribution to his films, quoted by Mervyn Cooke; original source not given.

clippings.speaker: Federico Fellini
clippings.quote: With Nino I can spend whole days listening to him play the piano in order to pin down a motif, to clarify some musical phrase that matches as exactly as possible the emotion I want to express in a sequence
clippings.original: Con Nino puedo pasarme días enteros, oyéndolo tocar el piano con el fin de precisar un motivo, de aclarar alguna frase musical que coincida lo más exactamente posible con la emoción que deseo expresar en una secuencia
clippings.title: Nino Rota, el otro yo musical de Fellini
clippings.context: Something Fellini wrote about working with Rota, quoted in Spanish translation in a Rota centenary piece by Fernando López.

clippings.speaker: Nino Rota
clippings.quote: If I hadn’t managed to replace the music Federico held so dear, tied to the world of the circus and to Chaplin, our partnership would probably have ended before it began. Instead, our friendship and collaboration have never been interrupted. It’s not that Federico is insensitive to music, it’s that he is too affected by it.
clippings.original: Se non fossi riuscito a sostituire le musiche tanto care a Federico, legate al mondo del circo e a Chaplin, probabilmente il nostro sodalizio sarebbe finito sul nascere. Al contrario la nostra amicizia e collaborazione non si sono mai interrotte. Non è che Federico sia insensibile alla musica, è che ne rimane troppo colpito.
clippings.title: Sulle musiche legate al circo si giocò il sodalizio fra Fellini e Rota
clippings.context: Rota in a public conversation with Fellini on his Radio2 program "Voi ed io", recalling The White Sheik; reported from a La Repubblica audio excerpt.

clippings.speaker: Nino Rota
clippings.quote: We had spent the whole day fiddling about at the piano, but nothing was coming. Finally, just as I was about to leave, I play a tune, Federico stops and says to me, this one’s good, we’ll do the whole film with it
clippings.original: Eravamo stati tutta la giornata a cincischiare al pianoforte, ma non usciva niente. Finalmente, al momento di andar via, suono un motivo, Federico si ferma e mi dice, questo va bene, ci facciamo tutto il film
clippings.title: HOT CORN RADIO | Fellini, Nino Rota e le colonne sonore più belle in una playlist
clippings.context: Rota describing in an unnamed interview how the Amarcord theme was found;

clippings.speaker: Nino Rota
clippings.quote: He might tell me, make a cheerful tune but one that’s sad. An oldish tune but one that’s new, carefree but poignant…
clippings.original: Magari mi dice, fai un motivo allegro ma che sia triste. Un motivo vecchiotto ma che sia nuovo, spensierato ma patetico…
clippings.title: HOT CORN RADIO | Fellini, Nino Rota e le colonne sonore più belle in una playlist
clippings.context: Rota, continuing the same unnamed interview, on Fellini's contradictory musical briefs;

clippings.speaker: Steven Spielberg
clippings.quote: The first movie was fraught with, 'I don't want to say anything that Tom's not going to like. I want to keep his friendship. I like this guy and his family. God, don't let me do anything that's going to screw that up.'
clippings.title: Hanks, Spielberg maintain 'Terminal' friendship
clippings.context: Joint AP interview for The Terminal, recalling his anxiety on their first film together.

clippings.speaker: Tom Hanks
clippings.quote: I sort of said, 'Look, you know ... you can't offend me. You're the boss. Tell me what you like, and if you don't like my ideas say: That's nice, but we're going to do something different.'
clippings.title: Hanks, Spielberg maintain 'Terminal' friendship
clippings.context: Same joint interview, responding to Spielberg's account; Hanks said the tiptoeing lasted a week.

clippings.speaker: Tom Hanks
clippings.quote: He can say anything to me and I think vice versa and whatever answer comes out is perfect. To be relaxed on a movie set means you can get stuff out that you haven't even imagined before, and that comes from knowing each other.
clippings.title: Hanks, Spielberg maintain 'Terminal' friendship
clippings.context: Joint AP interview for The Terminal.

clippings.speaker: Steven Spielberg
clippings.quote: I actively look for things for him. Literally, I actively try to find projects we can work together on.
clippings.title: Hanks, Spielberg maintain 'Terminal' friendship
clippings.context: Joint AP interview; he went on to note he had found Road to Perdition for Hanks.

clippings.speaker: Steven Spielberg
clippings.quote: It was going to be a tremendous performance opportunity for Tom, and I wanted to be in on that, around that...I wanted to be in his zone.
clippings.title: Hanks, Spielberg maintain 'Terminal' friendship
clippings.context: On asking to direct The Terminal after learning Hanks was considering the lead.

clippings.speaker: Steven Spielberg
clippings.quote: I guess my mantra is very simple. I say, 'That was great, that was brilliant! Once more. Once more.'
clippings.title: Steven Spielberg and Tom Hanks collaborate once again in "Bridge of Spies"
clippings.context: Asked by Gayle King how one tells Tom Hanks to do a take over.

clippings.speaker: Tom Hanks
clippings.quote: The best thing that can happen on the set is where Steven disappears, you don't know where he is, and then you see him out of the corner of your eye somewhere on the periphery of the set with a finder up to his eye… It means he's looking for something that's gonna be solid gold. And you just hope you're in it somewhere.
clippings.title: Steven Spielberg and Tom Hanks collaborate once again in "Bridge of Spies"
clippings.context: His advice to fellow Bridge of Spies actors who asked what to expect from Spielberg (two answers joined across Gayle King's question).

clippings.speaker: Gene Wilder
clippings.quote: I said you're going to be in a lot of trouble if you don't get the right person to play - well, the Richard Pryor part. I said the only one I can think of is Richard Pryor.
clippings.title: In This 2005 Interview, Gene Wilder Explains How He Learned To Get Laughs
clippings.context: Wilder tells Terry Gross how he urged Fox's Alan Ladd Jr. to cast Pryor opposite him; NPR rebroadcast the 2005 interview after Wilder's death.

clippings.speaker: Gene Wilder
clippings.quote: And we started working the next morning, and we hit it off really well. And he taught me how to improvise on camera. I had improvised a lot in classes and at the Actors Studio, but I never did it in front of the camera.
clippings.title: In This 2005 Interview, Gene Wilder Explains How He Learned To Get Laughs
clippings.context: Wilder on their first day of shooting together, the morning after they met in Calgary.

clippings.speaker: Gene Wilder
clippings.quote: It was the one scene that I was the most worried about, and I thought, well, if Richard doesn't mind my putting on the shoe polish in order to pass as black, then it must be OK because he's the teacher here.
clippings.title: In This 2005 Interview, Gene Wilder Explains How He Learned To Get Laughs
clippings.context: Wilder recounts how Pryor objected to the shoe-polish scene the night before filming and rewrote it; Wilder: "well, that's a better scene."

clippings.speaker: Gene Wilder
clippings.quote: Well, that's a real mystery. It's -- I hope this comes out right -- but it's a little bit like sex, you know. When you meet someone and the chemistry is there, you don't know why, you don't know how, but it's there.
clippings.title: Larry King Live: Interview with Gene Wilder
clippings.context: Asked by Larry King what worked so well between him and Pryor.

clippings.speaker: Gene Wilder
clippings.quote: I never improvised in a film before. In classes I did, but not in a film. But with him, I always improvised. Because if you don't you're not going to be anywhere, not with Richard.
clippings.title: Larry King Live: Interview with Gene Wilder
clippings.context: Same answer, continuing about their first scene together.

clippings.speaker: Gene Wilder
clippings.quote: Well, that was with Richard, and I don't think it would have happened to me alone if I didn't have Richard.
clippings.title: Larry King Live: Interview with Gene Wilder
clippings.context: Wilder, asked about being the number-one box-office star, credits the partnership.

clippings.speaker: Gene Wilder
clippings.quote: as close as we were on film, it just didn't carry over to our private lives. Richard traveled in his own circle. You could count on one hand the times that we saw each other when we weren't working
clippings.title: The Complicated Friendship of Comedy Duo Richard Pryor and Gene Wilder
clippings.context: Quoted from Wilder's 2005 memoir Kiss Me Like a Stranger.

clippings.speaker: Richard Pryor
clippings.quote: That man's a genius, and he's a good man, that's for sure.
clippings.title: Gene Wilder Remembered: Richard Pryor Adored "Good Man," His Daughter Says
clippings.context: Rain Pryor tells THR this is what her father always said of Wilder; recalled after Wilder's death.

clippings.speaker: Lauren Bacall
clippings.quote: he changed me. He was my teacher, my husband, my friend. In his life and his work, Bogie was integrity, truth and courage. He taught me how to live. That it was okay to trust. He taught me how to keep going no matter what.
clippings.title: Bacall on Bogart
clippings.context: TCM article quoting Bacall in the 1988 PBS Great Performances documentary Bacall on Bogart.

clippings.speaker: Lauren Bacall
clippings.quote: Off screen he bore little resemblance to the parts he played. He was a gent.
clippings.title: Bacall on Bogart
clippings.context: From the 1988 documentary Bacall on Bogart, as quoted by TCM, on the difference between his screen persona and the man she married.

clippings.speaker: Lauren Bacall
clippings.quote: I never imagined I would meet anyone like Bogie and marry him and have children. And obviously, the minute I fell in love with him that's all I wanted. Then, of course, after we were married I wanted more. But I was a kid. I was 19 when I met him…
clippings.title: Remembering Lauren Bacall
clippings.context: From Brad Goldfarb's April 2004 Interview Q&A, reprinted in the magazine's 2014 tribute.

clippings.speaker: Lauren Bacall
clippings.quote: I married a man who was exactly the same. If anyone asked Bogie about whether he thought a movie was good or not, regardless of whether he was in it, he'd answer honestly. He could not lie, and I'm the same.
clippings.title: Remembering Lauren Bacall
clippings.context: From the 2004 Interview Q&A reprinted in 2014, on speaking her mind in Hollywood.

clippings.speaker: Lauren Bacall
clippings.quote: Had I not met Bogie and then met all of his friends — his contemporaries — I never would've known Robert Benchley, Dorothy Parker, Louis Bromfield, all the journalists, sports figures, it's truly amazing.
clippings.title: Lauren Bacall Talks Favorite Hollywood Memories & Career in Unpublished Interview
clippings.context: Previously unpublished excerpts from a 1996 interview promoting The Mirror Has Two Faces.

clippings.speaker: Humphrey Bogart
clippings.quote: Do you realize what you do? You're a wife, a mother, an actress, you're running a house … that's a lot!
clippings.title: Lauren Bacall Talks Favorite Hollywood Memories & Career in Unpublished Interview
clippings.context: Bacall recalling, in a 1996 interview, what Bogart once said to her.

clippings.speaker: Humphrey Bogart
clippings.quote: I wish I were your age again – perhaps a few years older – and no ties of any kind – no responsibilities – it would be so lovely, for there would be so many long years ahead for us instead of the few possible ones.
clippings.title: Married at Malabar: The “Reel” Romance of Humphrey Bogart and Lauren Bacall
clippings.context: From a June 1944 letter Bogart wrote to Bacall while still married to Mayo Methot, quoted in a Mansfield/Richland County library blog post.

clippings.speaker: Humphrey Bogart
clippings.quote: Sure, Baby [his nickname for Bacall] and I are engaged. I know I open my fat yap too much and maybe this announcement is a little premature. But what the hell?
clippings.title: Married at Malabar: The “Reel” Romance of Humphrey Bogart and Lauren Bacall
clippings.context: Bogart to reporter Inez Robb in January 1945, as quoted in the library blog's history of the Malabar Farm wedding.

clippings.speaker: Akira Kurosawa
clippings.quote: Mifune had a kind of talent I had never encountered before… He reacts so swiftly to direction; if I say one thing to him, he understands 10. The ordinary Japanese actor might need 10 feet of film to get across an impression: Mifune needed only 3 feet … I decided to turn him loose.
clippings.title: Toshiro Mifune dead at 77
clippings.context: Variety's obituary of Mifune quoting Kurosawa's autobiography (Something Like an Autobiography, English translation) on their first film together.

clippings.speaker: Akira Kurosawa
clippings.quote: His sense of timing was the keenest I had ever seen in a Japanese actor… And yet with all his quickness, he also had surprisingly fine sensibilities.
clippings.title: Toshiro Mifune dead at 77
clippings.context: Continuation of the autobiography passage quoted in Variety's obituary of Mifune; translated from Japanese.

clippings.speaker: Akira Kurosawa
clippings.quote: I'm not usually impressed by actors, but Mifune impressed me. If I tell him one thing, he understands ten… If I had to think of a flaw, the only thing I can come up with is his voice is a little rough and sometimes it's hard to understand.
clippings.title: Seven Samurai (1954)
clippings.context: TCM article by Rob Nixon quoting Kurosawa's memoirs (a different translation of the autobiography passage).

clippings.speaker: Akira Kurosawa
clippings.quote: a young man reeling around the room in a violent frenzy. It was as frightening as watching a wounded beast trying to break loose. I was transfixed
clippings.title: Why did Toshiro Mifune fall out with Akira Kurosawa?
clippings.context: Kurosawa recalling first seeing Mifune at Toho's 1946 new-faces audition; originally from his autobiography, quoted without citation.

clippings.speaker: Toshirō Mifune
clippings.quote: Yes, on Yojimbo… One day Kurosawa said, 'I won't mention names, but the actors are late.' I said, 'What are you talking about? I'm the actor.' Every day after that, when Kurosawa arrived, I would be there already, in costume and makeup from 6 a.m. I showed him.
clippings.title: Film Review: A Perfunctory Documentary on Toshiro Mifune
clippings.context: Mifune answering critic Gerald Peary in a 1985 Montreal hotel interview, asked whether he and Kurosawa ever quarreled; recounted in Peary's 2016 review.

clippings.speaker: Toshirō Mifune
clippings.quote: No matter how much I drank the night before, I never once was late on his films. But with Kurosawa, sometimes people are waiting, and he never shows up. The people go to his house, and he says, 'I'm sorry. I don't feel well today.'
clippings.title: Film Review: A Perfunctory Documentary on Toshiro Mifune
clippings.context: Same 1985 interview with Gerald Peary, two decades after their last film together.

clippings.speaker: Toshirō Mifune
clippings.quote: I have never as an actor done anything that I am proud of other than with him.
clippings.title: Why did Toshiro Mifune fall out with Akira Kurosawa?
clippings.context: Mifune's widely repeated tribute after the split; Far Out gives no source (other sites trace it to Donald Richie's The Films of Akira Kurosawa).

clippings.speaker: Hoyte van Hoytema
clippings.quote: When I met with Chris it was just very inspiring meeting him. He is a very curious filmmaker that wanted to do new things and wanted to explore things and somehow we had a chemistry. … I'm not Wally. I'm not expected to be Wally and I just have to be myself and Chris has never ever given me the feeling that he needed me to be anybody who he's previously collaborated with.
clippings.title: Interview: Interstellar cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema
clippings.context: On stepping in after Wally Pfister for his first film with Nolan.

clippings.speaker: Hoyte van Hoytema
clippings.quote: Chris is just — he has a mystique around him but I can bring it all very much down to his pure love for filmmaking. … It literally is a very pure obsession with the medium of film itself. So that was kind of striking. And if you're on the same page with that, he's very accessible.
clippings.title: Interview: Interstellar cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema
clippings.context: Asked what surprised him most about working with Nolan.

clippings.speaker: Hoyte van Hoytema
clippings.quote: But what is very beautiful with Chris is that he is somebody that is not afraid of following his heart, and reacting to intuitive impulses, as well. He's a very sensitive and very much a feeling person. … But, as people call him sometimes, ‘Oh, he's very technical,’ I would definitely debate it. He is one of the most sensitive and most intuitive directors I work with.
clippings.title: 'Oppenheimer' Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema on IMAX, Not Using CGI, and Christopher Nolan's Process
clippings.context: Asked what would surprise fans about making a movie with Nolan.

clippings.speaker: Hoyte van Hoytema
clippings.quote: If I would ask Chris, 'So, how are we going to do this?' He would laugh at me. He would smile and say, 'That's for us to figure out.'
clippings.title: 'Oppenheimer' Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema on Breaking the Boundaries of Reality (Exclusive)
clippings.context: Academy interview after his Oscar win, on how their projects start with seemingly impossible challenges.

clippings.speaker: Hoyte van Hoytema
clippings.quote: We've done four films together now. In the first film, I was very scared and didn't know what was about to happen, but gradually we got to know each other better and got more courageous together. … I kind of hope that this is just sort of halfway through our journey.
clippings.title: Hoyte van Hoytema Talks About Film, Large Format, and Nolan
clippings.context: Press-room conversation after winning the BAFTA for Oppenheimer, as transcribed by Y.M.Cinema.

clippings.speaker: Christopher Nolan
clippings.quote: With Hoyte it's particularly fun, because he doesn't just have a cinematographer's eye; he has an engineer's brain. Set him a challenge, and he just won't quit until he's fully mapped out his vision and how to make it happen.
clippings.title: Christopher Nolan on Oppenheimer
clippings.context: Nolan interview in the October 2023 issue of American Cinematographer.

clippings.speaker: Christopher Nolan
clippings.quote: The unique quality that Hoyte brings to photography is that he's prepared to talk about an idea in abstract terms and not worry about the specifics of how we're going to execute it.
clippings.title: Christopher Nolan on Oppenheimer
clippings.context: Same American Cinematographer interview; highlighted as the article's pull quote.

clippings.speaker: Christopher Nolan
clippings.quote: …the way I like to block the action, the way I was working with first, Wally Pfister, who really pioneered this, and then Hoyte van Hoytema, who took it to the next level in terms of using this format for telling Hollywood stories…
clippings.title: Christopher Nolan Officially Reveals the Key Role 'The Dark Knight' Played in 'The Odyssey'
clippings.context: Nolan on how his IMAX framing evolved, in an interview about shooting The Odyssey entirely in IMAX.

clippings.speaker: Ingmar Bergman
clippings.quote: Sometimes I probably do mourn the fact that I no longer make films… Most of all I miss working with Sven Nykvist, perhaps because we are both utterly captivated by the problems of light, the gentle, dangerous, dreamlike, living, dead, clear, misty, hot, violent, bare, sudden, dark, springlike, falling, straight, slanting, sensual, subdue, limited, poisonous, calming, pale light. Light.
clippings.title: Sven Nykvist, cinematographer, master of light
clippings.context: Nykvist's obituary quoting Bergman's autobiography The Magic Lantern (translated from Swedish), written after he stopped making films.

clippings.speaker: Ingmar Bergman
clippings.quote: The only thing that I miss with not making films anymore is that I don’t get to work with Sven.
clippings.title: Nykvist was 'the master of light'
clippings.context: Variety's obituary quoting what Bergman said in Carl-Gustaf Nykvist's documentary Light Keeps Me Company.

clippings.speaker: Ingmar Bergman
clippings.quote: Sven and I saw things alike, thought things alike; our feeling for light was the same. We had the same basic moral positions about camera placement.
clippings.title: Sven Nykvist - Writer
clippings.context: Reference entry (Patricia Ferrara, updated by Rob Edelman) quoting Bergman in the documentary Light Keeps Me Company.

clippings.speaker: Sven Nykvist
clippings.quote: I was fortunate to work with Ingmar, especially at that early stage in my career. One of the things we believed was that a picture shouldn’t look lit. Whenever possible, I lit with one source and avoided creating shadows, because that pointed to the photography.
clippings.title: Beyond The Frame: Cries and Whispers
clippings.context: Nykvist speaking to American Cinematographer (AP dates the remark to 1995), resurfaced in the ASC's Beyond the Frame series.

clippings.speaker: Sven Nykvist
clippings.quote: That was a very nice way to work… Everyone did everything. Everyone helped everyone else. it was like a family. Even Cries and Whispers was produced on a $300,000 to $400,000 budget. I learned so much about composition, staging and the infinite varieties of light from Ingmar.
clippings.title: Beyond The Frame: Cries and Whispers
clippings.context: Nykvist on Bergman's tiny crews and budgets, from the same American Cinematographer interview.

clippings.speaker: Sven Nykvist
clippings.quote: Initially, I was quite apprehensive; Ingmar was known as the ‘demonic’ director. But from the first day, we worked well together. Perhaps we understood each other because we were both the sons of pastors.
clippings.title: Sven Nykvist interview from Cinematography Screencraft by Peter Ettedgui
clippings.context: Nykvist's first-person account in Peter Ettedgui's book, reproduced on a blog in 2010, on first meeting Bergman.

clippings.speaker: Sven Nykvist
clippings.quote: The next day, when we saw the rushes, Ingmar screamed, ‘God Damn it! How can there be shadows when the sun has gone down?’ The incident marked the beginning of our journey together into light… Had I not met him, in all probability I would have remained just another technician with no great awareness of the infinite possibilities of light.
clippings.title: Sven Nykvist interview from Cinematography Screencraft by Peter Ettedgui
clippings.context: Nykvist recalling adding artificial light to a night exterior on The Virgin Spring, his second film for Bergman.

clippings.speaker: John Carpenter
clippings.quote: Debra introduced me to Dean, who is a tremendously talented cameraman. Kind of a strange guy to deal with, and can be sarcastic on the set, but wow, what a cameraman.
clippings.title: On John Carpenter + Career Retrospective Interview
clippings.context: Word-association career interview by Justin Beahm for Fangoria's John Carpenter Legends issue, reposted in full on Beahm's site in 2016.

clippings.speaker: John Carpenter
clippings.quote: He and I discovered the Panavision anamorphic fast lenses together on ESCAPE FROM NEW YORK. It was a moment of pure joy when we discovered we could open the lenses to 2.2 or 1.8, and could shoot a scene in the middle of Ventura Boulevard. at midnight. You couldn’t do that before. … It changed how we made film.
clippings.title: On John Carpenter + Career Retrospective Interview
clippings.context: Same Fangoria Legends interview, continuing his answer to the prompt 'Dean Cundey'.

clippings.speaker: John Carpenter
clippings.quote: [Dean Cundey] doesn't know. He has no idea. He puts the lights up. He puts the lights up and we were in the snow. He has no clue. … You tell him that. Tell him he's full of shit.
clippings.title: John Carpenter Says ‘The Thing’ Cinematographer Is ‘Full of S—‘ Over His Ending Theory: He ‘Has No Clue,’ Only I Do and ‘I Cannot Tell You’
clippings.context: Carpenter teasingly dismissing Cundey's 'eye gleam' theory of The Thing's ending; originally said to ComicBook.com and reported by Variety.

clippings.speaker: Dean Cundey
clippings.quote: Working with John was a revelation because suddenly here was a guy who was interested in using the camera in a creative way, drawing the audience in. … I thought, Boy, this is just my cup of tea, where the camera is contributing and you’re telling the story with visuals.
clippings.title: The Making of John Carpenter's Halloween
clippings.context: David Konow's oral history of Halloween built from interviews from years past; first published October 2016, republished 2018.

clippings.speaker: Dean Cundey
clippings.quote: in the case of John, he was not afraid of having dark areas in the frame because he understood the importance. Compared to other directors, who would say, ‘Well, it’s dark, I can’t see the wall in the corner back there’, and so it was a case of being allowed the flexibility to experiment.
clippings.title: The Den Of Geek interview: Dean Cundey
clippings.context: Cundey on shooting in the dark on Halloween and The Thing, in a career interview with Simon Brew.

clippings.speaker: Dean Cundey
clippings.quote: When I first started with him on Halloween, I had worked on a lot of low budget movies, but he was the first director (I worked with) who I think really realized what visual storytelling was, how to use the camera to engage the audience and to tell the story. So I really appreciated that immediately. And you know, I think that continued, because we did five movies where that followed through.
clippings.title: [Interview] Cinematographer Dean Cundey on the Art of Illusion in Film
clippings.context: Interview by Matt Artz at the H40: Forty Years of Terror Halloween 40th anniversary convention.

clippings.speaker: Francis Ford Coppola
clippings.quote: there's a young actor that I know. He has never been in a movie, but every time I read the scenes with Michael Corleone in the book, like him walking in Sicily with the two bodyguards and the girl, I kept seeing his face. And when I read it, that's the only one whose face I saw.
clippings.title: The Godfather Speaks
clippings.context: Coppola recalls pitching Pacino to Paramount's Robert Evans for the role of Michael.

clippings.speaker: Francis Ford Coppola
clippings.quote: I finally realized why they didn't want Pacino, why they wanted Ryan O'Neal. Bob Evans wanted a Michael who looked like him. Someone who was handsome and tall. And I wanted a Michael who was more like me, who was more ethnic.
clippings.title: The Godfather Speaks
clippings.context: Coppola on the studio's resistance to casting Pacino.

clippings.speaker: Francis Ford Coppola
clippings.quote: Yeah, we remained close and we worked together. They went on to become movie stars. But they had never been the doubters. They were just these kids I brought in and they were hoping I wasn't gonna get fired.
clippings.title: The Godfather Speaks
clippings.context: Asked about Pacino, De Niro and Brando after the film's success.

clippings.speaker: Francis Ford Coppola
clippings.quote: But they also hated my casting ideas. They hated Al Pacino for the role of Michael, and they hated Marlon Brando for the role of the godfather.
clippings.title: To Make 'The Godfather' His Way, Francis Ford Coppola Waged A Studio Battle
clippings.context: Fresh Air interview with Terry Gross, originally aired 2016 and rebroadcast in 2021.

clippings.speaker: Al Pacino
clippings.quote: At that time in my life, I didn't have a choice. Francis wanted me.
clippings.title: Al Pacino: 'The Godfather gave me a new identity that was hard to cope with'
clippings.context: Pacino, asked by Dave Itzkoff how the role of Michael came up, for the film's 50th anniversary.

clippings.speaker: Al Pacino
clippings.quote: But here's the secret: For whatever reason, he wanted me and I knew that. You could feel that. And there's nothing like that, when a director wants you. It's the best thing an actor could have, really.
clippings.title: Al Pacino: 'The Godfather gave me a new identity that was hard to cope with'
clippings.context: Pacino on his Godfather screen tests while the studio rejected Coppola's cast.

clippings.speaker: Al Pacino
clippings.quote: And there, sitting on a tombstone, is Francis Ford Coppola, weeping like a baby. Profusely crying. And I went up to him and I said, ‘Francis, what's wrong? What happened?’ He says, ‘They won't give me another shot.’ … And I thought: OK. I guess I'm in a good film here. Because he had this kind of passion and there it is.
clippings.title: Al Pacino: 'The Godfather gave me a new identity that was hard to cope with'
clippings.context: Pacino recalls the end of shooting Vito Corleone's funeral scene.

clippings.speaker: Francis Ford Coppola
clippings.quote: I got along very well with Marlon. One of the most affectionate, warm men I’ve ever known. He’d come in late once in a while, but he’d make up for it with his sense of humor.
clippings.title: Francis Ford Coppola: Playboy Interview (1975)
clippings.context: Coppola to William Murray in Playboy's July 1975 interview, asked what it was like working with Brando.

clippings.speaker: Francis Ford Coppola
clippings.quote: As for Brando himself, what an improviser! I told him at one point that I didn’t really know how to shoot his final scene, just before he dies. What could we do to make his playing with his grandson believable? He said, ‘Here’s how I play with kids,’ and took an orange peel, cut it into pieces that looked like fangs and slipped them into his mouth.
clippings.title: Francis Ford Coppola: Playboy Interview (1975)
clippings.context: Coppola on how Brando invented Vito Corleone's death scene in the garden.

clippings.speaker: Francis Ford Coppola
clippings.quote: He was still wonderful. Brando was like a big kid. You know how sometimes a kid is -- you love them and everything, but he does these irresponsible things. Well, he arrived heavy, and he was a green beret colonel.
clippings.title: Extraordinary with Fareed Zakaria: Francis Ford Coppola
clippings.context: Coppola to Fareed Zakaria, asked whether Brando had gotten weirder by the time of Apocalypse Now.

clippings.speaker: Marlon Brando
clippings.quote: No, I liked the -- and I wasn't sure that I could do it, and Francis, fortunately, asked me if I would do a...
clippings.title: Encore Presentation: Interview with Marlon Brando
clippings.context: Brando to Larry King in October 1994 (re-aired 2004), on whether he liked The Godfather; King finishes the sentence: "Test?"

clippings.speaker: Marlon Brando
clippings.quote: I was good at bullshitting Francis (Coppola) and persuading him to think my way, and he bought it, but what I’d really wanted from the beginning was to find a way to make my part smaller so that I wouldn’t have to work as hard.
clippings.publication: The New York Review of Books
clippings.title: Stumbles and Mumbles
clippings.context: From Brando's 1994 memoir Songs My Mother Taught Me, as quoted in an NYRB review; on reshaping Kurtz.

clippings.speaker: Marlon Brando
clippings.quote: It was probably the closest I’ve ever come to getting lost in a part, and one of the best scenes I’ve ever played…I was hysterical; I cried and laughed, and it was a wonderful scene. Francis shot it twice—two 45-minute improvisations—but used hardly any of the footage in the picture.
clippings.publication: The New York Review of Books
clippings.title: Stumbles and Mumbles
clippings.context: From Brando's 1994 memoir Songs My Mother Taught Me, as quoted in an NYRB review; on Kurtz's death monologue.

clippings.speaker: Cary Grant
clippings.quote: I have only happy ones. They’re all vivid because they’re all interesting. It was a great joy to work with Hitch. He was an extraordinary man. I deplore these idiotic books written about him when the man can’t defend himself.
clippings.title: New Again: Cary Grant
clippings.context: Asked by Kent Schuelke for his memories of working with Hitchcock, four months before Grant's death; republished online in 2013.

clippings.speaker: Cary Grant
clippings.quote: A film’s a film. As Hitch would say when someone would get all upset on the set, ‘Come on, fellas, relax—it’s only a movie.’
clippings.title: New Again: Cary Grant
clippings.context: Grant, asked whether scholars over-analyze films made for entertainment, recalls Hitchcock's on-set refrain.

clippings.speaker: Cary Grant
clippings.quote: When we were making Notorious, Ingrid could do no wrong as far as Alfred Hitchcock was concerned. He simply adored her. … I always went to work whistling when I was working on a Hitchcock film because nothing ever went wrong. Hitch was so incredibly well prepared.
clippings.title: A Few Words with Cary Grant
clippings.context: Phone interview with Philip Wuntch ahead of Grant's Dallas 'Conversation' appearance; fan-site reprint of the newspaper article.

clippings.speaker: Alfred Hitchcock
clippings.quote: In the case of Suspicion, one of the early films you mention with Cary Grant, he should never have been in the picture in the first place. You run into this problem. You cast a man who is suspected of murder and then you have to compromise.
clippings.title: Alfred Hitchcock at the National Film Theatre
clippings.context: Interviewed by Bryan Forbes at London's National Film Theatre, broadcast by BBC One; transcript excerpt reproduced by Cinephilia & Beyond.

clippings.speaker: Alfred Hitchcock
clippings.quote: The scene I wanted, but it was never shot, was for Cary Grant to bring her a glass of milk that’s been poisoned … Fade out and fade in on one short shot: Cary Grant, whistling cheerfully, walks over to the mailbox and pops the letter in. That would have been a great twist.
