clippings.title: ‘Suspicion’: Proof that a True Artist Can Create Great Things Even Under the Crippling Harness of a Profit-Driven Studio
clippings.context: From Hitchcock's 1962 interviews with François Truffaut, describing the ending he wanted for Grant's character; book excerpt reproduced online.

clippings.speaker: Alfred Hitchcock
clippings.quote: Anyway, Cary Grant came up to me and said, ‘It’s a terrible script. We’ve already done a third of the picture, and I still can’t make head or tail of it.’ …Without realizing it he was using a line of his own dialogue.
clippings.title: 4K UHD Blu-ray Review: North by Northwest
clippings.context: Hitchcock to Truffaut on Grant's confusion during North by Northwest, which suited his bewildered character; excerpt quoted in a blog review.

clippings.speaker: Elia Kazan
clippings.quote: I just told him to get on his knees at the bottom of the staircase. But I didn't tell him what to do with his voice or how he should shout it. He just knew. But many, many things with him - many, many times with him, he was ahead of me…
clippings.title: Celebrating 30 Years Of 'Fresh Air': Filmmaker And Theater Legend Elia Kazan
clippings.context: Kazan to Terry Gross in 1988, when his autobiography came out, on directing the 'Stella' scene; rebroadcast 2017.

clippings.speaker: Elia Kazan
clippings.quote: He would've been damn good too, but not as good as Brando. I don't think anybody's as good as Brando.
clippings.title: Celebrating 30 Years Of 'Fresh Air': Filmmaker And Theater Legend Elia Kazan
clippings.context: Kazan on Frank Sinatra, first in line for Terry Malloy before the role went to Brando.

clippings.speaker: Elia Kazan
clippings.quote: Very, very little. I think we had a instinctive fraternity. I think we understood each other, almost from the word go, very well. And we would talk a lot about other things, but not a hell of a lot about the role.
clippings.title: Celebrating 30 Years Of 'Fresh Air': Filmmaker And Theater Legend Elia Kazan
clippings.context: Asked what questions Brando asked him about the Waterfront role.

clippings.speaker: Elia Kazan
clippings.quote: You adapt to what each one is. You - I talked more to Jimmy than I ever did to Marlon. … With Marlon, I didn't have to do anything like that.
clippings.title: Celebrating 30 Years Of 'Fresh Air': Filmmaker And Theater Legend Elia Kazan
clippings.context: Kazan comparing how he directed James Dean and Brando.

clippings.speaker: Marlon Brando
clippings.quote: Most actors don't get any help from directors. Emotional help, if you're playing an emotional part. Kazan is the only one I know who really gives you help.
clippings.title: Marlon Brando names the best director he ever worked with
clippings.context: From Chris Hodenfield's 1976 Rolling Stone interview, as quoted by Far Out Magazine in 2024.

clippings.speaker: Marlon Brando
clippings.quote: Kazan would say, 'Go out and rehearse this scene and bring me something back.' He'll take about eight points out of 12 or 11, and you argue with him. He'll give you points and there's no ego involved. He's a guy that works without ego.
clippings.title: Marlon Brando names the best director he ever worked with
clippings.context: Same 1976 Rolling Stone interview, as quoted by Far Out Magazine.

clippings.speaker: Marlon Brando
clippings.quote: Kazan was the best actors' director by far of any I've worked for . . . the only one who ever really stimulated me, got into a part with me and virtually acted it with me. . . . He was an arch-manipulator of actors' feelings, and he was extraordinarily talented; perhaps we will never see his like again.
clippings.title: 'On the Waterfront' and the Courage to Confront Evil
clippings.context: From Brando's 1994 autobiography, as quoted in a Word on Fire essay.

clippings.speaker: Marlon Brando
clippings.quote: They made the film to justify finking on their friends. Evidently, as Terry Malloy, I represented the spirit of the brave, courageous man who defied evil.
clippings.title: On the Waterfront (1954)
clippings.context: Brando's autobiography on Kazan and Schulberg's motives after Kazan named names to HUAC, as quoted by TCM.

clippings.speaker: Billy Wilder
clippings.quote: We meet at, say, 9:30 in the morning and open shop, like bank tellers, and we sit there in one room … Sometimes nothing happens. Sometimes it goes on until 12:30, and then I’ll ask him, ‘How about a drink?’’ And he nods, and then we have a drink and go to lunch.
clippings.title: Conversations with Billy Wilder & I.A.L. Diamond [Part 1]
clippings.context: Joint seminar-style interview (c. 1976, original publication unnamed) excerpted by Scott Myers; Wilder describing their daily routine.

clippings.speaker: Billy Wilder
clippings.quote: Oh, he collaborates with me all the time. He just doesn’t get the credit for it.
clippings.title: Conversations with Billy Wilder & I.A.L. Diamond [Part 4]
clippings.context: Same joint interview; Wilder jumping in when Diamond was asked whether he ever collaborated on the direction.

clippings.speaker: I. A. L. Diamond
clippings.quote: No, we don’t co-direct. I may sit on the sidelines, and I may make a suggestion occasionally, but I stay out.
clippings.title: Conversations with Billy Wilder & I.A.L. Diamond [Part 4]
clippings.context: Same joint interview; Diamond's answer, right after Wilder said he collaborates on the direction without credit.

clippings.speaker: I. A. L. Diamond
clippings.quote: Oh, I throw out ideas, and sometimes they’re listened to and sometimes they’re not.
clippings.title: Conversations with Billy Wilder & I.A.L. Diamond [Part 4]
clippings.context: Same joint interview; asked how involved he gets in casting and other matters once the script is done.

clippings.speaker: Billy Wilder
clippings.quote: Then I heard Diamond say, ‘Nobody’s perfect.’ I thought about it and I said, Well, let’s put in ‘Nobody’s perfect’ for now. But only for the time being. … When we screened the movie, that line got one of the biggest laughs I’ve ever heard in the theater.
clippings.title: Written Interview: Billy Wilder [The Paris Review]
clippings.context: James Linville's Spring 1996 Paris Review interview, excerpted on Go Into The Story; on writing the film's final line.

clippings.speaker: Billy Wilder
clippings.quote: We never talked about personal things. That was the beauty of it. … But Iz Diamond was a very taciturn guy, my partner. It was wonderful to talk about dialogue, or about structure. He was always on the set with me.
clippings.title: Seven Things to Know About I.A.L. Diamond
clippings.context: From Cameron Crowe's Vanity Fair interview with Wilder (later in Conversations with Wilder), as quoted by the blog.

clippings.speaker: Billy Wilder
clippings.quote: If I ever lost this guy, I'd be like Abercrombie without Fitch.
clippings.title: I.A.L. Diamond, the Oscar-winning writer whose 30-year association with...
clippings.context: Earlier Wilder remark recalled in UPI's obituary of Diamond.

clippings.speaker: I. A. L. Diamond
clippings.quote: Billy … is a writer who is also a director.
clippings.title: The Beginning of a Beautiful Affair Between Billy Wilder and I.A.L. Diamond
clippings.context: Asked by the Los Angeles Times who mattered most, writer, actor or director, Diamond chose the writer, then made Wilder the exception; quoted by PopMatters, original date unknown.

clippings.speaker: Robert De Niro
clippings.quote: We have known each other for long. And we have a special relationship, I can say. We get together from time to time. We talk about stuff that’s personal, help, give each other advice on things…
clippings.title: Talking With Al Pacino And Robert De Niro: An MW Exclusive
clippings.context: Joint interview with Mayank Shekhar during The Irishman press tour, asked how their relationship had evolved.

clippings.speaker: Al Pacino
clippings.quote: You know, we have been through a lot of the same things. And unusual stuff has happened to us in this profession. We knew each other when we were very young, too. Not well. But we had met. … But I think that even at that time, there was a certain comfort when we’d meet. … And there’s a lot of trust there between us. And love too.
clippings.title: Talking With Al Pacino And Robert De Niro: An MW Exclusive
clippings.context: Same joint interview, answering De Niro on their friendship.

clippings.speaker: Al Pacino
clippings.quote: And Bob saw this project (The Irishman). And he read it … He had the foresight to say there’s something that we can do here. Bob and Marty came together, and we discussed it in LA almost seven to eight years ago.
clippings.title: Talking With Al Pacino And Robert De Niro: An MW Exclusive
clippings.context: Pacino credits De Niro with finding the book behind The Irishman, after their Righteous Kill reunion.

clippings.speaker: Robert De Niro
clippings.quote: This movie went through all the twists and turns. From time to time Al would phone up and say, ‘Is it happening?’
clippings.title: De Niro and Pacino: ‘We are very close... We have known each other a long time’
clippings.context: De Niro to Donald Clarke on The Irishman's long development, in a joint interview with Pacino.

clippings.speaker: Al Pacino
clippings.quote: We have known each other for a long time – since ’68. I think early on in our careers we connected from time to time. Similar things happened to us. Then our lives would take different paths. It was that camaraderie that got us together. We are very close. We don’t see each other very much, but when we do it’s always there...
clippings.title: De Niro and Pacino: ‘We are very close... We have known each other a long time’
clippings.context: Pacino on their 50-year friendship, joint interview for The Irishman.

clippings.speaker: Al Pacino
clippings.quote: We’ve played it before: in the film Heat, we were actually on opposite ends, and in Righteous Kill we were close, and in this film we were close in a different way. It came relatively easy to come to that place. I don’t even think we talked about it consciously, but it was in the writing, of course. And in the nature of the two people’s relationship in real life, too.
clippings.title: De Niro and Pacino on The Irishman and the gangsterization of US politics
clippings.context: London audience with both actors, on the Sheeran-Hoffa relationship and their past pairings.

clippings.speaker: Al Pacino
clippings.quote: He’s so great, and he was smart because he said he didn’t want to rehearse the scene with me. He didn’t want to rehearse it. And at first I [had doubts about that]. But then I realized he was right. It really made a difference and that was very clever.
clippings.title: 'Heat' at 25: How Al Pacino hurt himself running away from Robert De Niro
clippings.context: From Yahoo's own 2017 Role Recall interview, on the Heat diner scene; brackets are Yahoo's.

clippings.speaker: John Huston
clippings.quote: No. I helped him. Knowing Bogart so well, and I saw Bogart as the role, as the part, and I was able to help him into it.
clippings.title: John Huston
clippings.context: TV interview transcript; Moyers asked whether Bogart disliked the Charlie Allnut role and had to be coaxed into it.

clippings.speaker: John Huston
clippings.quote: an ideal collaborator and companion...He's a joy to work with...his figure seemed to find its way into whatever I did.
clippings.title: The Big Idea
clippings.context: TCM's making-of article on The African Queen quotes Huston on Bogart; original source not given.

clippings.speaker: John Huston
clippings.quote: Both Bogie and I teased Katie unmercifully at the beginning. She thought we were rascals, scamps, rogues. We did everything we could to support this belief. We pretended to get roaring drunk.
clippings.title: Behind the Camera - The African Queen
clippings.context: TCM quotes Huston's 1980 autobiography An Open Book on how he and Bogart treated Katharine Hepburn on location.

clippings.speaker: John Huston
clippings.quote: The better I got to know him, the more I admired him. He was a very serious man. He took great pride in being an actor. There'll never be another Bogart.
clippings.title: Star of the Month: Humphrey Bogart
clippings.context: TCM profile quotes Huston speaking the night before Bogart's funeral in January 1957.

clippings.speaker: Humphrey Bogart
clippings.quote: I just want to pay a slight, as a matter of fact a very big tribute to Mr. John Huston and Miss Katharine Hepburn, because they helped me to be where I am now.
clippings.title: Humphrey Bogart Academy Awards Acceptance Speech
clippings.context: Bogart's Best Actor acceptance speech for The African Queen, directed by Huston.

clippings.speaker: Humphrey Bogart
clippings.quote: He's brilliant and unpredictable. Never dull. When I work with John, I think about acting. I don't worry about business.
clippings.title: The Big Idea
clippings.context: TCM's making-of article quotes Bogart on why he trusted Huston enough to shoot in Africa; original source not given.

clippings.speaker: Humphrey Bogart
clippings.quote: John wanted everything perfect. If he saw a nearby mountain that could serve for photographic purposes, that mountain was not good; too easy to reach.
clippings.film: The Treasure of the Sierra Madre
clippings.title: Trivia & Fun Facts About THE TREASURE OF THE SIERRA MADRE
clippings.context: TCM says Bogart told an unnamed interviewer this about Huston's exacting location choices.

clippings.speaker: Katharine Hepburn
clippings.quote: We balanced each other's natures,
clippings.title: TV tribute to Spencer Tracy -- by his closest friend
clippings.context: Said in her PBS documentary The Spencer Tracy Legacy: A Tribute by Katharine Hepburn, about their films and their friendship.

clippings.speaker: Katharine Hepburn
clippings.quote: ...you were, really the greatest movie actor. I say this because I believe it and I've heard so many people of standing in our business say it - from [Laurence] Olivier to Lee Strasberg, David Lean, name it. You could do it, and you could do it with that glorious simplicity, that directness. You could just...do it.
clippings.title: Spencer Tracy
clippings.context: From the letter Hepburn wrote to Tracy nearly twenty years after his death, quoted in TCM's tribute.

clippings.speaker: Katharine Hepburn
clippings.quote: Well, that's okay. I'm sure mine is for the two of us.
clippings.title: Spencer Tracy and Katharine Hepburn's years at MGM.
clippings.context: Her reply on hearing she had won the Best Actress Oscar and that Tracy, dead ten months, had not; recounted by Karina Longworth.

clippings.speaker: Katharine Hepburn
clippings.quote: You never really know anybody, do you? I never really knew Spencer, not really.
clippings.title: `An Affair To Remember' -- Drien By Demons, Tracy Drank And Had Affairs As Hepburn Chose To Look The Other Way
clippings.context: Hepburn reflecting on the 1986 letter she wrote to Tracy, in an excerpt from Christopher Andersen's book An Affair to Remember.

clippings.speaker: Spencer Tracy
clippings.quote: Not me, boy! … I don't want to get messed up in anything like this.
clippings.title: `An Affair To Remember' -- Tracy Was A Heel, Hepburn Was His Doormat In The Longest Running Star Partnership In History
clippings.context: Tracy to producer Joseph L. Mankiewicz right after first meeting Hepburn, as recounted in Christopher Andersen's book An Affair to Remember (excerpted).

clippings.speaker: Spencer Tracy
clippings.quote: We learned to be invisible … in all the right places.
clippings.title: `An Affair To Remember' -- Tracy Was A Heel, Hepburn Was His Doormat In The Longest Running Star Partnership In History
clippings.context: Tracy on how he and Hepburn kept their relationship out of public view, quoted in Christopher Andersen's book An Affair to Remember (excerpted).

clippings.speaker: James Stewart
clippings.quote: I agree with everything he [Hitchcock] said. I think probably as far as the actual making of the pictures, he was the most exciting of any, because -- he and John Ford had a lot in common -- you were never sure what was going to happen next . . . .
clippings.title: Jimmy Stewart; Hollywood didn't invent him
clippings.context: Interview ahead of his AFI Life Achievement Award, responding to Hitchcock's line that an actor's chief requisite is the ability to do nothing well.

clippings.speaker: James Stewart
clippings.quote: You never, in a Hitchcock or Ford picture, you never get the feeling you're sitting around waiting for something to happen, or arguing with somebody about the script. There's none of that. Hitchcock and Ford and a lot of the others came completely prepared as far as the basic mechanics of the picture were concerned, and the mood they wanted to get from every scene.
clippings.title: Jimmy Stewart; Hollywood didn't invent him
clippings.context: Same 1980 interview, on how Hitchcock and Ford ran a set.

clippings.speaker: James Stewart
clippings.quote: There have been books written about that and people saying that he was so terrible with women and that there was an evil-type thing — which is absolutely ridiculous. He kept an excitement on the set. How he did it, I don't know. But nothing seemed to upset him.
clippings.title: Jimmy Stewart's wonderful life
clippings.context: Bill Steigerwald's fall 1986 interview at Stewart's home, asked whether there was tension on Hitchcock's sets; expanded version reposted by the interviewer.

clippings.speaker: James Stewart
clippings.quote: Finally, just as they told Hitch they had enough lights, the lights tripped the sprinkler for the fire system. It started to rain — and I mean really rain. And he said, ‘See if you can get someone to turn off the rain, and while you're at it, someone might get me an umbrella’ And he sat under this umbrella until they got the sprinklers turned off. Nothing threw him.
clippings.title: Jimmy Stewart's wonderful life
clippings.context: Same 1986 interview: an anecdote about lighting the single courtyard set of Rear Window at Paramount.

clippings.speaker: James Stewart
clippings.quote: For instance, sometimes I'd do a scene with Hitchcock and he'd look up and say, ‘Jim’ -- he always called me Jim — ‘this scene is timed.’
clippings.title: Jimmy Stewart's wonderful life
clippings.context: Same 1986 interview, on learning to control his famous drawl.

clippings.speaker: James Stewart
clippings.quote: And Kim just came up to Hitchcock and said, ‘Mr. Hitchcock, I, just this next scene, it’s just not quite clear to me and I’d like to go over it with you because I’m not sure of the reason for the motivation that I have in dealing with the problem that I have with Mr. Stewart.’ And Hitchcock just looked at her and said, ‘Kim, it’s only a movie!’
clippings.title: Jimmy Stewart: The Interview
clippings.context: Maury Z. Levy's Video Review interview with a 78-year-old Stewart, reposted by the author; Stewart recalls early in the Vertigo shoot.

clippings.speaker: Harrison Ford
clippings.quote: I suppose you can just simply say that I love him. You know, he’s a bit of a mystery, old George. I mean, he’s got a head so crammed full of ideas and thoughts and ambitions, and yet at his heart he’s simply a father, a husband, a mentor, business man, an entrepreneur, a creative genius — just a guy. … And he’s my friend.
clippings.title: Harrison Ford on 'The Force Awakens' and the Return of Han Solo
clippings.context: Asked by Brian Hiatt what he made of Lucas then and now, around the release of The Force Awakens.

clippings.speaker: Harrison Ford
clippings.quote: Jesus, I didn’t know he liked me that much. Well, I like him that much, too.
clippings.title: Harrison Ford on 'The Force Awakens' and the Return of Han Solo
clippings.context: Ford's reaction on hearing Lucas's 1977 explanation of why he cast him: "Harrison is handsome, dashing, and sullen, with an underlying current of sensual hostility."

clippings.speaker: Harrison Ford
clippings.quote: I wouldn’t sit out front and wait for you, George. I love you, but I don’t wait out front.
clippings.title: Harrison Ford Building A Door For Francis Ford Coppola Landed Him Han Solo
clippings.context: Onstage with Lucas at Star Wars Celebration 2017, disputing Lucas's claim that he loitered outside the casting office pretending to work.

clippings.speaker: Harrison Ford
clippings.quote: I was not an overnight success. I struggled for about 15 years, going from acting job to carpentry and back to acting. Until I finally got a part in a wildly successful film. None of this happened on my own. Thank you, George Lucas. Thank you, Steven Spielberg.
clippings.title: Harrison Ford thanks Star Wars creator George Lucas for giving him "a part in a wildly successful film" during emotional SAG awards speech
clippings.context: From Ford's acceptance speech for the Screen Actors Guild Life Achievement Award on March 1, 2026.

clippings.speaker: George Lucas
clippings.quote: In American Graffiti, I could see he was a real talent, but he didn’t have a big part.
clippings.title: '40 Years Of Star Wars' Panel: George Lucas Says "There Aren't That Many People Like" Carrie Fisher
clippings.context: Lucas onstage with Ford at the 40 Years of Star Wars panel, Star Wars Celebration Orlando.

clippings.speaker: George Lucas
clippings.quote: He got the part because in the end I asked him, this is about spaceships and flying and stuff like that. I said ‘Do you know how to fly?’
clippings.title: '40 Years Of Star Wars' Panel: George Lucas Says "There Aren't That Many People Like" Carrie Fisher
clippings.context: Same Celebration panel; Ford replied, "I said, fly, yeah. Land?"

clippings.speaker: George Lucas
clippings.quote: I was wary of Harrison and I becoming like Scorsese and De Niro. I thought, ‘Let's create a new icon.’
clippings.title: The Making Of Raiders Of The Lost Ark
clippings.context: Lucas in Empire's oral history of Raiders, on why he first looked beyond Ford to play Indiana Jones.

clippings.speaker: George Lucas
clippings.quote: So then we were running short of time and Steven said, ‘There's always Harrison.’ I doubted he'd go for a three-picture deal - he didn't want to on Star Wars. … I went to Harrison and he read the script and said, ‘Yeah, I'll do a three-picture deal. I'd love to.’
clippings.title: The Making Of Raiders Of The Lost Ark
clippings.context: Lucas in Empire's oral history, on how Ford came to play Indiana Jones after Tom Selleck dropped out.

clippings.speaker: James Cameron
clippings.quote: Arnold was the one true believer … He was the only one who really thought it was going to be a hit.
clippings.title: A Kinder, Gentler Cyborg
clippings.context: On the set of Terminator 2, Cameron looks back on the low-budget first film; fan-site reprint of Rachel Abramovitz's Premiere story.

clippings.speaker: Arnold Schwarzenegger
clippings.quote: I think that with a director like this, I don't have to go home and say, 'I better work up this scene for tomorrow,' because you don't need to with him. He has worked it already ten times over.
clippings.title: A Kinder, Gentler Cyborg
clippings.context: Schwarzenegger, in his trailer during the T2 shoot, on why he feels no pressure working with Cameron.

clippings.speaker: Arnold Schwarzenegger
clippings.quote: He has still the two personalities when he shoots … When he shoots, he doesn't care for anything. It's not that he's mean-spirited; he just likes to have everyone at that point of being scared. So he will scream and go crazy, and then, as soon as the shot is over, he will be casual with everyone and very sweet and nice.
clippings.title: A Kinder, Gentler Cyborg
clippings.context: Schwarzenegger describes Cameron's on-set temperament during the T2 production.

clippings.speaker: Arnold Schwarzenegger
clippings.quote: He became a mentor in many ways. And to have him as my friend? I need any help, I need anything from him, he's there.
clippings.title: “It’s Going to Be Epic”: The Oral History of James Cameron
clippings.context: Schwarzenegger in The Ringer's oral history of Cameron's career, released alongside Avatar: The Way of Water.

clippings.speaker: James Cameron
clippings.quote: No, he and I are still besties, and I like to wind him up a little bit, and he likes to wind me up. But he was great, and he came with a will to make it everything that it could be.
clippings.title: James Cameron: The Ultimate Terminator Interview
clippings.context: For The Terminator's 40th anniversary, Cameron recalls his apprehension before first directing Schwarzenegger.

clippings.speaker: James Cameron
clippings.quote: Well, first of all, this character is as much your character as it is mine. I may have created it, but it's you now. You own it more than I do in the zeitgeist, in the public imagination. I'm not going to hold you back as a friend.
clippings.title: James Cameron: The Ultimate Terminator Interview
clippings.context: Cameron recounts what he told Schwarzenegger when Arnold asked his blessing to make Terminator 3 without him.

clippings.speaker: Ari Aster
clippings.quote: I’ve been working with Pawel for a long time—he’s one of my best friends and we understand how the other person works. We have a very satisfying shorthand and our own processes, which is great. I definitely plan on keeping on going with him.
clippings.title: The Ari Aster Q&A
clippings.context: Answering a Letterboxd member's question about whether he'd keep working with Pogorzelski, around the release of Midsommar.

clippings.speaker: Ari Aster
clippings.quote: Pawel spent long days in the field alone before we were shooting, seeing what times were best for the light and which areas and so he was in charge of the schedule day-to-day in terms of what we were shooting.
clippings.title: ‘Midsommar’: How Ari Aster and Pawel Pogorzelski Created a Technicolor Fairy Tale Nightmare
clippings.context: Joint IndieWire craft interview on shooting Midsommar in near-constant summer daylight.

clippings.speaker: Ari Aster
clippings.quote: So logistically, this was definitely the hardest thing I had ever done. And I'm sure it's the hardest thing the cinematographer, Pawel Pogorzelski, had ever done.
clippings.title: Director Ari Aster Dishes on ‘Midsommar’ as New Trailer Debuts: “This Isn’t Hereditary”
clippings.context: Interview on the eve of the Midsommar trailer release, on the difficulty of shooting in daylight.

clippings.speaker: Pawel Pogorzelski
clippings.quote: Well, Ari and I met at AFI in 2008. Almost from the first few weeks, we got a liking of each other's taste in movies. Then, we did a short together at AFI, and knew right away that we wanted to partner up (for other projects).
clippings.title: Interview: Cinematographer Pawel Pogorzelski on Working with Ari Aster to Create HEREDITARY
clippings.context: Interview for the release of Hereditary, on how the two first met as AFI students.

clippings.speaker: Pawel Pogorzelski
clippings.quote: We would jog together and he would pitch me this idea he had for Hereditary , and I thought it was so cool. So, I've been there since the infancy of Hereditary . From the ideas while we were jogging, all the way to the first script, and then on set.
clippings.title: Interview: Cinematographer Pawel Pogorzelski on Working with Ari Aster to Create HEREDITARY
clippings.context: Same interview, on how Aster first pitched Hereditary to him.

clippings.speaker: Pawel Pogorzelski
clippings.quote: Yeah, I hope we keep making movies together for a while. For me, he's family. I love working with. He really pushes the envelope, and I love being part of that.
clippings.title: Interview: Cinematographer Pawel Pogorzelski on Working with Ari Aster to Create HEREDITARY
clippings.context: Same interview, asked about Aster's next film for A24 (Midsommar).

clippings.speaker: Pawel Pogorzelski
clippings.quote: Ari is very prepared and has a very clear vision. We’ll watch a couple movies and send references. He very much knows what he wants, and I have to deliver. What makes me happy is when I show him a test during prep and he says, ‘This is what I wanted but even more.’
clippings.title: Journey of Extremes: Pawel Pogorzelski, 1st AC Dany Racine & Brian Mills on Beau Is Afraid
clippings.context: Panavision interview about the camera and lens work on Beau Is Afraid.

clippings.speaker: Brian De Palma
clippings.quote: Pino Donaggio wrote the score for DON'T LOOK NOW. I was put on to him by a good friend of mine, the ‘Time’ magazine film critic Jay Cocks, who had always liked his music and suggested him to me when Bernard Herrmann unfortunately passed away and I was looking for another composer. I listened to his records and talked it over with him and felt he was the right kind of combination.
clippings.title: Brian DePalma Cinefantastique interview
clippings.context: De Palma, interviewed by Mike Childs and Alan Jones for Cinefantastique (Vol. 6 No. 1, Summer 1977), explains how he found Donaggio for Carrie; transcribed on a fan site.

clippings.speaker: Brian De Palma
clippings.quote: Nobody writes those psycho dream things like Pino does, and there's a long section of Noomi's nightmare that has big surprises in it, and he's just the master of that. I mean, we did it in ‘Carrie,’ we did it in ‘Dressed to Kill,’ we did it in ‘Raising Cain.’
clippings.title: Brian De Palma Q & A: 'Passion,' McAdams vs. Rapace, Sex Tools UPDATED (New Trailer)
clippings.context: Anne Thompson asks De Palma about reuniting with Donaggio on Passion, their first film together since Raising Cain.

clippings.speaker: Brian De Palma
clippings.quote: Well, I've worked with Pino on seven films together. He knows how to do these long violent sequences that I create. The last cue at the end of the film, when the last nightmare takes place, no one writes music like that but him.
clippings.title: Interview: Brian De Palma Talks Passion
clippings.context: Phone interview ahead of Passion's US release, asked about scoring the film with Donaggio.

clippings.speaker: Pino Donaggio
clippings.quote: When I first told De Palma that I was going to score Joe Dante's film he said: ''if you feel like it, ashkksss''. Well, he made an unfriendly noise. … But Brian De Palma didn't like it even one bit.
clippings.title: Interview with Pino Donaggio: Oorlogswinter (Winter in Wartime)
clippings.context: Donaggio, interviewed in Amsterdam about Oorlogswinter, recalls De Palma's reaction to him scoring Joe Dante's Piranha.

clippings.speaker: Pino Donaggio
clippings.quote: And of course I would have liked to do all other films by Brian de Palma. He keeps on changing composers, but there is still something out there. He came to Venice to talk to me about The Toyer.
clippings.title: Interview with Pino Donaggio: Oorlogswinter (Winter in Wartime)
clippings.context: Donaggio on the gaps in their collaboration and De Palma's unmade project The Toyer.

clippings.speaker: Pino Donaggio
clippings.quote: For a long time Brian didn't listen to anything before the recording: he heard the music directly in the studio, with the orchestra. There were no demos, there was nothing. He trusted me. The first time I was risking a lot, because he didn't know what I would do. In fact, the night before recording in New York, I didn't sleep much!
clippings.original: Per molto tempo Brian non ascoltava nulla prima della registrazione: sentiva la musica direttamente in sala, con l’orchestra. Non c’erano provini, non c’era niente. Si fidava. «La prima volta rischiavo molto, perché non sapeva che cosa avrei fatto. Infatti, la notte prima di registrare a New York, non è che abbia dormito molto!
clippings.title: Pino Donaggio: «Volevano far cambiare il finale di Blow Out». L'intervista esclusiva, da De Palma a Refn
clippings.context: Donaggio, interviewed by Alessandro Gamma, describes De Palma hearing his scores for the first time at the recording session; translated from Italian.

clippings.speaker: Pino Donaggio
clippings.quote: When we watched it with the American distributors, they wanted to have the ending changed. But Brian was very tough, he refused to change it.
clippings.original: Quando lo vedemmo con i distributori americani, volevano far cambiare il finale. Ma Brian fu durissimo, non volle cambiarlo.
clippings.title: Pino Donaggio: «Volevano far cambiare il finale di Blow Out». L'intervista esclusiva, da De Palma a Refn
clippings.context: Donaggio recalls the fight over Blow Out's bleak ending; translated from Italian.

clippings.speaker: Pino Donaggio
clippings.quote: Brian De Palma and I often joked around. He used to tell me: ‘I pulled you out of the canals of Venice’.
clippings.original: Con Brian De Palma scherzavamo spesso. Lui mi diceva: ‘Ti ho tirato fuori dai canali di Venezia’.
clippings.title: Pino Donaggio: «Volevano far cambiare il finale di Blow Out». L'intervista esclusiva, da De Palma a Refn
clippings.context: Donaggio on a running joke between them; translated from Italian.

clippings.speaker: Jamie Foxx
clippings.quote: ‘He says, ‘What are you doing?’’ Foxx remembers of that day on set. ‘I say, ‘I’m trying to do my thing, Mike.’ He says, ‘How about you don’t do your thing. When was the last time you saw a guy who drove a taxi cab do his thing? He’s trying to get home because he’s tired. … So why don’t you be real.’’
clippings.title: How Jamie Foxx drew on lessons from Michael Mann for death row drama 'Just Mercy'
clippings.context: Promoting Just Mercy, Foxx recalls Mann cutting a scene short on Collateral to stop him performing.

clippings.speaker: Jamie Foxx
clippings.quote: Michael Mann, who's known for his intensity, but we had a great chemistry on this film. I think it has something to do with being in LA. We felt really comfortable doing it.
clippings.title: Collateral: Press Conference interviews with Tom Cruise, Jamie Foxx, Jada Pinkett-Smith, and Director Michael Mann
clippings.context: Collateral press conference with Mann, Cruise and Pinkett Smith.

clippings.speaker: Jamie Foxx
clippings.quote: Now this is like my thing I've been lucky enough to have. I was thrown Michael Mann, Tom Cruise saying we believe. You've got to have somebody who believes that you can actually make it happen.
clippings.title: Collateral: Press Conference interviews with Tom Cruise, Jamie Foxx, Jada Pinkett-Smith, and Director Michael Mann
clippings.context: Collateral press conference, asked about moving from comedy into dramatic roles.

clippings.speaker: Michael Mann
clippings.quote: Jamie's a renaissance man, he's a man for all seasons. He can do anything.
clippings.title: Collateral: Press Conference interviews with Tom Cruise, Jamie Foxx, Jada Pinkett-Smith, and Director Michael Mann
clippings.context: Mann at the Collateral press conference, after discussing Foxx's scene with Jada Pinkett Smith.

clippings.speaker: Michael Mann
clippings.quote: First of all, it’s all Jamie’s fault, because he talked me into this, starting in 2002, at Ali’s birthday party.
clippings.title: Colin Farrell, Jamie Foxx and Michael Mann on the Virtues of 'Miami Vice'
clippings.context: Asked why he returned to Miami Vice as a film; Foxx replied, "Yeah, I did."

clippings.speaker: Michael Mann
clippings.quote: I loved the idea of Jamie playing the cab driver. And we had just done Ali together, and knew each other really well,
clippings.title: Adam Sandler Was Almost Cast in 'Collateral,' Says Director Michael Mann
clippings.context: Mann on casting Foxx in Collateral, from his Hollywood Masters talk at Loyola Marymount.

clippings.speaker: Michael Mann
clippings.quote: We would get fares and explain to the fare what we were doing, and hanging around Jamie made it all hilarious and a lot of fun.
clippings.title: Michael Mann on ‘Collateral’ at 20: One Cab and One Night with Tom Cruise and Jamie Foxx
clippings.context: Mann on riding along with real cab drivers so Foxx could learn the job for Collateral.

clippings.speaker: Quentin Tarantino
clippings.quote: It’s just this cool connection that happened while we were doing Pulp Fiction. I mean, von Sternberg had Marlene Dietrich, Hitchcock had Ingrid Bergman, André Téchiné had Catherine Deneuve. It’s a special bond that I’m proud to have, and hopefully, one day, people will reference me and Uma like they do the others.
clippings.title: Quentin Tarantino and Uma Thurman: A Magnificent Obsession
clippings.context: Tarantino, asked by Erik Hedegaard how Thurman operates as his muse, during the Kill Bill Vol. 2 press.

clippings.speaker: Quentin Tarantino
clippings.quote: She’s one of my best friends on the planet, but if she doesn’t know you, she’s private and reserved. The feeling with Uma is, she’s got to let you inside.
clippings.title: Quentin Tarantino and Uma Thurman: A Magnificent Obsession
clippings.context: Tarantino describing Thurman's reserve in the same Rolling Stone profile of the pair.

clippings.speaker: Quentin Tarantino
clippings.quote: We love each other, but we’re almost too close now to be a couple. We had our life together on ‘Kill Bill.’ It was like a marriage in every way.
clippings.title: UMA RUMORS: Quentin Tarantino hasn’t exactly killed…
clippings.context: Said at a Lost in Translation DVD party in Los Angeles, as reported by USA Today and relayed in a Tribune gossip roundup.

clippings.speaker: Quentin Tarantino
clippings.quote: It affected me and Uma for the next two to three years. It wasn’t like we didn’t talk. But a trust was broken.
clippings.title: Uma Thurman said she'd work with Quentin Tarantino again despite 'Kill Bill' onset accident that injured her
clippings.context: Tarantino on the Kill Bill car-stunt crash, originally told to Deadline in February 2018 and quoted by ABC News.

clippings.speaker: Uma Thurman
clippings.quote: We got going back and forth and cooked up the character of The Bride together. Like, wouldn’t it be great to play this woman...assassin...wedding chapel massacre...and da da da da dah. Usually that kind of talk is cheap but not with him. He went and sculpted the seed ideas of the movie.
clippings.title: Uma Thurman is Tarantino's muse
clippings.context: Thurman recalling how the Bride was born in conversations during Pulp Fiction, in an AP interview for Kill Bill Vol. 2.

clippings.speaker: Uma Thurman
clippings.quote: I think we’re really different people actually, but that’s what’s fun about talking to each other. We have very different perspectives. He’s a very extroverted, public person. I’m a very introverted person.
clippings.title: Uma Thurman is Tarantino's muse
clippings.context: Thurman on the contrast she sees as the key to her relationship with the director.

clippings.speaker: Uma Thurman
clippings.quote: Anyway, I don’t think I did any musing. I think I listened to a lot of scenes and gave Quentin my opinions and killed myself trying to help him make the movie great. But I didn’t spend a lot of time on a pedestal, musing. It’s great if he finds me inspiring.
clippings.title: Quentin Tarantino and Uma Thurman: A Magnificent Obsession
clippings.context: Thurman pushing back on the 'muse' label over dinner with Rolling Stone.

clippings.speaker: Uma Thurman
clippings.quote: When you know someone for as long as I’ve known him, 25 years of creative collaboration...yes, did we have some tragedies take place? Sure. But you can’t reduce that type of history and legacy.
clippings.title: Uma Thurman said she'd work with Quentin Tarantino again despite 'Kill Bill' onset accident that injured her
clippings.context: Thurman to Entertainment Weekly, after her 2018 account of the Kill Bill crash, as quoted by ABC News.

clippings.speaker: Brad Pitt
clippings.quote: It's a fun set. There is no set like a Tarantino set. Because of his verve and love for film. Sometimes he'll say: 'That was fine, but we are going to do one more take. Why?' And the whole crew will chant: 'Because we love making movies!' Everyone's in.
clippings.film: Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood
clippings.title: Brad Pitt on Once Upon a Time in Hollywood: 'There's no set like a Tarantino set'
clippings.context: Pitt to Donald Clarke at Cannes, the day after the film's premiere.

clippings.speaker: Brad Pitt
clippings.quote: The Quentin I know is hilarious and verbose and great to have conversations with, amazing energy. It's almost like spring break with him, and you need a week to recover—the guy has got so much energy. But also there is a tenderness and sweetness to him.
clippings.title: Brad Pitt, Tarantino and a Bong Full of Hash: The Untold Origin Story of 'Inglourious Basterds'
clippings.context: From an excerpt of Jay Glennie's book The Making of Quentin Tarantino's Inglourious Basterds, recalling their first script meeting in France.

clippings.speaker: Brad Pitt
clippings.quote: Quentin and I met at the premiere of that. We had a lot in common. We were pretty much raised on the same television shows. We'd talk about Fantastic Voyage and The War of the Gargantuas, going to the drive-in theater, and Clint Eastwood. We were weaned on the same kinda movie magic.
clippings.title: Brad Pitt, Tarantino and a Bong Full of Hash: The Untold Origin Story of 'Inglourious Basterds'
clippings.context: Pitt, in Jay Glennie's book excerpt, on first meeting Tarantino at the True Romance premiere.

clippings.speaker: Quentin Tarantino
clippings.quote: The hillbilly dialect could be some actor we know who throws on a twang, but you buy it coming from him. There aren't many actors of my generation who can pull it off.
clippings.title: In 'Inglourious Basterds,' Tarantino, Pitt Kick the Crap Out of the Nazis
clippings.context: Tarantino on Pitt's Southern drawl as Aldo Raine, in an interview with ABC News Now's Popcorn with Peter Travers.

clippings.speaker: Quentin Tarantino
clippings.quote: But I could not see past anybody else playing Aldo Raine other than Brad, which is why I wanted him in the movie, not for any other fucking reasons. He was right for Aldo, okay?
clippings.title: Brad Pitt, Tarantino and a Bong Full of Hash: The Untold Origin Story of 'Inglourious Basterds'
clippings.context: Tarantino, in Jay Glennie's book excerpt, explaining the film's deal was set up without a star attached.

clippings.speaker: Quentin Tarantino
clippings.quote: That's right. He had a big brick of hash. He whipped out a knife, like Jesse James, and cut me off a big sliver. I thought, 'Oh, God, this should be in a movie,'
clippings.title: Brad Pitt, Tarantino and a Bong Full of Hash: The Untold Origin Story of 'Inglourious Basterds'
clippings.context: Tarantino recalling the all-night meeting at Pitt's home in the South of France where Pitt signed on.

clippings.speaker: Quentin Tarantino
clippings.quote: I loved the Cliff Booth character, I loved the way that Brad played him, and there was this aspect of him as sort of like a paperback hero.
clippings.film: Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood
clippings.title: Quentin Tarantino Shows Off First 17 Minutes of 'Cliff Booth' and Explains Decision to Revive Character
clippings.context: Tarantino at an AFI Fest Q&A explaining why he wrote the Cliff Booth follow-up for Pitt.

clippings.speaker: Robert Eggers
clippings.quote: Jarin and I have grown together as people, as fathers, as filmmakers — we’ve been working together since I was 25. I know that with some of my director colleagues, they design the shots and the DP lights them. With Jarin and me, it’s very collaborative.
clippings.title: Director Robert Eggers on Nosferatu
clippings.context: Eggers describes his collaborative relationship with his cinematographer in an ASC interview about Nosferatu.

clippings.speaker: Robert Eggers
clippings.quote: In scenes that had a whole lot of dialogue, I’d be working with the actors in a rehearsal room, and Jarin would be there [framing things] with his phone, trying different things. Sometimes I might grab the phone, and we’d both be trying to find ways to make the staging more elegant.
clippings.title: Director Robert Eggers on Nosferatu
clippings.context: Eggers on how he and Blaschke worked out shots during rehearsals for Nosferatu.

clippings.speaker: Robert Eggers
clippings.quote: Jarin and I have been working together for over 17 years. This film is the culmination of a long collaboration of mutual inspiration and trying to push each other in certain directions.
clippings.title: Nosferatu's Robert Eggers and Oscar-Nominated DP Jarin Blaschke
clippings.context: Joint interview with Iain Blair; Eggers asked what Blaschke brought to their sixth film together.

clippings.speaker: Jarin Blaschke
clippings.quote: I found a fellow hopeless perfectionist in Rob during that shoot. Up until then and sometimes in-between his movies, it can feel lonely, like you are just working for yourself. With Rob, I felt my quirks and obsessions were accepted, encouraged and even demanded. That is a rare, rare thing.
clippings.title: From a Rampaging Alexander Skarsgård to an Erupting Volcano: Shooting The Northman
clippings.context: Studio interview for The Northman; Blaschke recalls meeting Eggers on the short The Tell-Tale Heart.

clippings.speaker: Jarin Blaschke
clippings.quote: After that first short, we would just hang out all the time, because we weren’t working, and there’s like seven years of that, really, just becoming friends and kind of aesthetic snobs together, and really connecting.
clippings.title: Nosferatu’s Jarin Blaschke Chats Oscar Nomination, Robert Eggers, and That Ending Sunrise
clippings.context: Interview after his second Oscar nomination; on the years between their first short and The Witch.

clippings.speaker: Jarin Blaschke
clippings.quote: When I’m working with Rob, my brain just goes into Rob composition mode… So even if it’s a frame that I might find, I’m filtering it through the Rob filter.
clippings.title: Nosferatu’s Jarin Blaschke Chats Oscar Nomination, Robert Eggers, and That Ending Sunrise
clippings.context: Blaschke on their shared, symmetrical, storybook visual style.

clippings.speaker: Steven Soderbergh
clippings.quote: George is a notorious letter-writer, particularly when he's mad, and my first thought was that I had given an interview and said something I wasn't supposed to. Then I opened the letter and it said, 'I think I would like to try to do this.'
clippings.title: 'Solaris' is about more than just George Clooney's naked butt
clippings.context: Soderbergh recalling the letter Clooney sent while he was editing Ocean's 11, asking to play the lead in Solaris.

clippings.speaker: Steven Soderbergh
clippings.quote: As soon as I read the letter, I knew he was ready to play this role. Just the fact that he asked the question meant he was ready to take the leap. And his performance proves that I was right. It puts him in a totally different category as an actor. In terms of his career, this is his 'Five Easy Pieces.'
clippings.title: 'Solaris' is about more than just George Clooney's naked butt
clippings.context: Soderbergh on casting Clooney in Solaris, in a press interview at the film's release.

clippings.speaker: George Clooney
clippings.quote: Although it seems as if we have nothing in common … we think the same things are funny and important.
clippings.title: 'Solaris' is about more than just George Clooney's naked butt
clippings.context: Clooney on the friendship that began while filming Out of Sight (the writer's aside about extrovert vs. bookish is cut).

clippings.speaker: George Clooney
clippings.quote: He’s by far the biggest influence creatively I’ve had. Here’s the thing: I got to get firsthand, up-close and personal lessons on writing, storytelling, directing, producing, with someone who will be remembered as one of the greats. And I got to do it on a daily basis for years.
clippings.title: Dialogue: George Clooney
clippings.context: Clooney, asked to describe his creative partnership with Soderbergh, around his American Cinematheque Award.

clippings.speaker: George Clooney
clippings.quote: Steven and I were talking about it on the plane this morning, because we’re about to wrap up ‘(Ocean’s) Thirteen.’ And I looked over and said, ‘So how do you think we did?’ And he said, ‘I think we did pretty good.’ I said, ‘I think we did pretty good, too.’
clippings.title: Section Eight goes up in Smoke
clippings.context: Clooney looking back on Section Eight, the production company he and Soderbergh were closing down.

clippings.speaker: Steven Soderbergh
clippings.quote: When I first saw George in 'ER' on TV, I said, 'That guy is a movie star,' … When 'Out of Sight,' came up, I wanted him for it. I felt he was ready to pop, and I wanted to get on that train.
clippings.title: Clooney a loser in new film
clippings.context: Soderbergh, in an interview around The Good German, on why he cast Clooney in Out of Sight.

clippings.speaker: Steven Soderbergh
clippings.quote: He’s very patient, which makes him lethal when it comes to pranks.
clippings.title: George Clooney on 'Ocean's' Reboot, Jay Kelly and Slamming Trump
clippings.context: Soderbergh in a Variety cover profile of Clooney, introducing a story about a prank Clooney planned for producer Jerry Weintraub.

clippings.speaker: Joel Coen
clippings.quote: We’re lucky we found Roger. He understands what we are after, and frequently comes up with stuff on the spot that reflects what we want to do in the scene — but perhaps in a much better realization of it, given the setup.
clippings.title: Fargo: Cold-Blooded Scheming
clippings.context: Joel Coen on Deakins in American Cinematographer's 1996 Fargo production story, republished online by the ASC in 2020.

clippings.speaker: Joel Coen
clippings.quote: We always involve Roger very early. Basically, what we do after we finish the script is sit down with him and talk in general terms about how we were thinking about it from a visual point of view. … So he’s involved pretty much right from the beginning. The style of the shooting is worked out between the three of us.
clippings.title: Fargo: Cold-Blooded Scheming
clippings.context: Joel Coen describing how the brothers bring Deakins into pre-production and storyboarding.

clippings.speaker: Joel Coen
clippings.quote: He has been quietly bringing us around to longer lenses. It’s a joke between the three of us. We’re now up to 32mm and 35mm lenses!
clippings.title: Fargo: Cold-Blooded Scheming
clippings.context: On the running debate between Deakins and the Coens over their taste for wide-angle lenses.

clippings.speaker: Roger Deakins
clippings.quote: So Joel and Ethan had this small project up in Minnesota that they wanted to do, and they weren't sure if I would want to do it cause it was so low budget. I always remember that. I said, 'Well, you must be mad. Why wouldn't I want to do it?'
clippings.title: Oscar-winning cinematographer Roger Deakins on the funny reason he began working with Coens, 'disaster' of 'Shawshank' release and more
clippings.context: Deakins recalling how Fargo came to him after The Hudsucker Proxy flopped, in a career-retrospective interview.

clippings.speaker: Roger Deakins
clippings.quote: I remember Joel and Ethan saying, just a passing comment one day, … that they were gonna be writing a script of the novel No Country for Old Men. And the first thing I said was, 'Well, are you gonna direct it?' And they said, 'We don't know, really.' And I said, 'Dammit, I'll never talk to you again if you don't direct it and ask me to shoot it.'
clippings.title: Oscar-winning cinematographer Roger Deakins on the funny reason he began working with Coens, 'disaster' of 'Shawshank' release and more
clippings.context: Deakins on pushing the Coens to direct No Country for Old Men themselves.

clippings.speaker: Roger Deakins
clippings.quote: Obviously, with Joel and Ethan, I pretty much will do anything.
clippings.title: Roger Deakins
clippings.context: Deakins, interviewed by Jeff Bridges, on how he chooses projects.

clippings.speaker: Roger Deakins
clippings.quote: Joel and Ethan will do that sometimes. There will be storyboarding on a scene to have a lot of coverage, and we’ll go in in the morning and shoot, like, a two shot, and then I’ll say, ‘Well, we’ve got the overs now.’ And they’ll say, ‘Well, I don’t think we need them.’ … They’re also very confident when they feel they’ve got something.
clippings.title: Roger Deakins
clippings.context: Deakins, talking with Jeff Bridges, on the Coens' confidence on set.

clippings.speaker: Bill Murray
clippings.quote: Harold Ramis and I together did the 'National Lampoon Show' off Broadway, 'Meatballs,' 'Stripes,' 'Caddyshack,' 'Ghostbusters' and 'Groundhog Day.' … He earned his keep on this planet. God bless him.
clippings.title: Bill Murray Opens Up About Death of Harold Ramis
clippings.context: Murray's statement on Ramis's death, first obtained by Time magazine and reported by ABC News.

clippings.speaker: Bill Murray
clippings.quote: In the editing, I think we had a difference of opinion. We had a difference about the script too. That gets a little personal and that's not for sharing with everyone. But I just felt like a lot of what was in there was unnecessary. I thought there was a lot of overwriting in it. And I held Harold responsible for that.
clippings.title: Bill Murray talks about mending fences with Harold Ramis on Grantland podcast
clippings.context: Murray on the rift that began on the Groundhog Day set, speaking on a Grantland podcast with John Walsh, as reported by the Sun-Times.

clippings.speaker: Bill Murray
clippings.quote: And it was great. It was a beautiful day, obviously….There was sadness. I got to his beautiful home in the suburbs of Chicago. I went there. I sort of just showed up. I wasn't expected.
clippings.title: Bill Murray talks about mending fences with Harold Ramis on Grantland podcast
clippings.context: Murray on visiting the ailing Ramis in Glencoe to make peace before his death, from a Grantland podcast reported by the Sun-Times.

clippings.speaker: Harold Ramis
clippings.quote: He redefines quirky! [ Laughs ] He is the most fascinating and talented pain in the ass we know. … Hey, he couldn't be the actor he is if he didn't have that explosive potential. We watch him with such fascination because we genuinely don't know what he's going to do.
clippings.title: Harold Ramis 'Busts Bill Murray
clippings.context: Ramis, asked whether Murray is as quirky as people say, in an interview pegged to the Ghostbusters DVD set.

clippings.speaker: Harold Ramis
clippings.quote: In Danny's original script the characters weren't well defined; part of the fun was tailoring them for Bill, Danny and me. What we came up with was that Danny was the heart, I was the brain and Bill was the mouth of the Ghostbusters.
clippings.title: Harold Ramis 'Busts Bill Murray
clippings.context: Ramis on shaping the Ghostbusters roles around himself, Aykroyd and Murray.

clippings.speaker: Harold Ramis
clippings.quote: Bill has kind of moved on in his life since Groundhog Day. I've had no contact with him. I did ask him to appear in my new film, The Ice Harvest, [but] I didn't hear back from him. Too bad, he would have been great in it.
clippings.title: Harold Ramis 'Busts Bill Murray
clippings.context: Ramis, asked if they would work together again, during the long estrangement after Groundhog Day.

clippings.speaker: Matt Damon
clippings.quote: In Hollywood, by any measure, I was cold – cold as ice. And Steven was coming off his Oscar for Traffic and two of his movies were Best Picture nominees in the same year. By Hollywood standards, he was as hot as you could get. … And it was in that climate that he called me.
clippings.title: Exclusive Matt Damon Interview
clippings.context: Damon recalls Soderbergh offering him The Informant! in 2001, while he was stuck in Paris on Bourne reshoots and his career had stalled.

clippings.speaker: Matt Damon
clippings.quote: Formally, nobody has pushed the envelope more than Steven. He's done every kind of movie. He's totally fascinated by form. He's basically tried everything. And he's always in production.
clippings.title: Exclusive Matt Damon Interview
clippings.context: Asked what he admires about Soderbergh, in the same interview for The Informant!

clippings.speaker: Matt Damon
clippings.quote: I choose movies entirely based on who's directing them now. I have done movies with no script and they have turned out the way I wanted them to, just because of who the director was, so to have a director like Steven, and then on top of it, to have a script that was as good as any script I had read…
clippings.title: Behind the Candelabra - Interview with Matt Damon
clippings.context: Damon, at Cannes 2013, on why he didn't hesitate over playing Scott Thorson for Soderbergh.

clippings.speaker: Steven Soderbergh
clippings.quote: Well, that's Matt wanting to expand his experience as an actor and you got to give him credit for that. … You want somebody who's kind of fearless and we look at the complete transformation that Matt goes through in this. You're seeing somebody who sort of jumps off the cliff and doesn't look back, and that's what you want.
clippings.title: TIFF Interview: The Informant Director Steven Soderbergh
clippings.context: Soderbergh at the 2009 Toronto Film Festival, asked about pushing Damon as an actor in The Informant!

clippings.speaker: Steven Soderbergh
clippings.quote: Possibly, but I think Michael's point was that, at that stage in his life, in his career, he was I think more protective of his image as an actor than Matt is right now.
clippings.title: Interview: BEHIND THE CANDELABRA director Steven Soderbergh on the Liberace bio-pic
clippings.context: Soderbergh relays Michael Douglas's admiration for Damon's willingness to play Scott Thorson, comparing Damon to Douglas at the same age.

clippings.speaker: Steven Soderbergh
clippings.quote: Don't say anything around Matt when he's drunk that you don't want repeating because he does remember everything. He sort of embellished that story a little bit but I was shocked he remembered any of it, because at the time we were having this conversation he was not on this planet.
clippings.title: Soderbergh's Six: the Ocean's director on not panicking, not retiring and not trusting drunk Matt Damon
clippings.context: At Karlovy Vary 2024, Soderbergh on Damon being the one who first let slip, in 2013, that he was thinking of retiring.

clippings.speaker: Seth Rogen
clippings.quote: I mean, I couldn’t say enough great things about him. He’s the reason I’m not a homeless crackhead right now. Probably.
clippings.title: Interview with Seth Rogen
clippings.context: Responding to being told Apatow had raved about his writing, around the DVD release of Undeclared and The 40 Year Old Virgin.

clippings.speaker: Seth Rogen
clippings.quote: It was kind of the first legitimate thing a lot of us had really done, and the environment that Judd and Paul (Feig, the show’s co-creator) set was one of such camaraderie and working together and kind of communal attitude of making everything funnier… and it was a big influence on all of our lives.
clippings.title: Interview with Seth Rogen
clippings.context: On the bond among the Freaks and Geeks cast and crew.

clippings.speaker: Judd Apatow
clippings.quote: Seth Rogen, you know, we found him in Vancouver and he was just this odd, funny guy that, when we met him, was 16. … Then it turned out he was such a good writer that it was almost embarrassing, because his scripts were better than most everybody else’s scripts, and he was a kid, so we were all somewhat humiliated having him around.
clippings.title: Interview with Judd Apatow
clippings.context: Explaining how Rogen went from Freaks and Geeks actor to star and writer on Undeclared.

clippings.speaker: Judd Apatow
clippings.quote: Seth is one of the leads of the movie. And he kills so hard that I had to take some jokes out, because it was just weighing the movie in an odd way towards his character when it shouldn’t be that much about him. But people love Seth. I was very gratified, as a big Seth supporter, to see audiences really like him.
clippings.title: Interview with Judd Apatow
clippings.context: Just before The 40 Year Old Virgin opened.

clippings.speaker: Seth Rogen
clippings.quote: I didn’t know Judd when he was young so it’s kind of what I would imagine Judd would have been when he was young. Judd and I are very different — we don’t act anything alike. We are friends and we work together well but we are not very similar people.
clippings.title: Seth Rogen talks Funny People
clippings.context: Asked whether his Funny People character Ira was based on the young Apatow, for the film's DVD release.

clippings.speaker: Judd Apatow
clippings.quote: I saw The Studio and I was just blown away by what Seth and Evan had accomplished. … Like, wow, look how far they're taking it…. They're still getting better. It's incredible.
clippings.title: Judd Apatow chalks up his early career setbacks to being ‘cool enough to fail’
clippings.context: On Q with Tom Power, about the pride he feels as former protégés like Rogen and Evan Goldberg succeed on their own.

clippings.speaker: Seth Rogen
clippings.quote: At one time, when we were shooting ‘Knocked Up,’ we would improvise a lot, and we were improvising and Judd screamed from the other room, ‘Less semen, more emotion!’ … And honestly, as I’ve gone on to make films, it’s amazing how much I come back to ‘Less semen, more emotion.’
clippings.title: Seth Rogen Tells TIFF the Best Advice He’s Ever Received: ‘Less Semen, More Emotion!’
clippings.context: Onstage at TIFF before receiving the Norman Jewison Career Achievement Award, asked for the best advice from his mentor.

clippings.speaker: Seth Rogen
clippings.quote: A little, not really, we’ve never had those problems in our friendship. I think that’s why we’re so comfortable exploring it.
clippings.title: Day Four: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg Are Friends So They Made a Film About It
clippings.context: Joint interview before the UK premiere, asked whether the film's strained friendship mirrors their own.

clippings.speaker: Evan Goldberg
clippings.quote: Yeah, a good partnership is super boring.
clippings.title: Day Four: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg Are Friends So They Made a Film About It
clippings.context: Same joint interview, responding to Rogen saying the film's friendship drama was invented for the movie.

clippings.speaker: Seth Rogen
clippings.quote: But it’s not at all like that actually. I’ll tell you it’s completely equal. And if anything, he touched more so he probably gets the lead.
clippings.title: THE GREEN HORNET On Set Interview Seth Rogen Evan Goldberg
clippings.context: On-set interview, asked which of the two writers is the Green Hornet and which is the sidekick.

clippings.speaker: Evan Goldberg
clippings.quote: And if it started to get disbalanced, our writing would suck. We counterbalance one another quite well.
clippings.title: THE GREEN HORNET On Set Interview Seth Rogen Evan Goldberg
clippings.context: Same on-set interview, following Rogen's answer that their partnership has no leader.

clippings.speaker: Evan Goldberg
clippings.quote: We were children, and our brains forged a thing where it's like, ‘This is how you write with another person.’ So we just learned how to write together–and can't ignore the truth that we are just better together than apart.
clippings.title: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg Open Up On Sequels: “We’re Not Opposed to Revisiting Some”
clippings.context: Joint interview, asked the secret to their creative partnership lasting so long.

clippings.speaker: Evan Goldberg
clippings.quote: But no, Seth just works harder than everyone else. That's nice. He works harder than me. That's what I appreciate the most, is having a partner who works harder than me because who doesn't want that?
clippings.title: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg Open Up On Sequels: “We’re Not Opposed to Revisiting Some”
clippings.context: Same interview, asked what each admires most about the other's work.

clippings.speaker: Seth Rogen
clippings.quote: Evan co-wrote this movie. There's not a lot that we have done without each other [chuckles], but Evan made this movie with Jay Baruchel that is amazing.
clippings.title: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg Open Up On Sequels: “We’re Not Opposed to Revisiting Some”
clippings.context: Same interview, asked for his favorite project of Goldberg's.

clippings.speaker: Evan Goldberg
clippings.quote: Maybe there were 10 nerds, back when nerd was still an insult, who read comic books in my grade and the only one I connected with was Seth.
clippings.title: A kingpin of comedy
clippings.context: Alumni magazine profile of Goldberg, on how his friendship with Rogen began in high school.

clippings.speaker: Alex Garland
clippings.quote: Rob and I, I really think we work very well together. I think both of us are kind of spiky, and I'm not sure how well we'd work with other people or like, I don't know. But we work really well with each other. We have a lot of shorthand…
clippings.title: Alex Garland Breaks Down the Making of Men & Attack on Titan's Influence
clippings.context: Garland, promoting Men, asked how his relationship with Hardy has grown since Ex Machina.

clippings.speaker: Alex Garland
clippings.quote: I just saw the frames and I thought that looks beautiful, that looks smart. He doesn't overdo it… He's got quite a lot of restraint. So in some ways, I think he doesn't get the credit he deserves because he's not showy. He's often kind of understated, and I love that.
clippings.title: Alex Garland Breaks Down the Making of Men & Attack on Titan's Influence
clippings.context: Garland on what he first saw in Hardy's work that made him hire him for Ex Machina.

clippings.speaker: Alex Garland
clippings.quote: really picked up the ball and ran with it… He transcended whatever requirement I could possibly have made of him. He elevated everything.
clippings.title: Director Alex Garland Probes the Limits of Artificial Intelligence in Ex-Machina
clippings.context: Garland on Hardy's lighting of the glass-walled house sets in Ex Machina.

clippings.speaker: Rob Hardy
clippings.quote: He [initially] sent me the first two episodes, and like every Alex Garland script, it's always exciting and a pleasure to read, because the way he writes is so economical… It always has a sense of getting straight to the point, and then going beyond the point…
clippings.title: 'Devs' Cinematographer Rob Hardy Cultivates Beautifully Alien Look For Bay Area Sci-Fi Thriller
clippings.context: Hardy on first reading Garland's scripts for the FX series Devs.

clippings.speaker: Rob Hardy
clippings.quote: The world that Alex creates, and the one I photograph, are aesthetically aligned, and that world—once you've created the content, if you like—is designed to operate in a way that, when we're on set, the shots, the lighting, everything presents itself to you in the moment.
clippings.title: 'Devs' Cinematographer Rob Hardy Cultivates Beautifully Alien Look For Bay Area Sci-Fi Thriller
clippings.context: Hardy describing how he and Garland develop a look through conversation rather than references.

clippings.speaker: Rob Hardy
clippings.quote: My idea, at first, was, 'Just put the ring around the tree on the ground.' But [Alex] was like, 'Why don't we put it in the middle? Let's put it up in the air,'… I was like, 'F**k yes!'
clippings.title: 'Devs' Cinematographer Rob Hardy Cultivates Beautifully Alien Look For Bay Area Sci-Fi Thriller
clippings.context: Hardy recalling how the halo light rings on the Devs set came about.

clippings.speaker: Rob Hardy
clippings.quote: At the very beginning, Alex always described it as the sort of silence in the chaos… You dropped out of this kind of chaotic moment into something of pure elegance and stillness.
clippings.title: “Think of Chaos”
clippings.context: Hardy on Garland's idea for the still-photo moments inside the Civil War siege.

clippings.speaker: Ron Perlman
clippings.quote: What I didn't realize was the campaign he mounted over the course of 6  years. He really could have made the film on 20 different occasions if he had used this actor or that actor or this actor. … It's the most generous gesture I have ever witnessed and certainly been the recipient of.
clippings.title: Hellboy: An Interview with Ron Perlman
clippings.context: Press interview for Hellboy, asked how it felt knowing del Toro would not make the film without him.

clippings.speaker: Ron Perlman
clippings.quote: First and foremost, from the moment we met, even before we started shooting ‘Cronos’, there was this instant friendship. Regardless of whether we ever worked together or will work together in the future, this friendship will endure. So, working with your best pal on something that you both are such geeks over which is moviemaking and cinema in general is as good as it gets.
clippings.title: Hellboy: An Interview with Ron Perlman
clippings.context: Same Hellboy press interview, on their third collaboration and how they met.

clippings.speaker: Ron Perlman
clippings.quote: Everybody accused me of improvising my way through the first Hellboy, but everything I said was scripted by Guillermo and it just sounded like me. I don’t know how he did it, but I had this gift bestowed upon me and you never want to look a gift horse in the mouth.
clippings.title: I, Hellboy: An Interview with Ron Perlman
clippings.context: Interview by Ed Gross tied to the Hellboy II DVD release, on del Toro's writing of the character.

clippings.speaker: Guillermo del Toro
clippings.quote: Hellboy’s a guy you could hang out with and kick back a couple of six packs with, and then all of a sudden he has to go out and kick some monster ass. Ron has that nonchalant, very aloof attitude, but has a very powerful voice and presence, too.
clippings.title: I, Hellboy: An Interview with Ron Perlman
clippings.context: Del Toro explaining Perlman's casting, quoted in the introduction to a Perlman interview; original setting not stated.

clippings.speaker: Guillermo del Toro
clippings.quote: Ron and I were talking while we were making Cronos; I was at his house. We had watched Gunga Din and then Elmer Gantry. He said, ‘You know, there’s a movie called Nightmare Alley, with Tyrone Power, and I would love to remake it.’ I went and got the book, by William Lindsay Gresham.
clippings.title: Guillermo del Toro talks about bringing Nightmare Alley To the Big Screen
clippings.context: Q&A with del Toro on Nightmare Alley, asked how Perlman was the progenitor of the adaptation some 30 years earlier.

clippings.speaker: Guillermo del Toro
clippings.quote: Ron was born for Hellboy
clippings.title: Dreaming of Hell: A Reflection on Guillermo del Toro’s ‘Hellboy’ Journey Following His Beyond Fest Appearance
clippings.context: Said at a 2025 Beyond Fest appearance, recalling how he fought studios that pitched bigger names for the role.

clippings.speaker: James Cameron
clippings.quote: I was petrified of you. I had been writing for months with your picture up on the wall right in front of my little writing station. I was desperately trying to channel what you and Ridley had created for Ripley, and extrapolate forward with my own post-traumatic-stress-syndrome motif.
clippings.title: Aliens 40th Cast Reunion: ‘We’re Still The Same Punks We Were Then,’ Says James Cameron
clippings.context: Cameron to Weaver in Empire's 40th-anniversary Aliens reunion interview, recalling their first meeting.

clippings.speaker: Sigourney Weaver
clippings.quote: Because I read this script that came out of nowhere by this person James Cameron, and it was one of the most extraordinarily structured, thematic, loaded scripts I’d ever read. I felt like it was this beautiful aria between Ripley and the Alien Queen.
clippings.title: Aliens 40th Cast Reunion: ‘We’re Still The Same Punks We Were Then,’ Says James Cameron
clippings.context: Weaver in Empire's Aliens reunion interview, recalling first reading Cameron's script.

clippings.speaker: Sigourney Weaver
clippings.quote: And I was thrilled that Jim would entrust me with such a character. I felt an immediate connection to her. I knew it would be probably the biggest challenge I’ve ever taken on, but I thought, with his help, with his amazing writing, with our wonderful cast, I would definitely give it my best shot.
clippings.title: Sigourney Weaver on Playing Kiri in Avatar: The Way of Water
clippings.context: Weaver on how Cameron pitched her the teenage Na'vi role of Kiri over lunch in 2010.

clippings.speaker: James Cameron
clippings.quote: I thought, 'Wow, if we could do that, what if Sigourney played her own daughter, or at least the daughter of her avatar self?' … I said, 'Sigourney, are you up for this? You want to try playing a 15-year-old?' And we'd joke about it. I'd say, 'Well, emotionally you're 15.' And so am I, by the way, I think we all are to some extent.
clippings.title: James Cameron Marvels at How Sigourney Weaver Played a Teen in “Avatar: Fire and Ash”: She Was 'a Different Person' (Exclusive)
clippings.context: Cameron to People, explaining his decision to cast Weaver as the teenage Kiri after she played Grace in Avatar.

clippings.speaker: Sigourney Weaver
clippings.quote: In fact, I don't really think he tells us where we're going. He wants to find out through us where the character is going, and that's why he's not in video village or anything … He is right there with us. … He does everything possible to make sure you get to try everything you want to try. So, it's kind of like the perfect job for an actor.
clippings.title: Sigourney Weaver says working with James Cameron on the Avatar series is "like the perfect job for an actor": "He does everything possible to make sure you get to try everything you want to try"
clippings.context: Weaver to GamesRadar+ in London on how Cameron directs performance-capture scenes in the Volume.

clippings.speaker: James Cameron
clippings.quote: We kind of meet in that sort of quest for perfection … She's amazing. She always brings it every time.
clippings.title: James Cameron Reflects on Decades-Long Friendship, Working Relationship with Sigourney Weaver (Exclusive)
clippings.context: Cameron to People at the Saturn Awards in March 2026, on his decades-long working relationship with Weaver.

clippings.speaker: Brad Pitt
clippings.quote: Then I go meet with Finch, and he was just talking about films like I'd never heard anyone speak about film. I just got the jones back. Finding that thing kind of … it just reinvigorated what I wanted out of this thing.
clippings.title: Brad Pitt Says David Fincher ‘Reinvigorated’ His Love of Acting During ‘Se7en’
clippings.context: Pitt on Dax Shepard's Armchair Expert podcast, recalling meeting Fincher about Se7en in 1994 when he was considering quitting; quoted by IndieWire.

clippings.speaker: Brad Pitt
clippings.quote: Man, I swore I would never do prosthetics. I’ve done some glue-on beards, and they’re not fun. Then Fincher came with this one and I said, ‘I’m in.’ One of his other great talents is subverting and perverting whatever existing technology there is to his own evil devices.
clippings.film: The Curious Case of Benjamin Button
clippings.title: Brad Pitt: The Rolling Stone Interview
clippings.context: Rolling Stone Q&A at the release of Benjamin Button, their third film together.

clippings.speaker: Brad Pitt
clippings.quote: He's one of the funniest [expletive] I've ever met. … He'll be muttering the whole time: 'That shot works. That's a bad handoff. Why would you go to the insert of the glove there? Stabilize!' It's like watching a football game with Bill Belichick.
clippings.title: Brad Pitt Describes Movie Nights with David Fincher: ‘He’ll Mutter the Whole Time’
clippings.context: Pitt describing their regular movie nights to The New York Times for a 2020 Fincher profile; quoted by IndieWire.

clippings.speaker: David Fincher
clippings.quote: Brad fucks with me all the time. … When we did Fight Club, the studio said, ‘This is awesome; this is going to be great,’ because we were going to have a scene with Brad opening the door naked. When it came time to shoot it, being Brad, he said, ‘I should open the door and have a big yellow dishwasher scrub glove on.’ I said, ‘Perfect.’
clippings.title: The Playboy Interview with David Fincher
clippings.context: Asked by Playboy's Stephen Rebello about the dynamic between him and Pitt; read in a 2023 Substack repost of the interview.

clippings.speaker: David Fincher
clippings.quote: I offer everything to Brad, not because I’m pathetic but because he’s good for so many things. Both Brad and Ben have a default ‘affable’ setting. Neither wants you to be uncomfortable.
clippings.title: The Playboy Interview with David Fincher
clippings.context: Asked why, given his relationship with Pitt, he cast Ben Affleck in Gone Girl.

clippings.speaker: David Fincher
clippings.quote: Brad’s idea was that this is a guy who wears a leather jacket out in the rain. He wears a suit because he has to wear a suit and he wears a tie because he has to wear a tie. He doesn’t really know how to tie a tie. So he leaves them pre-tied on a hanger.
clippings.title: Sinnin’ Ain’t Easy: David Fincher on the lasting legacy of Se7en’s pervasive horror
clippings.context: Interview for Se7en's 30th-anniversary 4K release, on Pitt devising his character's ties.

clippings.speaker: David Fincher
clippings.quote: Pitt came up with a lot of stuff. On Fight Club, [Se7en screenwriter] Andy Walker and I used to go to his house at seven in the morning to wake him up because he was always saying, ‘I think I need to do a little more work on the script.’ … Pitt came down one day in this ridiculous terry cloth pink robe that was covered with coffee cups, and he said, ‘I know you want one, but this is mine and Tyler Durden is wearing it.’
clippings.title: Sinnin’ Ain’t Easy: David Fincher on the lasting legacy of Se7en’s pervasive horror
clippings.context: Same Se7en anniversary interview, on Pitt shaping Tyler Durden in Fight Club.

clippings.speaker: Tom Hanks
clippings.quote: I must say, Meg and I are not real close pals. We see each other every now and again. It's like, we don't hang out for coffee. ... But when we pick up, we just pick up where we left off and it's an effortless thing that I don't think either one of us examines it too much because if we did, it'd be a problem.
clippings.title: 'You've Got Mail' Turns 25! Tom Hanks Explains 'Natural' Chemistry With Meg Ryan (Flashback)
clippings.context: From ET's 1998 press-tour interviews for You've Got Mail, republished from the vault for the film's 25th anniversary.

clippings.speaker: Tom Hanks
clippings.quote: I just go along for the ride. But it's like playing tennis with someone who's a better tennis player than you are. Now, maybe you can beat them if you're really on the game, but chances are, they're going to beat you. And so it just makes you better. Then afterwards you have a nice lunch.
clippings.title: 'You've Got Mail' Turns 25! Tom Hanks Explains 'Natural' Chemistry With Meg Ryan (Flashback)
clippings.context: Hanks on how acting opposite Ryan pushes him, from ET's 1998 You've Got Mail press interviews.

clippings.speaker: Tom Hanks
clippings.quote: I'm not quite sure really what makes her tick, and I think she kind of revels in the fact that I don't know what makes her tick. I think she protects that.
clippings.title: 'You've Got Mail' Turns 25! Tom Hanks Explains 'Natural' Chemistry With Meg Ryan (Flashback)
clippings.context: Said to ET at the You've Got Mail premiere in 1998.

clippings.speaker: Meg Ryan
