clippings.quote: He's a very inventive actor and really, really, really tries to find new things to do for every take. He really challenges himself. You know, Nora could be done 10 takes ago, and he'd still be trying new and equally great things.
clippings.title: 'You've Got Mail' Turns 25! Tom Hanks Explains 'Natural' Chemistry With Meg Ryan (Flashback)
clippings.context: Ryan on Hanks's work on set under Nora Ephron, from ET's 1998 You've Got Mail press interviews.

clippings.speaker: Meg Ryan
clippings.quote: He's just beyond being a generous person, he's just incredibly generous with his energy, with everyone, you know? Not just the actors in the movie, all the crew in the movie, the people on the street.
clippings.title: 'You've Got Mail' Turns 25! Tom Hanks Explains 'Natural' Chemistry With Meg Ryan (Flashback)
clippings.context: From ET's 1998 You've Got Mail press interviews.

clippings.speaker: Meg Ryan
clippings.quote: It was such a wonderful experience making that film with Tom. We all loved the script, we loved the story and we loved the time we all spent together. When there's so much love on a project, it doesn't really matter if the critics don't like.
clippings.title: Meg Ryan talks about love, directing, and the importance of having Tom Hanks for a friend
clippings.context: Talking to fans and reporters after an Ithaca screening at the Sonoma International Film Festival, March 2016.

clippings.speaker: Meg Ryan
clippings.quote: And Tom Hanks, he was so supportive. I literally could not have made this film without his involvement.
clippings.title: Meg Ryan talks about love, directing, and the importance of having Tom Hanks for a friend
clippings.context: At a post-screening interview at the Sonoma International Film Festival about her directorial debut, which Hanks acted in and produced.

clippings.speaker: Meg Ryan
clippings.quote: It took [Hanks] a day to [shoot his scene]. At the end of his time, he says to the crew, 'All right, gather 'round. Listen, I know we've gotten to know each other very well over the last 10 hours together, but I just want to thank you for being here for my friend Meg.' ... It was such an act of friendship. I love him so much.
clippings.title: Meg Ryan talks onscreen reunion with Tom Hanks: 'I love him so much'
clippings.context: TODAY quoting Ryan's Entertainment Weekly interview about Hanks's one-day cameo in Ithaca; original EW piece not located.

clippings.speaker: Walter Matthau
clippings.quote: How could you not be friendly with him? This man is amenable, delightful... Generous, no ego problem. He has no ego problem. This man is without an ego.
clippings.title: Encore Presentation: Jack Lemmon, Walter Matthau: Great Friends and Costars
clippings.context: Joint Larry King interview recorded July 3, 1997 while promoting Out to Sea, rebroadcast June 30, 2001; Matthau's reply is split across two of King's prompts.

clippings.speaker: Walter Matthau
clippings.quote: No, he's the perfectionist and I'm not, and we never clash.
clippings.title: Encore Presentation: Jack Lemmon, Walter Matthau: Great Friends and Costars
clippings.context: Same 1997 joint Larry King interview, when King asked which of them was the perfectionist.

clippings.speaker: Walter Matthau
clippings.quote: Yes, I think the magic is that he's neat and nifty and I'm slow and sloppy.
clippings.title: Encore Presentation: Jack Lemmon, Walter Matthau: Great Friends and Costars
clippings.context: Asked in the 1997 joint interview whether they sensed it was working right away on The Fortune Cookie; he then joked the reverse is true in real life.

clippings.speaker: Jack Lemmon
clippings.quote: we're on the same wave length when we work, obviously. We seem to think the same in comedy. In other words, what I think may be funny, Walter will probably think will be funny.
clippings.title: Encore Presentation: Jack Lemmon, Walter Matthau: Great Friends and Costars
clippings.context: Lemmon's answer when King asked what the magic between them was, in the 1997 joint interview.

clippings.speaker: Jack Lemmon
clippings.quote: When we get on that set, he's there. He's cold with the lines. I mean, he knows them cold and we're set and we go. And he's knocking it out from take one on or from the first read through.
clippings.title: Encore Presentation: Jack Lemmon, Walter Matthau: Great Friends and Costars
clippings.context: Lemmon pushing back on Matthau's self-effacing claim that he wasn't a perfectionist, 1997 joint interview.

clippings.speaker: Jack Lemmon
clippings.quote: Totally. It was like sitting down, as Carol was intimating I think. No acting showed. He would be the character, and he wasn't the same all the time.
clippings.title: Remembering Walter Matthau
clippings.context: Larry King tribute two weeks after Matthau's death, asked whether his rapport with Matthau came naturally.

clippings.speaker: Jack Lemmon
clippings.quote: Walter was nominated for best actor: not because of my direction, because I shut my mouth up and let him alone.
clippings.title: Remembering Walter Matthau
clippings.context: Same 2000 tribute, showing a set photo from Kotch, which Lemmon directed.

clippings.speaker: Gene Wilder
clippings.quote: I met Mel backstage in Anne's dressing room. He was wearing one of those pea coats, pea jackets that were made famous by the Merchant Marines. And I admired it, and he said, you know, they used to call this a urine jacket, but it didn't sell. And I laughed, and he laughed.
clippings.title: In This 2005 Interview, Gene Wilder Explains How He Learned To Get Laughs
clippings.context: Wilder to Terry Gross in 2005, rebroadcast after his death, on meeting Brooks while acting opposite Anne Bancroft.

clippings.speaker: Gene Wilder
clippings.quote: And then when I met him, there was a closeness because I loved that kind of humor, his kind of humor. It wasn't any part of my life, in my humor, but I just appreciated it. There was an affinity there somewhere. And in so many ways we're not at all alike, and in some ways we're very much alike.
clippings.title: In This 2005 Interview, Gene Wilder Explains How He Learned To Get Laughs
clippings.context: Wilder to Terry Gross in 2005 on admiring Brooks's writing for Your Show of Shows before they met.

clippings.speaker: Gene Wilder
clippings.quote: He said, are you crazy? This is frivolous. You're just being frivolous. Well, my temperature rose, and after 20 minutes or so of arguing, my color went from red to, I think, blue or purple. I was - started screaming and then all of a sudden, he said, OK, it's in. And I said, well, why did you put me through this? And he said, I wasn't sure if it was right.
clippings.title: In This 2005 Interview, Gene Wilder Explains How He Learned To Get Laughs
clippings.context: Wilder to Terry Gross in 2005 on their one fight, over the "Puttin' On The Ritz" number.

clippings.speaker: Mel Brooks
clippings.quote: I've been very close to Gene all our adult lives, and I knew. First of all, he was a brave guy.
clippings.title: Mel Brooks Salutes 'Magnificent' Gene Wilder, Spills Secrets of 'Young Frankenstein' — Including the Classic Scene That Was Almost Cut and the Upcoming Musical Reboot (Exclusive)
clippings.context: Brooks interviewed days after Wilder's death in August 2016.

clippings.speaker: Mel Brooks
clippings.quote: He was incredible in my first movie, The Producers. He had that blue blanket — hysterical. It was just amazing — nobody else in the world could have done that.
clippings.title: Mel Brooks Salutes 'Magnificent' Gene Wilder, Spills Secrets of 'Young Frankenstein' — Including the Classic Scene That Was Almost Cut and the Upcoming Musical Reboot (Exclusive)
clippings.context: Brooks naming his favorite Wilder performance.

clippings.speaker: Mel Brooks
clippings.quote: So we went back and argued, and I said, ‘Look, Gene Wilder insists!’ I blamed it on Gene, but it was really me.
clippings.title: Mel Brooks Salutes 'Magnificent' Gene Wilder, Spills Secrets of 'Young Frankenstein' — Including the Classic Scene That Was Almost Cut and the Upcoming Musical Reboot (Exclusive)
clippings.context: Brooks on fighting Columbia to shoot Young Frankenstein in black and white.

clippings.speaker: Mel Brooks
clippings.quote: And I called Gene, and I said, you're absolutely right all the time, and I'm glad we're - it's in, totally.
clippings.title: A 'Fresh Air' Halloween treat: Revisiting 'Young Frankenstein'
clippings.context: Brooks to David Bianculli in 2013, rebroadcast in 2025, on conceding the "Puttin' On The Ritz" scene after seeing it cut in.

clippings.speaker: Michael Palin
clippings.quote: A few years after my father died, John Cleese, who had known him, told me he was writing a new film in which one member of a desperately dysfunctional gang of crooks had a stutter. He asked if I could help him understand how a stutter worked and where it came from.
clippings.title: The King's Speech
clippings.context: Palin's own blog post on stammering, recalling how Cleese brought him the character of Ken Pile.

clippings.speaker: John Cleese
clippings.quote: Oh, much more famous, especially more famous than Michael Palin. (laughs) Mike Palin is a charming guy, just, there's not much talent. Oh, no, no, no, he doesn't have the fame, but that's because he doesn't have the talent. (laughs)
clippings.title: Extended transcript: John Cleese
clippings.context: Cleese teasing his old friend after the interviewer called him arguably the most famous Python.

clippings.speaker: John Cleese
clippings.quote: Michael is just the same, sweet, kind, slightly boring man.
clippings.title: Michael Palin says John Cleese "couldn't have done without" him in ongoing 'Monty Python' feud
clippings.context: Said on Zoe Ball's BBC Radio 2 Breakfast Show after Palin's 81st birthday dinner, as reported by NME.

clippings.speaker: Michael Palin
clippings.quote: You go back to Python, and I always played the boring character, but John couldn't have done without me. You had to have someone selling the parrot, or someone in the argument sketch to play off. So I think I'm going to continue to bask in John's compliment that I'm boring.
clippings.title: Michael Palin says John Cleese "couldn't have done without" him in ongoing 'Monty Python' feud
clippings.context: Palin's reply on ITV's This Morning to Cleese calling him boring, as reported by NME.

clippings.speaker: John Cleese
clippings.quote: He's terribly boring. Lorraine. He's the most boring man I've ever met in my life but he's so nice you forgive him. You'd forgive him anything.
clippings.title: John Cleese calls Michael Palin 'the most boring man I've met in my life'
clippings.context: Said on ITV's Lorraine after Cleese, Palin and Terry Gilliam dined together for Palin's 81st birthday.

clippings.speaker: Michael Palin
clippings.quote: I'm generally a conciliator. I don't seek arguments, I don't seek opposition. Some do it very well; John does it very well. John thrives on argument. He's very, very good at arguing, I'm not really.
clippings.title: Michael Palin responds to Monty Python co-star John Cleese calling him 'boring'
clippings.context: Said on The Louis Theroux Podcast, responding to Cleese's remark that Palin put all his effort into being affable.

clippings.speaker: Michael Palin
clippings.quote: I have done things that John doesn't much like. Me and my wife were friends with all of John's ex-wives and John didn't much like this. … I think that sometimes he probably looks at my life and says, 'I wish I didn't have all these complications and could be like Michael, looking at things in a sort of detached way'. But that's not John.
clippings.title: Michael Palin reveals strain in John Cleese relationship over ex-wives
clippings.context: Palin speaking to The Times about staying warm friends with Cleese, as reported by the Express.

clippings.speaker: Emmanuel Lubezki
clippings.quote: Terry came to me and he said, ‘Chivo, please don’t read the script.’ The script was very, very long. … He wanted me to document this as if it was somebody’s memory. That’s it, we never talked about anything else.
clippings.title: Emmanuel Lubezki on ‘The Revenant’ and ‘Knight of Cups’
clippings.context: Interview after his third straight Oscar, on shooting Knight of Cups without reading the script.

clippings.speaker: Emmanuel Lubezki
clippings.quote: The only way I have to know if we’re getting the scene or not, I’d turn sometimes to Terry and see if I could get a feeling from his expression.
clippings.title: Emmanuel Lubezki on ‘The Revenant’ and ‘Knight of Cups’
clippings.context: On the fun and fear of shooting scenes without knowing the script.

clippings.speaker: Emmanuel Lubezki
clippings.quote: That only tells me how incredible Terry is, because he’s so daring. This is a crazy experiment in a way – not crazy, I wouldn’t say crazy. It’s a wonderful experiment.
clippings.title: Emmanuel Lubezki on ‘The Revenant’ and ‘Knight of Cups’
clippings.context: Responding to the idea that Knight of Cups feels like the work of a much younger filmmaker.

clippings.speaker: Emmanuel Lubezki
clippings.quote: I think some of the Terry DNA must have come out because I’m his pupil, he’s my teacher.
clippings.title: Emmanuel Lubezki on ‘The Revenant’ and ‘Knight of Cups’
clippings.context: On how working with Malick prepared him for shooting Iñárritu's The Revenant.

clippings.speaker: Emmanuel Lubezki
clippings.quote: Working with Terry, sometimes I can shoot a whole day and not know if there’s anything that’s going to be usable. … That can sometimes be frustrating but ultimately it’s rewarding because it allows for the special or spontaneous moment, and Terry also encourages me to take risks.
clippings.title: Contender: Director of Photography Emmanuel Lubezki, The Tree of Life
clippings.context: Awards-season trade profile on shooting The Tree of Life; the two joke that each day is a fishing trip.

clippings.speaker: Emmanuel Lubezki
clippings.quote: You learn so much by watching an artist like Terry at work. … For me, he has been an extraordinary film teacher and much more.
clippings.title: Cosmic Questions
clippings.context: From American Cinematographer's August 2011 Tree of Life cover story, excerpted with credit by Cinephilia & Beyond (the ASC page itself was blocked).

clippings.speaker: Kevin Williamson
clippings.quote: So, here is the director of the movie, in the middle of his stressful, busy first day giving this novice kid from Goose Creek a master class in building tension.
clippings.title: 'Scream' Writer Kevin Williamson Pens Tribute to Wes Craven: He Gave Me "a Master Class in Building Tension"
clippings.context: From Williamson's written tribute after Craven's death, recalling the first day of shooting Drew Barrymore's opening scene; quoted by Out from THR.

clippings.speaker: Kevin Williamson
clippings.quote: Scream changed my life forever… Knowing Wes Craven changed my life forever. I am grateful. I am blessed.
clippings.title: 'Scream' Writer Kevin Williamson Pens Tribute to Wes Craven: He Gave Me "a Master Class in Building Tension"
clippings.context: Closing lines of Williamson's THR tribute to Craven, as quoted by Out.

clippings.speaker: Kevin Williamson
clippings.quote: I got to pick the brain of Wes Craven. Not just that, I had a really long relationship and really great friendship. He was a mentor and friend to me and also a co-conspirator for many years. So I got my dream, my dream did come true.
clippings.title: Scream Writer Kevin Williamson Reflects on the Franchise's Legacy and Connecting With Fans
clippings.context: Asked for the 25th anniversary which filmmaker he would have wanted to learn from.

clippings.speaker: Kevin Williamson
clippings.quote: Wes created a very family environment. You felt like you were safe, and that you were with your uncle or your father or somebody.
clippings.title: Your Favorite Scary Movie: The Oral History of 'Scream'
clippings.context: Williamson in The Ringer's 25th-anniversary oral history, on the atmosphere of the 1996 shoot.

clippings.speaker: Wes Craven
clippings.quote: Scream is a great example of something that is very innovative and has drawn top talent, inspired by great scripts written by Kevin. It has allowed me to do some of my best work and most popular work. Kevin is a great writer, and I love doing his material.
clippings.title: Constant Craven: The Franchise that Doesn't Die (Unlike Everyone In It)
clippings.context: Craven interviewed by Steven Prigge ahead of Scream 4, asked whether he had grown to enjoy horror.

clippings.speaker: Wes Craven
clippings.quote: It was the result of Kevin's original master script, and Ehren did a decent amount of work on specific scenes and areas of it. I also wrote sections of the film myself. But, it very much is Kevin's concept, characters, situations and over-arcing framework for the film.
clippings.title: Wes Craven Interview SCREAM 4
clippings.context: At the Scream 4 press day, responding to talk of Ehren Kruger's rewrites of Williamson's script.

clippings.speaker: Wes Craven
clippings.quote: When we were shooting the ending sequence in a house in Santa Rosa, every time the sun set, Neve and I would go outside for five minutes and watch the sunset together. I think we sort of felt like, ‘This is where you find your calm.'
clippings.title: Interview: Neve Campbell
clippings.context: Craven recalling the Scream shoot for a Rolling Stone profile of Campbell during the Scream 2 era; the reporter's attribution "recalls director Wes Craven" is cut from the middle.

clippings.speaker: Wes Craven
clippings.quote: I think Neve runs very, very deep, … and is incredibly physically strong, so she can deal with the really killing schedule that she is on.
clippings.title: Interview: Neve Campbell
clippings.context: Craven on Campbell in the same 1997 Rolling Stone profile, while she juggled Party of Five and the Scream films; "he adds" attribution cut.

clippings.speaker: Wes Craven
clippings.quote: Neve tried to think of one clever line after another to replace that, … I said, ‘Well, just say it once.'
clippings.title: Interview: Neve Campbell
clippings.context: Craven on Campbell resisting Sidney's mean "I'd get Tori Spelling" line in Scream, from the 1997 Rolling Stone profile.

clippings.speaker: Neve Campbell
clippings.quote: Wes has a really great eye and ear, and taste in people, with the casting, writing and all the people who get involved in the film. He’s also just phenomenal with timing, humor and scaring people.
clippings.title: Neve Campbell, Courteney Cox and David Arquette Interview SCREAM 4
clippings.context: Campbell at the Scream 4 press day, asked what keeps Craven's sequels scary.

clippings.speaker: Neve Campbell
clippings.quote: My life wouldn’t be what it is without him. I will be forever grateful for his brilliant direction, his wicked sense of humor and his consummate kindness and friendship.
clippings.title: Neve Campbell, Courteney Cox Remember Horror Master Wes Craven
clippings.context: Campbell's statement after Craven's death in August 2015; Moviefone quotes the statement she gave to Entertainment Weekly.

clippings.speaker: Neve Campbell
clippings.quote: Wes was a master. He was the best with this genre. Well, with other genres as well, but just a phenomenal talent and amazing energy and a father figure to us.
clippings.title: Scream's Neve Campbell And David Arquette Reminisce About Working With Wes Craven - Exclusive
clippings.context: Campbell on making the 2022 Scream, the first in the series without Craven.

clippings.speaker: Neve Campbell
clippings.quote: He would sort of glide onto set, and sit down, and get behind the monitor, and you would do these horrific things, and you would just hear [laughter].
clippings.title: Neve Campbell Remembers Wes Craven: "He Just Loved Making Movies"
clippings.context: Campbell on Craven's twisted sense of humor on the Scream set; originally said on a podcast interview (The Evolution of Horror's Hello Sidney), reported by HorrorGeekLife.

clippings.speaker: Willem Dafoe
clippings.quote: Robert had so much stuff to give me and he pretty much turned me on to everything I needed
clippings.title: Robert Eggers and Willem Dafoe on The Lighthouse
clippings.context: Joint London interview; Dafoe on how Eggers's period research fed his preparation for Thomas Wake.

clippings.speaker: Robert Eggers
clippings.quote: It builds your confidence when Willem Dafoe sees The Witch and his team contacts you for a meeting and says 'I want to be in whatever you're doing next'
clippings.title: Robert Eggers and Willem Dafoe on The Lighthouse
clippings.context: Eggers recalls how their collaboration began after Dafoe saw The Witch.

clippings.speaker: Robert Eggers
clippings.quote: Dafoe comes from the theater, and has more energy than my one-year-old son. He can bring it all fucking day long in rehearsals and then go 25-percent more when we're shooting.
clippings.title: Drunken Sailors and Movie Stars: Robert Eggers on Making 'The Lighthouse'
clippings.context: Eggers on rehearsing The Lighthouse with Dafoe and Robert Pattinson.

clippings.speaker: Willem Dafoe
clippings.quote: I thought that this guy's the full package. I mean, besides seeing ‘The Witch,’ you get this beautiful script, you get this beautiful set to work in and the shots are constructed so beautifully.
clippings.title: Before 'Nosferatu,' Robert Eggers Recalls Almost Getting Willem Dafoe Set on Fire
clippings.context: Joint Nosferatu interview; Dafoe looks back on their first collaboration.

clippings.speaker: Robert Eggers
clippings.quote: Why wouldn't you want to continue to work with one of the greatest actors of all time?
clippings.title: Before 'Nosferatu,' Robert Eggers Recalls Almost Getting Willem Dafoe Set on Fire
clippings.context: Asked whether The Lighthouse felt like the start of a long partnership.

clippings.speaker: Willem Dafoe
clippings.quote: I want to try to be that guy that he thinks I am. But it's a mutual respect and he inspires me terrifically. And not just his way of working and what he does, but his character, where creating this stuff fits into his life.
clippings.title: Before 'Nosferatu,' Robert Eggers Recalls Almost Getting Willem Dafoe Set on Fire
clippings.context: Dafoe responding to Eggers calling him one of the greatest actors of all time.

clippings.speaker: Robert Eggers
clippings.quote: Different actors need different things. I know what Willem needs. And I knew that some people needed a more complete backstory for the kind of work that they do to get into the character.
clippings.title: Before 'Nosferatu,' Robert Eggers Recalls Almost Getting Willem Dafoe Set on Fire
clippings.context: On why he didn't share his Nosferatu backstory novella with Dafoe.

clippings.speaker: Nora Ephron
clippings.quote: Well, Meg can do everything. Meg is both funny and smart, and you rarely get that in one person. She's a brilliantly gifted actress. She really is.
clippings.title: Nora Ephron | Academy of Achievement
clippings.context: Ephron, asked in her Academy of Achievement interview in Washington, D.C., why she kept casting Ryan.

clippings.speaker: Nora Ephron
clippings.quote: We had a read-through, and Billy Crystal and Meg Ryan read the script, and at the end of the read-through, Meg said, ‘You know, I think this scene would be much funnier if it took place in a restaurant,’ … and then Meg said, ‘And then I think at the end of the scene, she should have an orgasm,’
clippings.title: Nora Ephron | Academy of Achievement
clippings.context: Ephron explaining how Ryan reshaped the famous Katz's Deli scene at the read-through.

clippings.speaker: Nora Ephron
clippings.quote: And you know, you hear an idea like that, and you think, ‘I am so lucky to be working with these people.’ Thank God people believe in collaboration.
clippings.title: Nora Ephron | Academy of Achievement
clippings.context: Ephron's reaction to Ryan's (and Crystal's and Reiner's) ideas for the orgasm scene.

clippings.speaker: Meg Ryan
clippings.quote: She was very prepared. Her love of creating was contagious … The set felt like going to a great dinner party. You just didn't want to leave.
clippings.title: Meg Ryan Honors Late Rom-Com Legend Nora Ephron: 'So Many Blessings in My Life Because of Her' (Exclusive)
clippings.context: Ryan to People while promoting What Happens Later, which she dedicated to Ephron; two consecutive quoted sentences joined.

clippings.speaker: Meg Ryan
clippings.quote: Almost the whole time, I thought about her. I am so grateful to her in general. … This is a piece of work that says, ‘I was paying attention, lady, and thank you because my life is full of blessings.’
clippings.title: Meg Ryan on Dedicating Her First Movie in Eight Years to Nora Ephron
clippings.context: Ryan on why What Happens Later ends with a dedication to Ephron.

clippings.speaker: Meg Ryan
clippings.quote: She had pure delight on a movie set, and now I understand that. I also understand she was tough, and she had a way of being in the world of Hollywood — very intellectual and stern — sometimes to get what she wanted.
clippings.title: Meg Ryan on what romance means to her — and why her new movie isn't really a rom-com
clippings.context: Ryan on All Things Considered, reflecting on Ephron after directing her own film.

clippings.speaker: Meg Ryan
clippings.quote: I think it shares some DNA with some of the movies Nora did. In her movies, she had a belief in kismet and destiny.
clippings.title: 'What Happens Later' co-stars Meg Ryan and David Duchovny talk about rom-coms, fame and Nora
clippings.context: Ryan in an AP joint interview with David Duchovny, on the airport voice in What Happens Later.

clippings.speaker: Ridley Scott
clippings.quote: And coming in, I had a very good run with Hans. We had done some good stuff. So with Hans I said, ‘There’s this guy called Baaba Maal…’
clippings.title: 'Black Hawk Down': When Ridley Scott Went To War
clippings.context: Scott, revisiting Black Hawk Down, on what he asked of Zimmer for the score.

clippings.speaker: Ridley Scott
clippings.quote: So Baaba and Hans and I sat in a Sony room and Baaba would say, ‘Okay, run it.’ … Now, Hans is very much a prepared, orchestral, knowledgeable musician and composer but Baaba was much more of a ‘from the hip’ musician, because that’s how he functions.
clippings.title: 'Black Hawk Down': When Ridley Scott Went To War
clippings.context: Scott describing the scoring sessions with Zimmer and Senegalese singer Baaba Maal.

clippings.speaker: Hans Zimmer
clippings.quote: And I woke up to Ridley being right in the guy's face, 'Don't you ever talk to my composer like this.' And you know how those little things give you a sense of a bonding experience.
clippings.title: Ray Colcord Interviews Hans Zimmer
clippings.context: Zimmer recalls fainting after a producer berated him at a Black Rain preview, their first film together.

clippings.speaker: Hans Zimmer
clippings.quote: Then Ridley [Scott] came in, and he was going, ‘I don't know about this.’ He literally said, and this was on a Friday, he said, ‘Let me come back on Monday.’ … Monday I played him the main theme. He actually added a scene at the beginning of the movie because he loved that tune so much.
clippings.title: Composer Hans Zimmer On The Questions That Drive Him [Interview]
clippings.context: Zimmer on the pressure of writing the Thelma & Louise main theme.

clippings.speaker: Hans Zimmer
clippings.quote: Somehow Ridley Scott and his Gladiator made it possible for me to just play again and so on a strictly personal level, Gladiator was a great way of rediscovering my joy in music.
clippings.title: Hans Zimmer and the Gladiator
clippings.context: Interview with Ian Lace; Zimmer says Gladiator restored his love of writing after The Thin Red Line.

clippings.speaker: Hans Zimmer
clippings.quote: All those sequences, all the action music was written before Ridley had finished shooting. Part of it was written on the battlefield. Ridley would cut the film at my Lilly Yard Studio so we were actually 'joined at the hip' every day.
clippings.title: Hans Zimmer and the Gladiator
clippings.context: Same interview, on writing the battle music while Scott was still shooting.

clippings.speaker: Hans Zimmer
clippings.quote: I would somehow figure out what would help Ridley to be poetic, because I know that’s what he wants to do.
clippings.title: Hollywood Masters: Hans Zimmer
clippings.context: Zimmer at LMU's Hollywood Masters series, calling Scott a painter and a poet.

clippings.speaker: Samuel L. Jackson
clippings.quote: He told me, ‘Hopefully you’ll be able to find a character that, when you make bad movies and they don’t make any money, you can always go back to this character everybody loves,’ … ‘He said, ‘Arnold’s got Terminator. Sylvester’s got Rocky and Rambo. I’ve got John McClane.’ I’m like, ‘Oh, okay,’’ … ‘And it didn’t occur to me until I got that Nick Fury role — and I had a nine-picture deal to be Nick Fury — that, ‘Oh, I’m doing what Bruce said,’
clippings.title: Samuel L. Jackson Shares The Honest Advice Bruce Willis Gave Him About Movies
clippings.context: Jackson recalling advice Willis gave him on the Die Hard With a Vengeance set, from a Vanity Fair tribute for Willis' 70th birthday, as reported by HuffPost.

clippings.speaker: Samuel L. Jackson
clippings.quote: Bruce and I have been around together for quite a bit, so… it was kind of easy for us to kind of listen to Night and look at each other and go, ‘ Yeah , wait till this kid finds out.’
clippings.title: An Oral History of Unbreakable With M. Night Shyamalan and Samuel L. Jackson
clippings.context: Jackson on how he and Willis, as veterans, handled the young Shyamalan's line readings on Unbreakable.

clippings.speaker: Samuel L. Jackson
clippings.quote: It looked kind of like Bruce, but Bruce hadn't started shaving his head yet and this guy had no hair,’ … ‘I was like, ‘Hmm, could it be?’ Then I heard his voice and said, 'It is Bruce.'‘ … ’And Bruce went, 'Sam, there's this guy who's writing a script for us.'
clippings.title: A Chance Meeting Between Bruce Willis And Samuel L. Jackson Set The Stage For Unbreakable
clippings.context: Jackson recalling running into Willis in a Moroccan casino, which led to Unbreakable; from EW's 15th-anniversary oral history, quoted by SlashFilm.

clippings.speaker: Bruce Willis
clippings.quote: I was in a casino in Marrakech, in Morocco, and I saw this guy and I said, 'Somebody over there is trying to impersonate Sam Jackson.'
clippings.title: A Chance Meeting Between Bruce Willis And Samuel L. Jackson Set The Stage For Unbreakable
clippings.context: Willis's side of the chance casino meeting that put Jackson in Unbreakable; from EW's oral history, quoted by SlashFilm.

clippings.speaker: Bruce Willis
clippings.quote: I talked to [Shyamalan] over the holidays, and he is still thinking about doing the fight movie between me and Sam that we were going to do,
clippings.title: Bruce Willis says M. Night Shyamalan ‘Still Thinking’ About ‘Unbreakable 2’
clippings.context: Willis to MTV News on a possible Unbreakable sequel pitting his hero against Jackson's villain; reposted by a fan site.

clippings.speaker: Bruce Willis
clippings.quote: As long as Sam can make it, I’m up for it,
clippings.title: Bruce Willis says M. Night Shyamalan ‘Still Thinking’ About ‘Unbreakable 2’
clippings.context: Willis to MTV News, conditioning an Unbreakable sequel on Jackson's availability; reposted by a fan site.

clippings.speaker: Dante Spinotti
clippings.quote: When I work with Michael Mann, Michael is usually very keen on his camera angles. Very rarely, if I step in, was I consulted about where or what kind of lens to use in how to do a shot. Sometimes, it happens.
clippings.title: Dante Spinotti on Michael Mann’s Preparedness, Remastering Classics, and New Technologies
clippings.context: Interviewed at Camerimage, Spinotti describes how the division of labor works on a Mann set.

clippings.speaker: Dante Spinotti
clippings.quote: I know Michael very well. We are friends and have been friends for a long, long time. Michael is, for sure, the kind of director who, if you agree with him and understand what he has in mind to do, you can work with him. If you are someone who discusses or does disagree, you better not do that.
clippings.title: Dante Spinotti on Michael Mann’s Preparedness, Remastering Classics, and New Technologies
clippings.context: Asked about Mann's famous sense of control, Spinotti describes their friendship and how to work with him.

clippings.speaker: Dante Spinotti
clippings.quote: I always found, even when I did my first movie with Michael… the way I describe it is that, for me, coming from Italy and some good television, he was like finding a way of making movies that maybe I dreamed of, in my mind, but that I actually never worked on. … He was great, and I have always highly admired him; I learned a lot from Michael Mann.
clippings.title: Dante Spinotti on Michael Mann’s Preparedness, Remastering Classics, and New Technologies
clippings.context: Spinotti recalls arriving from Italy to shoot Manhunter, his first film with Mann.

clippings.speaker: Dante Spinotti
clippings.quote: At some point, Michael turned to me and said, ‘Dante, why did you turn this up in the forest?’ I said, ‘Michael, that is the sun.’ He hadn’t realized that the sun was up!
clippings.title: Dante Spinotti on Michael Mann’s Preparedness, Remastering Classics, and New Technologies
clippings.context: Spinotti's anecdote about dimming tungsten lights up with the dawn during a night exterior with Magua.

clippings.speaker: Dante Spinotti
clippings.quote: I think the allure for Michael Mann, and obviously for myself, was to be able to shoot this period film in a very modern, agile, aggressive and, I think, dynamic camera style.
clippings.title: Michael Mann Takes a Shot in the Dark With Public Enemies
clippings.context: Spinotti on why he and Mann shot their 1930s gangster film on Sony F23 digital cameras.

clippings.speaker: Michael Mann
clippings.quote: If people are as ambitious as you are, you keep them close to you. … Cinematographer Dante Spinotti and I have done five movies together.
clippings.title: The Study of Mann
clippings.context: Asked by F.X. Feeney how he assembles his recurring team, Mann names Spinotti among his longtime collaborators.

clippings.speaker: Keanu Reeves
clippings.quote: One day I got an email from Lana, ‘How’s it going? I’m thinking about…’ And I was like, ‘What!?’ Then, it was a conversation—she shared with me some of what was happening with her personally, and what had brought her to a place of telling a story with The Matrix. And she asked me how I would feel about it. ‘YES.’ On these films, with Lana, it’s ‘YES.’
clippings.title: It was a “YES” when Keanu Reeves was asked to return to The Matrix
clippings.context: Q&A ahead of The Matrix Resurrections' release, on being asked back to play Neo.

clippings.speaker: Keanu Reeves
clippings.quote: So, my experience [of the trilogy] was with her behind a monitor, now she’s in front—of course, she’ll reference the monitor. Her evolution as a filmmaker is extraordinary. So, what we have now is an artist who’s interested in natural light, who wants to be next to the camera and literally connects herself to the camera and becomes this other thing, which I’ve never seen before.
clippings.title: It was a “YES” when Keanu Reeves was asked to return to The Matrix
clippings.context: Same Q&A, asked how Lana had evolved as a filmmaker since the original trilogy.

clippings.speaker: Keanu Reeves
clippings.quote: You can go to either of them and ask a question and much more often than not they’ll agree and tell you the same thing. They are independent and together.
clippings.title: Filmmaking Wachowski brothers hide in the shadows of ‘The Matrix’
clippings.context: Profile of the then-press-shy Wachowskis at the release of The Matrix Reloaded; Reeves speaks of the two siblings together.

clippings.speaker: Keanu Reeves
clippings.quote: They’re one of the most sensitive people I’ve ever met.
clippings.title: Filmmaking Wachowski brothers hide in the shadows of ‘The Matrix’
clippings.context: Same 2003 profile; Reeves describing the Wachowski siblings as almost a single person.

clippings.speaker: Lana Wachowski
clippings.quote: We showed the film to Keanu, and he really was blown away by it, and he said something that was typically Keanu, where it’s incredibly insightful. He’s just sort of sitting there, and you don’t expect some incredible revelation to come out of him at that moment, like casual brilliance just kind of rolls off of Keanu.
clippings.title: The Matrix 4 “Describes the Next 20 Years of Digital Life”
clippings.context: Said on a panel at the Berlin International Literature Festival with co-writers Aleksandar Hemon and David Mitchell, reported by Den of Geek.

clippings.speaker: Lana Wachowski
clippings.quote: How do you tell an actor that they’re going to have to spend four months training and learning Kung Fu when they could make another movie in that same time? That’s what impressed us about Keanu. He understood why it was necessary and the dedication it required.
clippings.title: The Making of The Matrix
clippings.context: Joint statement credited to both Wachowskis (Lana then credited as Larry) in the studio's 1999 production notes.

clippings.speaker: Lana Wachowski
clippings.quote: Keanu did some amazing work in this scene which included 6 hours every morning of prosthetic makeup. And he had to sit in a freezing cold vat of goo for another six hours..
clippings.title: Chat Transcript: Wachowski Brothers
clippings.context: Live online chat during a screening of The Matrix; answers are credited jointly to 'WachowskiBros', commenting on the pod scene.

clippings.speaker: Kurt Russell
clippings.quote: I love working with John. He is a heralded filmmaker but he’s also very underrated, in my opinion. I’ve always felt people don’t quite understand what he does. He’s funny. He sees the world differently, and I’ll always love working with him.
clippings.title: Kurt Russell: The Hollywood Interview
clippings.context: Alex Simon's career interview with Russell, around the release of The Art of the Steal.

clippings.speaker: Kurt Russell
clippings.quote: John and I are not tremendously communicative... I mean, I talk more than he does. He's pretty quiet. He says things pretty concisely, but he's so damn much fun and he's such a good thinker. It's always fun to do a show and you're always doing a show with John, not just a movie.
clippings.title: AICN Legends: Quint chats up Kurt Russell about everything from Walt Disney to John Carpenter!
clippings.context: Long breakfast interview with Quint covering Russell's career, here on how the two first clicked on Elvis.

clippings.speaker: Kurt Russell
clippings.quote: John just did that so easily. I look back on that and think ‘Man, John had guts.’ He was stuck!
clippings.title: AICN Legends: Quint chats up Kurt Russell about everything from Walt Disney to John Carpenter!
clippings.context: Russell on Carpenter coming aboard Elvis after Russell had already been cast in the title role.

clippings.speaker: Kurt Russell
clippings.quote: That's one of the cool things about our relationship. We always said ‘Only if you see it. We'll only do the ones we see together.’ There were a couple of things that I took to him and he kinda went ‘Nope.’
clippings.title: AICN Legends: Quint chats up Kurt Russell about everything from Walt Disney to John Carpenter!
clippings.context: Russell on how he and Carpenter decide which projects to make together.

clippings.speaker: John Carpenter
clippings.quote: They were uncertain about Kurt as a hero. They said, ‘Well, he’s just this Disney kid.’ I said, ‘No, no, no. He can play this. He can play anything. Believe me, he can play anything. He played Elvis, he can play Snake Plissken.’
clippings.title: ‘Escape From New York’: My Interview with John Carpenter
clippings.context: David Weiner's interview, originally done for Famous Monsters magazine around the film's 35th anniversary, on the distributor's doubts about casting Russell.

clippings.speaker: John Carpenter
clippings.quote: There is no other Snake Plissken than Kurt. None.
clippings.title: FUCK ‘EM! I DON’T CARE: John Carpenter
clippings.context: Phone interview with Roel Haanen (April 2014), asked whether he could imagine another actor as Snake in a remake.

clippings.speaker: John Carpenter
clippings.quote: Kurt Russell had become somewhat of a draw. This would be in the early nineties, mid-nineties. He wanted to do an Escape sequel. He wanted to play that character again. [chuckles] So he conned me into writing the script, and it really wasn’t something that I was burning to do.
clippings.title: An interview with director John Carpenter
clippings.context: Tim Kelly interview; Carpenter on how the Escape from New York sequel came about.

clippings.speaker: John Carpenter
clippings.quote: No, we talked all the time! Just not about the character. There’s no need to talk about it. He knows what’s going on, I know what’s going on.
clippings.title: An interview with director John Carpenter
clippings.context: Carpenter, laughing, after saying he and Russell never discussed Snake's character on set.

clippings.speaker: David Fincher
clippings.quote: Sometimes I’d break Jeff off [on his own] and say, ‘Go across the street and find me a shot.’ I say this with humility: There aren’t a lot of people that I’d just [ask] to ‘go get me a shot.’ I’m not talking about trust so much as the knowledge that he wouldn’t need any handholding. I knew he’d come back with exactly what we needed.
clippings.title: Jeff Cronenweth, ASC: An Adventurous Eye
clippings.context: Fincher recalling Cronenweth operating on 2nd-unit reshoots for Seven, in an ASC career profile of the cinematographer.

clippings.speaker: David Fincher
clippings.quote: He might look at Fight Club as this big break, but I look at it as the natural evolution of what we were already doing. On Alien3, he and his father had been like one person.
clippings.title: Jeff Cronenweth, ASC: An Adventurous Eye
clippings.context: Fincher, calling Cronenweth "very humble," on handing him his first feature as cinematographer.

clippings.speaker: David Fincher
clippings.quote: I love when a cinematographer figures out a way to key someone without just setting a light and focusing it on them… The cinematographers I’ve always admired and worked with are very conscious of this. Jordan was excellent that way, and Jeff innately has that sensibility, too.
clippings.title: Jeff Cronenweth, ASC: An Adventurous Eye
clippings.context: Fincher comparing Jeff's lighting instincts to those of his father, Jordan Cronenweth.

clippings.speaker: Jeff Cronenweth
clippings.quote: Although I knew it would be rough, I had so much trust in David as a filmmaker that I had the confidence to do the film. He has such a distinct eye and is such a talented storyteller that the visuals in his films are always a collaboration in the truest sense.
clippings.title: Beyond The Frame: Fight Club
clippings.context: Retrospective drawing on AC's 1999 Fight Club feature, where Cronenweth discussed taking on his first feature with Fincher.

clippings.speaker: Jeff Cronenweth
clippings.quote: It would be tough for anybody to walk into a Fincher movie… When I met David in Zurich, he looked like he had been in a 12-round fight. He was beat just trying to keep up to the aesthetic level he was accustomed to; it was a lot of work.
clippings.film: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo
clippings.title: Fincher's SOS to d.p. gets quick reply
clippings.context: Cronenweth on replacing the original DP mid-shoot on The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo.

clippings.speaker: Jeff Cronenweth
clippings.quote: Truly, not much has changed other than the ability to sleep a little more comfortably. I think we have become more decisive and efficient, but that could be as much about the years we have collaborated together and experience as it could be from the transformation to digital capture–or more likely a combination of both.
clippings.title: Road To Oscar Prequel: Artists On "Gone Girl," "Birdman" Emerging As Awards Season Contenders
clippings.context: Asked how his working relationship with Fincher had evolved, during Gone Girl's awards campaign.

clippings.speaker: Jeff Cronenweth
clippings.quote: Even from a time when I was a camera assistant and had the opportunity to work with him a few times, aesthetically we saw eye to eye. We kind of share some of the same sensibilities and that made it really easy each time to discover what it is that particular film’s language would be…
clippings.title: An Interview with Jeff Cronenweth
clippings.context: Cronenweth on the partnership in a career interview.

clippings.speaker: Wes Anderson
clippings.quote: I sat in the corner, away from the table, and there was another person in that corner, who turned out to be Owen. During the entire class, we never once had a conversation. I wrote a play in that class and the next semester, it was produced, and I asked Owen to be in it.
clippings.title: Production notes from Bottle Rocket
clippings.context: Anderson recalls meeting Wilson in a University of Texas playwriting class, in the studio press notes for Bottle Rocket.

clippings.speaker: Wes Anderson
clippings.quote: Owen and I were roaming around, constantly doing things, but we weren't exactly focused. It was from that feeling that we started writing the film,
clippings.title: Production notes from Bottle Rocket
clippings.context: Anderson on how the unstructured end of college with Wilson became the seed of their first script.

clippings.speaker: Wes Anderson
clippings.quote: We were rehearsing a scene, and Owen was kind of mumbling and reading off the page and we had Gene Hackman there… [I said,] 'You're supposed to have it memorized.' Owen's like, 'I don't memorize before the rehearsal.' [I said,] 'What are you talking about?' [He said,] 'Wes, this is my seventh movie. This is the way I do it.' Somewhere around 'Anaconda,' he made a shift which I didn't even know about.
clippings.title: The Royal Tenenbaums
clippings.context: Anderson on rehearsing Wilson for The Royal Tenenbaums, five years after Bottle Rocket; SBIFF reprints the excerpt credited to latimes.com.

clippings.speaker: Wes Anderson
clippings.quote: As soon as Owen Wilson and I started making a movie, well, I wanted Owen to be involved with the other movies I would do.
clippings.title: This famous actor was Wes Anderson's roommate. Now he's one of the director's favorite actors
clippings.context: Anderson on keeping his early collaborators; the article cites it as told to Rolling Stone.

clippings.speaker: Owen Wilson
clippings.quote: My roommate in college in Austin, Texas, was Wes Anderson. Wes always wanted to be a director. I was an English major in college, and he got us to work on a screenplay together. And then, in working on the screenplay, he wanted my brother, Luke, and me to act in this thing.
clippings.title: Owen Wilson
clippings.context: Wilson, asked by Valentino's designers why he became an actor, credits Anderson.

clippings.speaker: Owen Wilson
clippings.quote: I think for Wes and me, the most important thing was James L. Brooks producing our first movie and giving us a chance to come to Hollywood… I think Wes and I could go to dinner tonight and spend the whole dinner thinking and talking about things that Jim has said to us over the years.
clippings.title: Owen Wilson
clippings.context: Wilson names the most important moment of his career, shared with Anderson.

clippings.speaker: Owen Wilson
clippings.quote: The Grand Budapest Hotel might be my favorite of Wes' movies; I really loved it. I thought that was so great, it would be fun to write something with Wes again, but you know, I have fun just going to dinner with him.
clippings.title: Owen Wilson: "You just go with it"
clippings.context: Asked whether he'd reignite their writing partnership, unused since The Royal Tenenbaums.

clippings.speaker: Lana Wachowski
clippings.quote: My brother quickly stepped in, ‘Look, just so we’re clear,’ he says, ‘if somebody asks something or says something about my sister that I don’t like, understand that I will break a bottle over their head.’ [applause] Few words express love clearer than these.
clippings.title: Lana Wachowski’s HRC Visibility Award Acceptance Speech (Transcript)
clippings.context: Lana's Human Rights Campaign Visibility Award speech, recalling a Cloud Atlas press interview soon after she came out; Lilly had not yet come out and is referred to as her brother.

clippings.speaker: Lana Wachowski
clippings.quote: And I would say, though, that as we’ve gotten older and we’ve met other teachers, and due to the kindness and generosity of my brother, we’ve agreed to do press recently on this movie for a lot of reasons.
clippings.title: Wachowskis, Tom Tykwer on ‘Cloud Atlas,’ ‘Matrix’ Sequels, and Out-of-Line Journalists (Q&A)
clippings.context: Joint Q&A with Tom Tykwer on why the siblings, who had avoided press since The Matrix, agreed to promote Cloud Atlas.

clippings.speaker: Lana Wachowski
clippings.quote: ‘When mom and dad passed, I went to [Lilly] and said, ‘Look, this idea came to me. I can see that it’s about me working with my grief, and I was thinking, do you want to work on it together?’’ … ‘That’s what grief does. Grief spirals us off in different directions… I wanted to go back and feel this thing again, and she wanted to go off and do this other thing.’
clippings.title: Matrix creator Lilly Wachowski shares agonising reason she turned down Resurrections
clippings.context: Lana at the San Francisco premiere of The Matrix Resurrections, as told to The Hollywood Reporter and relayed by PinkNews, on asking Lilly to co-direct.

clippings.speaker: Lilly Wachowski
clippings.quote: I’m out to my friends and family. Most people at work know too. Everyone is cool with it. Yes, thanks to my fabulous sister they’ve done it before, but also because they’re fantastic people.
clippings.title: Second Wachowski filmmaker sibling comes out as trans
clippings.context: Lilly's coming-out statement, given to Windy City Times four years after Lana came out.

clippings.speaker: Lilly Wachowski
clippings.quote: But for me, what makes ‘Bound’ unique and interesting is that it is the start of a conversation that me and my sister are having with ourselves, and that is apparent in the very first shot of the film — which is a closet. So, you begin to understand this idea of two closeted trans women making a film about wanting out.
clippings.title: ‘Matrix’ filmmaker Lilly Wachowski on making movies about trans identity and liberation
clippings.context: Interview ahead of a Chicago screening of Bound, the sisters' first film as writer-directors.

clippings.speaker: Lilly Wachowski
clippings.quote: ‘And so, like Lana made [Matrix Resurrections] for different reasons… I can’t speak for her, but that’s what I was feeling at the time.’
clippings.title: Matrix creator Lilly Wachowski shares agonising reason she turned down Resurrections
clippings.context: Lilly, at a Showtime TCA panel relayed by PinkNews, on why she sat out the sequel Lana directed alone.

clippings.speaker: Denis Villeneuve
clippings.quote: I remember having dinner alone with Hans, it was his birthday and we were alone in a Montreal restaurant. And I said Hans,  'I would love you to do the dual scoring' and he said, 'Denis this is my oldest dream. And I will say yes.' But he said, 'I'm just afraid that maybe it's a very dangerous idea to tackle your oldest dream. But let's try it.'
clippings.title: Interview: Denis Villeneuve Talks 'Dune', Assembling The Cast, Hans Zimmer's Score, Hopes For Part Two & More
clippings.context: Roundtable interview ahead of Dune's release, recalling how he asked Zimmer to score it.

clippings.speaker: Denis Villeneuve
clippings.quote: You know, when you put Hans Zimmer on the score, it always takes a lot of space. So there was a way to try and find a balance with sound design, and it was a beautiful artistic dance between the sound and music.
clippings.title: Interview: Denis Villeneuve Talks 'Dune', Assembling The Cast, Hans Zimmer's Score, Hopes For Part Two & More
clippings.context: Same roundtable, on blending Zimmer's music with the film's sound design.

clippings.speaker: Denis Villeneuve
clippings.quote: didn't hear from Hans for a long time. He took a long time to experiment.‘ Then, during editing, ’we started receiving tons of music for weeks. It was like a big creative rush. It became a storm. When the movie was totally finished, Hans was still sending me music.
clippings.title: Hans Zimmer on 'Dune' Score's Electronic Textures and Made-Up Language
clippings.context: Villeneuve speaking to Variety about how Zimmer's Dune score arrived during editing.

clippings.speaker: Hans Zimmer
clippings.quote: But when Denis very quietly asked me, there was something in the way he said had I ever read the book, that I knew he had made the same movie in his head that I was making in my head. And correct me if I'm wrong, but I think part of our process was that whenever we discussed things somehow, it was a full on conclusion that we felt the same way about certain things.
clippings.title: On The Scene: Denis Villeneuve & Hans Zimmer Talk 'Dune' at NYFF Q&A
clippings.context: Joint Q&A with Villeneuve at the New York Film Festival premiere of Dune.

clippings.speaker: Hans Zimmer
clippings.quote: And I think that it's pretty provocative, let's be honest, it's a pretty provocative score. Thank you Denis for letting me do this.
clippings.title: On The Scene: Denis Villeneuve & Hans Zimmer Talk 'Dune' at NYFF Q&A
clippings.context: Same NYFF Q&A, said to Villeneuve on stage.

clippings.speaker: Hans Zimmer
clippings.quote: You know those sort of dogs that get really excited? … I became one of those. He [Denis] never let me read the script because he wanted me to stay pure. He wanted one person who was like, I know the book, I know what this is all about, I know what the complications are as well of telling this story.
clippings.title: Hans Zimmer on Unearthing New Sounds for "Dune: Part Two"
clippings.context: MPA's The Credits interview on scoring Dune: Part Two; the article splits the quote with "Zimmer joked."

clippings.speaker: Jason Statham
clippings.quote: We have both come a long way since we started working together over 20 years ago. And what you really want to do in a situation like this is see if anything has changed, but the truth is that it hasn't. I fell in love with this profession thanks to a lottery ticket that Guy handed me called 'Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels'.
clippings.title: Jason Statham on working with Guy Ritchie on 'Wrath of Man'
clippings.context: IANSlife interview for the release of Wrath of Man, asked how it felt to work with Ritchie again.

clippings.speaker: Jason Statham
clippings.quote: I remember when we were shooting our first movie together and he pulled me into his room and told me to stop acting and just focus on saying my words. He just has this real way of getting out of you all the bad habits that actors can have.
clippings.film: Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels
clippings.title: Jason Statham on working with Guy Ritchie on 'Wrath of Man'
clippings.context: Same IANSlife interview, recalling Ritchie's direction on their first film.

clippings.speaker: Jason Statham
clippings.quote: If all I did for the rest of my career is work for Guy Ritchie, I would be a very happy man.
clippings.title: Jason Statham on working with Guy Ritchie on 'Wrath of Man'
clippings.context: Same IANSlife interview, asked whether he would take another Ritchie role.

clippings.speaker: Jason Statham
clippings.quote: The only difference is we're a little older and a little chubbier ... He called me up about this idea that he had. It was a very short pitch and I liked the premise. And I was quick to say 'yes,'
clippings.title: Guy Ritchie back working with Jason Statham for 'Wrath of Man'
clippings.context: Reuters interview on reuniting with Ritchie 16 years after Revolver.

clippings.speaker: Guy Ritchie
clippings.quote: I thought this would be the perfect story for Jason and I to be reunited on. It's not funny, this film. It's serious and the theme is serious and it's very violent, very aggressive. But I thought it'd be the perfect role for Jason to occupy,
clippings.title: Guy Ritchie back working with Jason Statham for 'Wrath of Man'
clippings.context: Reuters interview on why he brought Statham back for Wrath of Man.

clippings.speaker: Guy Ritchie
clippings.quote: Jason is one of my most favorite people in the entire world.
clippings.title: Guy Ritchie on Why He Loves 'Grumpy' Jason Statham
clippings.context: Yahoo Movies interview during the King Arthur: Legend of the Sword press tour.

clippings.speaker: Guy Ritchie
clippings.quote: He's grumpy, and he's one of the few grumpy people that doesn't annoy me in any way.
clippings.title: Guy Ritchie on Why He Loves 'Grumpy' Jason Statham
clippings.context: Same Yahoo Movies interview, on their friendship.

clippings.speaker: Park Chan-wook
clippings.quote: in a situation where you can imagine I'd find myself very lonely; to have somebody I was very close to was a very reassuring thing. … I had to rely on Chung-hoon.
clippings.title: Interview: Park Chan-Wook Talks STOKER
clippings.context: Park on having Chung beside him for his first English-language film, in a New York interview with The Lady Miz Diva.

clippings.speaker: Park Chan-wook
clippings.quote: to have somebody who I've been collaborating with for a long time, especially when I find myself on a film set where everything had to happen at a much faster pace, I had to have somebody who I was familiar with; we know each other very well. If it wasn't for that fact, I wouldn't have been able to finish this film in the 40-day shoot that it was.
clippings.title: Interview: Park Chan-Wook Talks STOKER
clippings.context: Same interview: Park on why Chung mattered creatively on the fast Hollywood shoot.

clippings.speaker: Park Chan-wook
clippings.quote: Ever since I made Oldboy, I worked with the same cinematographer. Even though we are not co-writing the script, we talk a lot about the story, and from the step of making the storyboard, we are always together.
clippings.title: Interview with Park Chan-wook
clippings.context: Park, interviewed at the Brussels International Fantastic Film Festival, asked how he works with Chung.

clippings.speaker: Chung Chung-hoon
clippings.quote: I've worked with a lot of different film directors but Park Chan-wook is one of the directors who have readily accepted a lot of my ideas. I am really grateful for your comment about my work being beautiful but from my perspective it really is director Park's choosing of specific styles that ultimately made the films what they are.
clippings.title: Chung Chung-hoon: analogue in a digital world
clippings.context: London group interview at the Korean Cultural Centre UK, asked how much of the look of Park's films was his idea.

clippings.speaker: Chung Chung-hoon
clippings.quote: he gave me the job of cinematographer on Oldboy without him ever having seen any of my work … After Oldboy, Park Chan-wook finally saw my earlier movie and said, ‘What on earth was that?’… He hated it and perhaps if he had seen that film before he spoke to me he would never have employed me.
clippings.title: Chung Chung-hoon: analogue in a digital world
clippings.context: Same group interview: how Park hired him for Oldboy on an editor's recommendation.

clippings.speaker: Chung Chung-hoon
clippings.quote: With director Park, we often show each other various images and in fact he is still constantly sending me pictures. … There is not text or explanation at all, just a photo. … All joking aside, it does allow me to know what the director is thinking and how he is working on a script.
clippings.title: Chung Chung-hoon: analogue in a digital world
clippings.context: Same group interview: Chung showing reference images Park emails him in the middle of the night.

clippings.speaker: Chung Chung-hoon
clippings.quote: To them, I am not just a cinematographer but also someone to discuss the story and characters with. Especially the time I spent with PARK has been tremendously helpful for me.
clippings.title: CHUNG Chung-hoon, Cinematographer of It
clippings.context: Korean Film Council email interview around It, asked about working with Park and his Hollywood directors.

clippings.speaker: Christopher Guest
clippings.quote: Eugene and I were talking about this idea of him having two left feet. And you’d think, on the face of it, Well, that’s just insane . But to play it completely real is a way of dealing with that in a different way. And I thought it worked. I guess that’s sort of self-serving, but I think it worked—because of Eugene, who was just extraordinary in that part.
clippings.title: The Oral History of 'Best in Show'
clippings.context: Guest on Levy's character Gerry Fleck, in a 20th-anniversary oral history of the film.

clippings.speaker: Eugene Levy
clippings.quote: We had done Guffman , and then [Guest] came back with this other idea about a dog show. It was a funny idea, but I said, ‘What do we do for a third act?’ … So we kind of set it aside and started working on something else. Then about a year after that, it was ‘What about the dog show idea?’
clippings.title: The Oral History of 'Best in Show'
clippings.context: Levy, the film's cowriter, recalls how Guest pitched the dog-show idea and how long it sat before they cracked it.

clippings.speaker: Christopher Guest
clippings.quote: I remember during ‘Waiting for Guffman’ near the end of the movie where Eugene was playing a comic in Florida, and I was watching the movie, and of course I didn’t know what he was going to do, and I was laughing so hard that I couldn’t look at the monitor. I was literally doubled over.
clippings.title: Interview: How to Write Your Own Script
clippings.context: Roundtable with Boston reporters promoting For Your Consideration; asked whether he finds his own films funny.

clippings.speaker: Eugene Levy
clippings.quote: You just don’t have this kind of creative flexibility and freedom. And this is the only experience that I’ve had where the creative input is exactly what you see when the movie comes out. The studio doesn’t creatively interfere. Chris [Guest] has final cut on the movie.
clippings.title: Interview: How to Write Your Own Script
clippings.context: Same Boston roundtable; Levy on why the Guest films are unlike his other movie work.

clippings.speaker: Christopher Guest
clippings.quote: The hopefully simple answer is I come up with an idea and I get together with Eugene, and we talk about whether that could be something viable in terms of its interest for both of us, and whether it can be funny and interesting, and then we set about to writing what will be a 25-page outline.
clippings.title: Christopher Guest and Eugene Levy, For Your Consideration
clippings.context: Joint interview; asked how the two work as a writing team.

clippings.speaker: Eugene Levy
clippings.quote: same sensibility that Chris and I write in our movies
clippings.title: Eugene Levy Reflects on 'SCTV,' 'A Mighty Wind,' 'Schitt's Creek'
clippings.context: Levy describing the concept for Schitt's Creek that his son Dan brought him, likening it to his films with Guest.

clippings.speaker: Terry Gilliam
clippings.quote: Fantastic. Mike and I balance each other, because he is so clever with character and dialogue. His imagery isn’t as good as mine. I have big ideas, but Mike takes them and makes them brilliant, that’s the difference.
clippings.title: “Hollywood has been very timid these days”: Terry Gilliam on his 50-year directing career
clippings.context: Gilliam, asked how his collaboration with Palin changed over the years, in a career-spanning BFI interview.

clippings.speaker: Terry Gilliam
clippings.quote: That was the big idea. Then Mike gave us evil, that great character, and he gave great character to all the bandits.
clippings.title: “Hollywood has been very timid these days”: Terry Gilliam on his 50-year directing career
clippings.context: Gilliam on co-writing Time Bandits with Palin: Gilliam had the premise, Palin wrote the characters.

clippings.speaker: Terry Gilliam
clippings.quote: We all sort of help each other; we'll work in different combinations. Michael Palin always turns up in my films.
clippings.title: The Saga Of BRAZIL
clippings.context: Gilliam, in a 1986 interview with David Morgan after Brazil, on how the Pythons keep working together.

clippings.speaker: Michael Palin
clippings.quote: Terry came over – he lived very close by, still does – and said: ‘I've got this idea’ and showed me this one-page outline for the film, which I loved. He said, ‘will you help me write it? You're good with characters and that's what I need help with.’ So Terry Gilliam handled the storyline, which I find a chore, and I had great fun writing characters in all the different time periods…
clippings.title: Mustard interview: Michael Palin
clippings.context: Palin on how Time Bandits began, in a Mustard magazine interview compiled from conversations in 2005, 2008 and 2014.

clippings.speaker: Michael Palin
clippings.quote: I believe the story is true, at least Terry tells me it is. He safeguarded the role for me because we had such a strong idea in our minds of how I could play it.
clippings.title: Mustard interview: Michael Palin
clippings.context: Palin on the story that Gilliam turned down Robert De Niro for the part of Jack Lint to keep it for Palin.

clippings.speaker: Michael Palin
clippings.quote: I've had many happy filming experiences with Terry Gilliam, and he's one of the most inventive and original film-makers of our generation. But it can be quite a physically demanding experience, acting in a Gilliam movie – blood and shit are never far away.
clippings.title: Mustard interview: Michael Palin
clippings.context: Palin, asked whether he would team up with Gilliam again.

clippings.speaker: Michael Palin
clippings.quote: I think Terry was almost too deferential to actors, too respectful, and didn't really know quite how you got the best performances out of actors.
clippings.title: Michael Palin on BRAZIL
clippings.context: Palin on Gilliam's first solo film, from an interview recorded for the 1996 Criterion laserdisc of Brazil but first published on this site.

clippings.speaker: Michael Palin
clippings.quote: And he was always sort of, 'All right, I will show you, I will show you something wonderful and then you can tell me whether you like it or not,' rather than, 'What do you want me to make? How should I do this? Please give me your advice. Tell me.'
clippings.title: Michael Palin on BRAZIL
clippings.context: Palin on Gilliam's working method on Jabberwocky and Time Bandits, from the same 1996 interview.
